eras.title: A Peace of Exhaustion
eras.overview: The First World War is over, but the world of 1920 is exhausted, grieving and unstable. Some 15 to 22 million soldiers and civilians died in the war and tens of millions more in the 1918-1919 influenza pandemic. Four empires, German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman, have collapsed, and new states such as Poland, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia fill central Europe. The Treaty of Versailles came into force in January, blaming Germany and making it pay reparations, and the new League of Nations meets in Geneva, though the United States has refused to join. Russia is in the final stage of a brutal civil war that the Bolsheviks under Lenin are winning; their Red Army is stopped outside Warsaw in August. Britain and France, the victors, have taken Germany's colonies and the Ottoman Arab lands as League 'mandates', bringing the British Empire to its greatest size. Meanwhile nationalists from Ireland and Egypt to India and China are demanding independence, and in America women have just won the vote.

regions.southern-africa: Former German colonies have been handed out as League of Nations mandates: South West Africa to South Africa, Tanganyika to Britain, and Ruanda-Urundi to Belgium. The Union of South Africa is led by Prime Minister Jan Smuts, Belgium rules the Congo, and the British South Africa Company still administers the Rhodesias. Kenya became a British Crown colony in 1920, and Portugal holds Angola and Mozambique.
regions.northern-africa: Egypt, still a British protectorate under Sultan Fuad I, was shaken by the 1919 revolution led by Saad Zaghloul and will win nominal independence in 1922. Germany's Kamerun and Togoland have been split between Britain and France, which also rules the Maghreb and huge federations in West and Equatorial Africa. Italy struggles against Senussi resistance in Libya. Ethiopia is ruled by Empress Zewditu, with her cousin Ras Tafari (the future Haile Selassie) as regent and heir.
regions.europe: The peace treaties have redrawn Europe: Germany, now the Weimar Republic under President Friedrich Ebert, lost territory and its army; Austria and Hungary are small separate states, and the Treaty of Trianon (June 1920) stripped Hungary of two-thirds of its land; Admiral Horthy rules Hungary as regent. New or restored states include Poland (Jozef Pilsudski), Czechoslovakia (President Tomas Masaryk), Yugoslavia, Finland and the Baltic states. The Poles defeat the Red Army at Warsaw in August 1920, the last White army is evacuated from Crimea in November, and Ireland is fighting its War of Independence against Britain.
regions.middle-east-south-asia: The Ottoman Empire is being dismantled: Sultan Mehmed VI signed the harsh Treaty of Sevres in August 1920 in Allied-occupied Constantinople, while Mustafa Kemal's rival nationalist government in Ankara fights on against Greek and Allied forces. At San Remo the Allies gave Britain mandates over Palestine and Mesopotamia (Iraq, where a major revolt breaks out) and France mandates over Syria and Lebanon; French troops crushed King Faisal's Arab kingdom in Damascus in July. Sharif Hussein is King of the Hejaz, Ibn Saud rules Nejd, Persia is under Ahmad Shah, and Afghanistan under Amir Amanullah Khan won full independence in 1919. In India, under Viceroy Lord Chelmsford, Gandhi launches the Non-Cooperation Movement after the 1919 Amritsar massacre.
regions.north-central-asia: The Red Army is conquering Central Asia: in 1920 the khan of Khiva and the emir of Bukhara were overthrown and replaced by Soviet-backed 'people's republics', while Muslim Basmachi rebels resist. White leader Admiral Kolchak was executed in Irkutsk in February, and Siberia falls to the Bolsheviks, who set up a buffer Far Eastern Republic while Japanese troops still occupy parts of the Russian Far East. A Kirghiz (Kazakh) autonomous republic is created on the steppe.
regions.east-asia: China has broken up into the Warlord Era: a weak government in Beijing under President Xu Shichang is fought over by northern militarist cliques, Zhang Zuolin rules Manchuria, and Sun Yat-sen leads a rival government in Guangzhou. The May Fourth Movement of 1919 sparked a wave of nationalism after the Versailles treaty gave Germany's Shandong rights to Japan. Japan, under Emperor Taisho and Prime Minister Hara Takashi, is a victor and a League Council member and rules Korea, where it brutally suppressed the March First independence movement of 1919. Tibet under the 13th Dalai Lama is de facto independent, while Chinese troops have reoccupied Mongolia.
regions.southeast-asia: Colonial rule continues unchanged: France governs Indochina, Britain rules Burma and Malaya, the Dutch rule the East Indies, where the Communist Party of Indonesia is founded in 1920, and the United States administers the Philippines under a mostly Filipino legislature. Siam, under King Vajiravudh, joined the Allies in 1917 and gained a seat at the League of Nations.
regions.northern-north-america: Canada, whose 60,000 war dead gave it a separate signature on the Versailles treaty, is led by Arthur Meighen from July 1920 after Robert Borden retired; the Winnipeg General Strike of 1919 reflected postwar unrest. Newfoundland remains a separate dominion, Alaska a US territory, and Greenland a Danish colony.
regions.southern-north-america: The United States, under the ailing Woodrow Wilson, has rejected the Versailles treaty and the League; Prohibition began in January 1920, the 19th Amendment gave women the vote in August, and Warren Harding won the November election promising a 'return to normalcy'. Mexico's Revolution winds down: President Carranza was overthrown and killed in May 1920, and Alvaro Obregon became president in December. US Marines occupy Haiti, the Dominican Republic and Nicaragua.
regions.northern-south-america: Brazil is governed by President Epitacio Pessoa under a republic dominated by coffee planters. Augusto Leguia has seized power in Peru, beginning an eleven-year rule, a July 1920 coup in Bolivia brings Bautista Saavedra to power, and Juan Vicente Gomez continues his dictatorship in Venezuela, where oil is starting to flow. Colombia is led by Marco Fidel Suarez.
regions.southern-cone: Argentina is governed by Hipolito Yrigoyen, its first president elected under universal male suffrage, and remains wealthy from exports, though strikes were violently repressed in 1919. Chile elects the reformer Arturo Alessandri in 1920 as its nitrate economy suffers from the invention of synthetic nitrates. Uruguay, under Baltasar Brum, is a stable democracy, and Paraguay is led by Manuel Gondra.
regions.australasia: Australia, under Prime Minister Billy Hughes, lost about 60,000 men in the war and now holds former German New Guinea as a League mandate. New Zealand, under William Massey, administers Western Samoa, Britain, Australia and New Zealand share Nauru, and Japan rules the former German islands of Micronesia as the South Seas Mandate. Hawaii is a US territory.

eras.title: The Great Depression Begins
eras.overview: The Wall Street Crash of October 1929 has tipped the world into the Great Depression. In 1930 factories close, farm prices collapse and unemployment soars from Detroit to Berlin to Sydney; the US raises tariffs and world trade begins to shrink. Hard times strengthen extremists: in Germany's September election Hitler's Nazi party jumps from 12 to 107 seats, while Mussolini's Fascists already rule Italy. In the Soviet Union, Joseph Stalin is forcing peasants onto collective farms and driving rapid industrialisation at terrible human cost. Military coups topple governments in Argentina, Brazil and Peru. Colonial empires still look solid, yet Gandhi's Salt March challenges British rule in India, and nationalist risings shake Vietnam and Burma. In China, Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists have nominally unified the country but are fighting warlords and Communists. Radio, cinema with sound and cars are reshaping daily life in rich countries, while Uruguay hosts the first football World Cup.

regions.southern-africa: The Union of South Africa, under Prime Minister J. B. M. Hertzog, extends the vote to white women in 1930 while further restricting Black Africans. Southern Rhodesia is a self-governing British colony, Northern Rhodesia's Copperbelt is being opened up, and Britain also rules Tanganyika, Nyasaland and Bechuanaland. Belgium governs the Congo, and Portugal, where Antonio de Oliveira Salazar is rising to power, tightens control of Angola and Mozambique.
regions.northern-africa: Ras Tafari is crowned Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia in November 1930 after Empress Zewditu's death. Egypt is a kingdom under King Fuad I with British troops still guarding the Suez Canal, and the Sudan remains an Anglo-Egyptian condominium. France celebrates the centenary of its conquest of Algeria and rules Morocco, where Sultan Mohammed V reigns, and Tunisia. Italy, led in the field by General Rodolfo Graziani, is brutally crushing the Libyan resistance of Omar Mukhtar.
regions.europe: Europe is sliding into crisis: Germany's Chancellor Heinrich Bruning governs by emergency decree under President Hindenburg as the Nazis surge, while Mussolini rules Italy as Fascist dictator under King Victor Emmanuel III. Britain has a minority Labour government under Ramsay MacDonald, France is governed under President Gaston Doumergue, and in Spain the dictator Primo de Rivera resigned in January, with the monarchy about to fall in 1931. Dictators or strongmen also rule Poland (Pilsudski), Yugoslavia (King Alexander), Hungary (Horthy) and Portugal, and Allied troops left the German Rhineland in June 1930.
regions.middle-east-south-asia: Turkey is a secular republic led by Mustafa Kemal (later Ataturk) from Ankara, and Iran is ruled by Reza Shah Pahlavi, both modernising rapidly. Iraq, under King Faisal I, signs a treaty with Britain in 1930 that will end the mandate in 1932; Britain also rules Palestine and Transjordan, and France holds Syria and Lebanon. Ibn Saud is King of the Hejaz and Nejd (renamed Saudi Arabia in 1932), and Nadir Shah rules Afghanistan. In India, Congress declares the goal of full independence, and Gandhi leads the Salt March in March-April 1930; Viceroy Lord Irwin jails tens of thousands, and the first Round Table Conference opens in London.
regions.north-central-asia: Soviet Central Asia has been divided into national republics, including the Uzbek, Turkmen and new Tajik Soviet republics and autonomous Kazakh and Kirghiz republics. Stalin's forced collectivisation is beginning a catastrophic famine among Kazakh nomads (1930-1933), and the Turkestan-Siberian Railway is completed in 1930. Mongolia is a Soviet-aligned People's Republic, and labour camps of the Gulag are spreading across Siberia.
regions.east-asia: Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist government in Nanjing claims all of China after its Northern Expedition (1928), but in 1930 it fights the huge Central Plains War against rival warlords and launches its first campaign against Mao Zedong's Communists in their Jiangxi base area. Manchuria is held by the 'Young Marshal' Zhang Xueliang, coveted by Japan. Japan, under Emperor Hirohito (Showa era), is hit hard by the Depression; Prime Minister Hamaguchi Osachi is shot by a nationalist in November 1930. Korea and Taiwan are Japanese colonies, and Tibet is ruled by the 13th Dalai Lama.
regions.southeast-asia: Nationalist and communist challenges are growing: the Yen Bai mutiny shakes French Indochina in February 1930 and Ho Chi Minh founds the Indochinese Communist Party; in Burma the Saya San peasant rebellion erupts in December. The Dutch have jailed Indonesian nationalist leader Sukarno, and the US governs the Philippines amid demands for independence. Siam, under King Prajadhipok (Rama VII), is the last absolute monarchy in the region and will be overthrown in 1932.
regions.northern-north-america: Canada, battered by the Depression and a prairie drought, elects Conservative R. B. Bennett as prime minister in July 1930. Newfoundland is a separate British dominion and Alaska a US territory, while Norway and Denmark dispute ownership of East Greenland. The 1931 Statute of Westminster will soon make the dominions fully independent in law.
regions.southern-north-america: The United States, under President Herbert Hoover, plunges deeper into depression; the Smoot-Hawley Tariff of June 1930 sparks retaliation around the world. Mexico is ruled by figurehead presidents, Pascual Ortiz Rubio from 1930, under the 'Jefe Maximo' Plutarco Elias Calles and his new National Revolutionary Party. Rafael Trujillo seizes power in the Dominican Republic, Gerardo Machado rules Cuba as a dictator, and Augusto Sandino fights US Marines in Nicaragua.
regions.northern-south-america: The Revolution of 1930 brings Getulio Vargas to power in Brazil in November, ending the coffee planters' Old Republic. In Peru, Augusto Leguia is overthrown by Luis Sanchez Cerro in August, and Bolivia's President Hernando Siles is ousted in June. Colombia peacefully elects Liberal Enrique Olaya Herrera, and Juan Vicente Gomez still rules oil-rich Venezuela.
regions.southern-cone: On 6 September 1930 the Argentine army overthrows the elected Hipolito Yrigoyen and installs General Jose Felix Uriburu, Argentina's first modern military coup and the start of the 'Infamous Decade'. Chile is ruled by the strongman Carlos Ibanez del Campo as the nitrate and copper markets collapse. Uruguay celebrates the centenary of its constitution by hosting and winning the first FIFA World Cup, and Paraguay and Bolivia are edging toward war over the Chaco.
regions.australasia: Australia, under Labor Prime Minister James Scullin, is among the countries worst hit by the Depression, with unemployment heading toward 30 percent; the Sydney Harbour Bridge is under construction. New Zealand, led by George Forbes from May 1930, also suffers hard times, and its rule in Western Samoa faces the peaceful Mau independence movement. Australia administers Papua and the New Guinea mandate, and Japan rules Micronesia.

eras.title: The Road to War
eras.overview: By 1938 the peace settlement of 1919 is falling apart and the world is drifting toward another great war. Adolf Hitler, dictator of Germany since 1933, has rearmed the country, absorbed Austria in March, and at the Munich conference in September won the Sudetenland from Czechoslovakia as Britain and France chose 'appeasement' over war. In November, the Kristallnacht pogrom shows the violence of Nazi persecution of Jews. Mussolini's Italy has conquered Ethiopia, and General Franco, backed by both dictators, is winning Spain's civil war. In Asia, Japan has been at full-scale war with China since 1937, capturing Nanjing, Wuhan and Canton and forcing Chiang Kai-shek's government deep inland. Stalin's Great Purge is killing hundreds of thousands in the Soviet Union. The democracies, Britain, France and the United States, are still recovering from the Depression and reluctant to fight. Across Asia and Africa, colonial rule continues, but nationalist movements grow stronger.

regions.southern-africa: South Africa is governed by J. B. M. Hertzog's United Party, with Jan Smuts as deputy, and the 1938 centenary of the Great Trek inflames Afrikaner nationalism. Britain rules the Rhodesias, Bechuanaland, Nyasaland and the Tanganyika mandate, which Nazi Germany demands back, while Belgium holds the Congo. Angola and Mozambique are ruled by Salazar's authoritarian Estado Novo in Portugal, and Madagascar is French.
regions.northern-africa: Italy conquered Ethiopia in 1935-1936 with poison gas and joined it with Eritrea and Somaliland as Italian East Africa, ruled from Addis Ababa by the Duke of Aosta, while Haile Selassie lives in exile in England. Italy also rules Libya under Governor Italo Balbo. Egypt, under young King Farouk, gained more independence by the 1936 treaty, though British forces guard Suez, and France rules Algeria, Tunisia, Morocco and the great African federations. Spanish Morocco was the base from which Franco launched his rebellion.
regions.europe: Hitler's Germany annexed Austria (the Anschluss) in March 1938, and the Munich Agreement of 30 September, signed by Chamberlain, Daladier, Mussolini and Hitler, handed it Czechoslovakia's Sudetenland; Poland and Hungary then grabbed slices of Czechoslovakia too. Spain's civil war (1936-1939) rages, with Franco's Nationalists defeating the Republic at the Ebro. Britain (King George VI, PM Neville Chamberlain) and France (PM Edouard Daladier from April) begin rearming, while Stalin's purges devastate the Soviet officer corps.
regions.middle-east-south-asia: Mustafa Kemal Ataturk, founder of modern Turkey, dies in November 1938 and is succeeded by Ismet Inonu. Reza Shah rules Iran, King Ghazi reigns in Iraq, and in Saudi Arabia, under King Ibn Saud, American engineers strike oil at Dammam in March 1938. Palestine is torn by the Arab Revolt (1936-1939) against British rule and Jewish immigration, and France holds Syria and Lebanon. In India, under Viceroy Lord Linlithgow, Congress governs most provinces after the 1937 elections, and Zahir Shah rules Afghanistan.
regions.north-central-asia: Soviet Central Asia now consists of five union republics, Kazakh, Uzbek, Turkmen, Kirghiz and Tajik, whose local Communist leaders are being executed in Stalin's purges. The Gulag camps of Siberia and Kolyma hold over a million prisoners, and Soviet and Japanese forces clash at Lake Khasan in the summer of 1938. Mongolia is a Soviet satellite dominated by the strongman Khorloogiin Choibalsan, and Xinjiang's warlord Sheng Shicai depends on Soviet support.
regions.east-asia: The Second Sino-Japanese War has raged since July 1937: after the Nanjing Massacre, Japan captures Xuzhou, Wuhan and Canton in 1938, and Chiang Kai-shek moves his government to Chongqing, even breaching the Yellow River dikes to slow the enemy. Mao Zedong's Communists, based at Yan'an, are in an uneasy united front with the Nationalists. Japan, under Emperor Hirohito and Prime Minister Konoe Fumimaro, rules Korea, Taiwan and the puppet state of Manchukuo under the last Qing emperor Puyi. Tibet is governed by a regent while the newly found 14th Dalai Lama is a small child.
regions.southeast-asia: The Philippines has been a self-governing Commonwealth under President Manuel Quezon since 1935, with independence promised for 1946. Burma was separated from India in 1937, Britain opened its great naval base at Singapore in February 1938, France rules Indochina, and the Dutch rule the East Indies. In Siam (renamed Thailand in 1939), the nationalist military strongman Plaek Phibunsongkhram becomes prime minister in December 1938 under the boy-king Ananda Mahidol.
regions.northern-north-america: Canada, under Prime Minister William Lyon Mackenzie King, supports appeasement but begins modest rearmament. Newfoundland, bankrupt in the Depression, has given up self-government to a British-appointed Commission (1934). Alaska is a US territory, and Greenland a Danish colony after an international court confirmed Danish sovereignty in 1933.
regions.southern-north-america: The United States, under President Franklin D. Roosevelt, is still fighting the Depression with the New Deal and remains officially neutral, though Roosevelt warns about the dictators. In Mexico, President Lazaro Cardenas nationalises the foreign oil companies on 18 March 1938, creating PEMEX. Strongmen rule much of the Caribbean and Central America, including Trujillo in the Dominican Republic, Anastasio Somoza in Nicaragua and Fulgencio Batista behind the scenes in Cuba.
regions.northern-south-america: Getulio Vargas rules Brazil as dictator under his Estado Novo (New State) of 1937 and crushes a fascist Integralist putsch in May 1938. Bolivia, defeated by Paraguay in the Chaco War, is led by the military reformer German Busch, Peru by General Oscar Benavides, and Colombia elects Eduardo Santos. Venezuela is moving toward democracy under Eleazar Lopez Contreras after Gomez's death.
regions.southern-cone: Argentina is ruled by Roberto Ortiz, elected by fraud in the 'Infamous Decade', and Chile elects Pedro Aguirre Cerda of the Popular Front in October 1938. The Chaco Peace Treaty of July 1938 awards Paraguay most of the disputed Gran Chaco after its victory over Bolivia. Uruguay is led by Alfredo Baldomir from June 1938.
regions.australasia: Australia, under Prime Minister Joseph Lyons, marks 150 years since British settlement, and Aboriginal activists hold a 'Day of Mourning' on 26 January 1938. New Zealand's Labour government under Michael Joseph Savage passes a pioneering Social Security Act. Australia rules Papua and the New Guinea mandate, and Japan has closed its mandated islands in Micronesia to outsiders, fuelling suspicion that it is fortifying them.

eras.title: Victory, Ruin and the Atom
eras.overview: 1945 is the year the Second World War ends, the deadliest conflict in history, which killed an estimated 60 to 85 million people, including six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust. Germany surrendered in May after Hitler's suicide in the ruins of Berlin, and Japan surrendered in August after American atomic bombs destroyed Hiroshima and Nagasaki and the Soviet Union invaded Manchuria. Two superpowers emerge: the United States, the richest country on Earth and sole owner of the atomic bomb, and the Soviet Union, whose Red Army now occupies Eastern Europe. At Yalta and Potsdam the victors divided Germany and Austria into occupation zones, and in San Francisco fifty nations founded the United Nations. Britain and France are victorious but bankrupt, and their empires are starting to crack: Indonesia and Vietnam declare independence, India is heading toward freedom, and China slides back into civil war. Much of Europe and East Asia lies in rubble, with millions of refugees on the move.

regions.southern-africa: South Africa's Prime Minister Jan Smuts helps draft the United Nations Charter, while his country keeps the mandate of South West Africa and its system of racial segregation. Uranium from the Belgian Congo's Shinkolobwe mine supplied the Manhattan Project that built the atomic bomb. Britain rules the Rhodesias, Tanganyika, Nyasaland and Kenya, Portugal still holds Angola and Mozambique, and Madagascar is under Free French rule after Britain seized it from Vichy France in 1942.
regions.northern-africa: Haile Selassie was restored to Ethiopia's throne in 1941 after British and Ethiopian forces drove out the Italians. Italy's former colonies of Libya, Eritrea and Somalia are under British (and, in Libya's Fezzan, French) military administration. Egypt, under King Farouk, hosts the founding of the Arab League in March 1945. In French Algeria, protests on VE Day at Setif lead to a massacre of thousands of Algerians, and France also rules Morocco, Tunisia and West and Equatorial Africa.
regions.europe: Nazi Germany surrendered on 7-8 May 1945; Germany and Austria are divided into American, British, French and Soviet zones, with Berlin and Vienna also split, and Germany's lands east of the Oder-Neisse line handed to Poland, except northern East Prussia, which the Soviet Union annexed and, in northern East Prussia, the Soviet Union. The Red Army occupies Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania and Bulgaria, where Communist-dominated governments are being installed, while Tito's partisans rule Yugoslavia. Britain elects Clement Attlee's Labour government in July, replacing Winston Churchill, and France is led by Charles de Gaulle's Provisional Government. Franco's Spain and Salazar's Portugal, neutral in the war, remain dictatorships.
regions.middle-east-south-asia: India is still ruled by Britain under Viceroy Lord Wavell, but independence is clearly coming, and the Muslim League under Muhammad Ali Jinnah demands a separate Pakistan. Iran, under the young Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, remains occupied by British and Soviet troops, and a Soviet-backed separatist movement emerges in Azerbaijan. Syria and Lebanon are winning independence from France, Britain holds the Palestine mandate amid rising Jewish-Arab conflict, and Ibn Saud of Saudi Arabia met President Roosevelt in February, beginning the US-Saudi oil partnership. Turkey, under Ismet Inonu, joined the Allies only in February 1945.
regions.north-central-asia: Soviet Central Asia and Siberia were transformed by the war, receiving evacuated factories and entire peoples deported by Stalin, such as Volga Germans, Chechens and Crimean Tatars, many of them sent to Kazakhstan. The USSR annexed Tuva in 1944. Mongolia, under Choibalsan, votes for independence in an October 1945 plebiscite that China soon recognises, and in Xinjiang a Soviet-backed East Turkestan Republic controls the Ili region.
regions.east-asia: Japan surrendered on 15 August 1945 and formally on 2 September; Emperor Hirohito remains, but the country is occupied by the Americans under General Douglas MacArthur. Korea, freed from Japanese rule, is divided at the 38th parallel into a Soviet-occupied north and an American-occupied south, and Taiwan is handed back to China. Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists and Mao Zedong's Communists hold peace talks in Chongqing, but both race to seize Japanese-held territory, and civil war is about to resume. Tibet is governed by a regent for the young 14th Dalai Lama.
regions.southeast-asia: Japan's occupation of Southeast Asia has shattered European prestige. Sukarno proclaims Indonesia's independence on 17 August and Ho Chi Minh proclaims the Democratic Republic of Vietnam on 2 September, while the last Vietnamese emperor, Bao Dai, abdicates; British and Indian troops arrive to restore Dutch and French rule and fight Indonesian nationalists at Surabaya. The Philippines, liberated in the bloody Battle of Manila, is led by President Sergio Osmena toward independence in 1946. Britain retakes Burma and Malaya, and Thailand, under King Ananda Mahidol, escapes punishment for its alliance with Japan.
regions.northern-north-america: Canada, under Prime Minister Mackenzie King, ends the war as a major military and industrial power; in September a Soviet cipher clerk, Igor Gouzenko, defects in Ottawa, exposing Soviet spy rings in an early warning of the Cold War. Newfoundland is still run by a British commission and will join Canada in 1949. Alaska, linked by the new Alaska Highway, is a US territory, and Greenland hosts US bases while Denmark was under German occupation.
regions.southern-north-america: Franklin Roosevelt died in April 1945, and President Harry S. Truman led the United States to victory, ordering the atomic bombings after the first test in New Mexico in July. The US emerges with half the world's industrial output. Mexico, under Manuel Avila Camacho, sent an air squadron to fight in the Philippines, Guatemala's democratic 'revolution' of 1944 brings Juan Jose Arevalo to the presidency, and Trujillo still rules the Dominican Republic.
regions.northern-south-america: Brazil, the only Latin American country to send combat troops to Europe, sees the army depose Getulio Vargas in October 1945, and General Eurico Gaspar Dutra is elected president in December. In Venezuela, an October coup brings Romulo Betancourt's Democratic Action party to power. Peru elects Jose Luis Bustamante y Rivero, and Colombia is led by Alberto Lleras Camargo from August 1945.
regions.southern-cone: Argentina, under a military government with General Edelmiro Farrell as president, declared war on the Axis only in March 1945; Colonel Juan Peron, the powerful labour minister, was arrested in October but freed after a mass workers' rally on 17 October, launching Peronism. Chile, under Juan Antonio Rios, celebrates poet Gabriela Mistral, Latin America's first Nobel Prize winner in literature. Uruguay is led by Juan Jose de Amezaga and Paraguay by the dictator Higinio Morinigo.
regions.australasia: Australia's wartime Prime Minister John Curtin died in July 1945 and was succeeded by Ben Chifley; Australian troops ended the war fighting in New Guinea and Borneo. New Zealand is led by Peter Fraser. The Pacific islands, from the Solomons to Iwo Jima and Okinawa, have been bloody battlefields, and Japan's former Micronesian mandate is now held by the United States.

eras.title: The Year of Africa
eras.overview: In 1960 the world is split by the Cold War between the American-led West and the Soviet-led Communist bloc, each armed with hydrogen bombs and racing into space. In May, the Soviets shoot down an American U-2 spy plane, wrecking a summit in Paris. Meanwhile the European empires are rapidly dissolving: seventeen African countries, including Nigeria, Congo and most of French Africa, win independence in what is called the 'Year of Africa'. British Prime Minister Harold Macmillan speaks of a 'wind of change' blowing through the continent. The newly independent Congo immediately plunges into crisis. China, under Mao Zedong, is suffering a catastrophic famine caused by the Great Leap Forward and is breaking with the Soviet Union. Western Europe and Japan are booming, Cuba's revolutionary Fidel Castro is turning toward Moscow, and in November John F. Kennedy is elected US president. Television, jet airliners and consumer goods are spreading across rich countries.

regions.southern-africa: The Belgian Congo became independent on 30 June 1960 under President Joseph Kasa-Vubu and Prime Minister Patrice Lumumba, but within weeks the army mutinied, Katanga seceded under Moise Tshombe, UN troops arrived, and Colonel Joseph Mobutu seized power in September. Madagascar gained independence under Philibert Tsiranana. In South Africa, police killed 69 protesters at Sharpeville in March, and Prime Minister Hendrik Verwoerd's apartheid government wins a referendum to become a republic. Britain still rules the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland, Kenya and Tanganyika, and Salazar's Portugal holds Angola and Mozambique.
regions.northern-africa: Most of French West and Equatorial Africa becomes independent in 1960, including Senegal (Leopold Senghor), Mali (Modibo Keita), Ivory Coast (Felix Houphouet-Boigny), Niger and Chad, along with French-run Cameroon, while Nigeria, Africa's most populous country, becomes independent from Britain on 1 October under Prime Minister Abubakar Tafawa Balewa, and Somalia unites in July. Algeria is still fighting a brutal independence war against France. Gamal Abdel Nasser leads Egypt, joined with Syria as the United Arab Republic, and begins the Aswan High Dam; Kwame Nkrumah makes Ghana a republic, and Emperor Haile Selassie survives a coup attempt in Ethiopia in December.
regions.europe: Europe is divided by the Iron Curtain: West Germany under Chancellor Konrad Adenauer is in NATO and booming, while Walter Ulbricht's East Germany, in the Warsaw Pact, is losing citizens through Berlin, a flow the Berlin Wall will stop in 1961. The six-nation European Economic Community is rivalled by the new European Free Trade Association. Charles de Gaulle leads France's Fifth Republic, which tests its first atomic bomb in the Algerian Sahara; Elizabeth II reigns in Britain, Khrushchev rules the Soviet Union, and Cyprus becomes independent in August. Franco and Salazar still rule Spain and Portugal.
regions.middle-east-south-asia: India is led by Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru, a founder of the Non-Aligned Movement, and signs the Indus Waters Treaty with Pakistan, which is ruled by General Ayub Khan. Ceylon elects Sirimavo Bandaranaike, the world's first female prime minister. A military coup in May overthrows Turkey's government, Abd al-Karim Qasim rules revolutionary Iraq, and the Shah rules Iran; in September, oil-producing states found OPEC in Baghdad. David Ben-Gurion leads Israel, whose agents capture Nazi war criminal Adolf Eichmann in Argentina.
regions.north-central-asia: Soviet Central Asia is home to the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan, from which Sputnik was launched in 1957 and Yuri Gagarin will fly in 1961, and Khrushchev's Virgin Lands campaign has ploughed up millions of hectares of Kazakh steppe for wheat. The Semipalatinsk site hosts Soviet nuclear tests, and giant dams are being built in Siberia. Mongolia, under Yumjaagiin Tsedenbal, stays firmly in the Soviet camp as Moscow withdraws its advisers from China in July 1960.
regions.east-asia: The People's Republic of China, under Chairman Mao Zedong, with Liu Shaoqi as head of state and Zhou Enlai as premier, is in the depths of a famine caused by the Great Leap Forward that will kill tens of millions. The Sino-Soviet split breaks into the open, and Tibet has been under direct Chinese control since the 1959 uprising sent the Dalai Lama into exile in India. In Japan, mass protests against the US security treaty force Prime Minister Kishi Nobusuke to resign, and Ikeda Hayato begins a plan to double incomes. South Korea's April Revolution topples Syngman Rhee, Kim Il-sung rules North Korea, and Chiang Kai-shek rules Taiwan.
regions.southeast-asia: Vietnam is divided between Ho Chi Minh's Communist North and Ngo Dinh Diem's US-backed South, where the National Liberation Front (Viet Cong) is founded in December 1960; neighbouring Laos is torn by a coup and civil war. Indonesia's Sukarno rules under 'Guided Democracy' and demands Dutch-held West New Guinea. Malaya, under Tunku Abdul Rahman, ends its long Communist Emergency, Singapore is self-governing under Lee Kuan Yew, Prince Sihanouk leads Cambodia, and Field Marshal Sarit Thanarat rules Thailand under King Bhumibol.
regions.northern-north-america: Canada, under Prime Minister John Diefenbaker, is a NATO and NORAD ally of the United States, with radar lines across the Arctic to watch for Soviet bombers. In Quebec, Jean Lesage's election in June 1960 begins the 'Quiet Revolution'. Alaska became the 49th US state in 1959, and Greenland, now a county of Denmark, hosts the large US air base at Thule.
regions.southern-north-america: President Dwight D. Eisenhower's America is the world's richest society; Hawaii became the 50th state in 1959, and in November 1960 John F. Kennedy narrowly defeats Richard Nixon. Black students' sit-ins in Greensboro energise the civil rights movement. Fidel Castro's Cuba nationalises American property and turns to the Soviet Union, and the US imposes a trade embargo in October. Mexico is governed by Adolfo Lopez Mateos of the long-ruling PRI, and dictators such as Trujillo and the Somoza family still rule parts of the Caribbean and Central America.
regions.northern-south-america: Brazil inaugurates its futuristic new capital, Brasilia, on 21 April 1960 under President Juscelino Kubitschek, and Janio Quadros wins the October election. Venezuela, under the democrat Romulo Betancourt, co-founds OPEC. Colombia is governed by Alberto Lleras Camargo under the National Front power-sharing deal, Victor Paz Estenssoro returns to power in Bolivia, and the Guianas remain under British, Dutch and French rule.
regions.southern-cone: On 22 May 1960 the Valdivia earthquake, the most powerful ever recorded (magnitude 9.5), devastates southern Chile, governed by President Jorge Alessandri. Argentina is led by Arturo Frondizi, with Peron in exile and his movement banned, and Israeli agents abduct Eichmann from Buenos Aires in May. Paraguay is ruled by the dictator Alfredo Stroessner, and Uruguay by a collective National Council of Government; the Treaty of Montevideo creates a Latin American free-trade association.
regions.australasia: Australia, under the long-serving Prime Minister Robert Menzies, is a close US ally and still keeps its 'White Australia' immigration policy; it governs Papua and New Guinea. New Zealand elects Keith Holyoake as prime minister in November 1960, and Western Samoa is preparing for independence in 1962. Hawaii has just become a US state, and the Dutch still hold West New Guinea.

eras.title: After the Cold War
eras.overview: The Cold War is over: the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991 into fifteen independent states, and the United States stands as the world's only superpower. Hopes run high for a new era of democracy and open markets. Nelson Mandela becomes South Africa's first Black president after the country's first all-race elections, the Channel Tunnel links Britain and France, the North American Free Trade Agreement takes effect, and Israel signs peace with Jordan as Palestinian self-rule begins. Yet 1994 is also a year of horror: in Rwanda, extremists murder an estimated 500,000 to 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi along with moderate Hutu, in about a hundred days, while war rages in Bosnia and Russia invades breakaway Chechnya in December. China's economy is booming under market reforms, India is liberalising, and the internet and mobile phones are starting to spread. Boris Yeltsin's Russia struggles with economic collapse, and North Korea's founder Kim Il-sung dies in July.

regions.southern-africa: South Africa's first democratic elections on 27 April 1994 end apartheid, and Nelson Mandela is inaugurated as president on 10 May. In Rwanda, a genocide from April to July kills an estimated 500,000 to 800,000 people before Paul Kagame's Rwandan Patriotic Front takes power, sending a million Hutu refugees into Zaire, still ruled by Mobutu Sese Seko. Mozambique holds its first multiparty elections after its civil war, Malawi votes out its dictator Hastings Banda, and Angola's government and Jonas Savimbi's UNITA sign the Lusaka Protocol. Robert Mugabe rules Zimbabwe and Sam Nujoma leads newly independent Namibia.
regions.northern-africa: Algeria is in a savage civil war between the military government of Liamine Zeroual and Islamist insurgents. Egypt is ruled by Hosni Mubarak, Libya's Muammar Gaddafi is under UN sanctions, and Sudan's Islamist military regime under Omar al-Bashir hosts Osama bin Laden. Somalia has collapsed into clan warfare after the failed UN and US intervention, Eritrea became independent from Ethiopia in 1993, and Nigeria is ruled by the dictator Sani Abacha. Civil wars ravage Liberia and Sierra Leone.
regions.europe: Europe is reuniting after the Cold War: Germany has been one country since 1990, the European Union was created by the Maastricht Treaty (1993), Austria, Finland and Sweden vote to join, and the last Russian troops leave Germany, Estonia and Latvia in August 1994. The Channel Tunnel opens in May. But Yugoslavia's breakup has brought war to Bosnia, where Sarajevo is under siege, and Russia, under President Boris Yeltsin, invades Chechnya in December. Helmut Kohl leads Germany, Francois Mitterrand France, John Major Britain, and the IRA declares a ceasefire in Northern Ireland.
regions.middle-east-south-asia: The Oslo peace process brings Palestinian self-rule to Gaza and Jericho, Yasser Arafat returns from exile, and Israel's Yitzhak Rabin signs a peace treaty with Jordan's King Hussein in October. Saddam Hussein's Iraq is under heavy UN sanctions, Iran is led by Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and President Rafsanjani, and Yemen fights a short civil war. Afghanistan is torn by warring mujahideen factions, and the Taliban movement emerges in Kandahar late in 1994. India, under P. V. Narasimha Rao, is opening its economy, and Benazir Bhutto is prime minister of Pakistan.
regions.north-central-asia: Five Central Asian republics have been independent since 1991, mostly ruled by former Soviet Communist bosses: Nursultan Nazarbayev in Kazakhstan, Islam Karimov in Uzbekistan, Saparmurat Niyazov in Turkmenistan, and Askar Akayev in Kyrgyzstan, while Tajikistan is in civil war under Emomali Rahmonov. Kazakhstan has agreed to hand its Soviet nuclear warheads back to Russia and leases the Baikonur Cosmodrome to Russia. Siberia remains part of Russia, and Mongolia has been a democracy since 1990.
regions.east-asia: China, under President Jiang Zemin with Deng Xiaoping still the paramount elder, is booming after market reforms, and construction of the Three Gorges Dam begins in December. Hong Kong (British until 1997) and Macau (Portuguese until 1999) await handover to China, and Taiwan is democratising under Lee Teng-hui. North Korea's Kim Il-sung dies in July and is succeeded by his son Kim Jong-il, whose government signs a nuclear freeze deal (the Agreed Framework) with the US in October. Japan, under Emperor Akihito, has three prime ministers in 1994 as its economic bubble deflates, while South Korea is led by Kim Young-sam.
regions.southeast-asia: The US lifts its trade embargo on Vietnam in February, as Vietnam pursues market reforms under Communist rule. Cambodia, after UN-run elections in 1993, is again a kingdom under Norodom Sihanouk, though the Khmer Rouge still fight on. Indonesia is ruled by Suharto, who occupies East Timor, and Myanmar's military junta keeps democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi under house arrest. Mahathir Mohamad's Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Fidel Ramos's Philippines are fast-growing 'tiger' economies.
regions.northern-north-america: Canada, under Prime Minister Jean Chretien, joins the North American Free Trade Agreement on 1 January 1994, and Quebec elects a separatist government under Jacques Parizeau, setting up a 1995 independence referendum. An agreement to create the Inuit territory of Nunavut (1999) has been signed. Greenland governs itself under Danish home rule, and Alaska is a US state.
regions.southern-north-america: Bill Clinton's America is the sole superpower and enjoying an economic boom, but Republicans win Congress in the November 1994 midterms. NAFTA takes effect on 1 January, the same day the Zapatista rebels rise up in Chiapas, Mexico; presidential candidate Luis Donaldo Colosio is assassinated, Ernesto Zedillo is elected, and a peso crisis strikes in December. A US-led force restores Haiti's elected President Jean-Bertrand Aristide in October, and thousands of Cubans flee Castro's island on rafts.
regions.northern-south-america: Brazil introduces the real currency to tame hyperinflation and elects its architect, Fernando Henrique Cardoso, as president, and wins the football World Cup. Alberto Fujimori rules Peru with strong powers after his 1992 'self-coup' and the capture of the Shining Path's leader. Colombia elects Ernesto Samper amid the power of drug cartels, and Venezuela is led by the veteran Rafael Caldera.
regions.southern-cone: Democracy has returned across the region: Argentina, under Carlos Menem, keeps its peso pegged to the dollar and reforms its constitution, but suffers the deadly AMIA bombing of a Jewish centre in Buenos Aires in July. Chile is led by Eduardo Frei Ruiz-Tagle, though former dictator Augusto Pinochet still commands the army. Paraguay has its first civilian president in decades, Juan Carlos Wasmosy, and the Mercosur trade bloc agrees a customs union in December.
regions.australasia: Australia, under Labor Prime Minister Paul Keating, debates becoming a republic and has recognised Aboriginal land rights in its Native Title Act (1993). New Zealand is led by Jim Bolger, and Papua New Guinea struggles with a separatist war on Bougainville. Palau becomes independent in October 1994, ending the last UN trust territory, and France has paused its nuclear tests in French Polynesia, which it will resume in 1995.

eras.title: Into a New Millennium
eras.overview: The world greets the year 2000 with fireworks and relief that the feared 'Y2K' computer bug caused little trouble. Globalisation is the word of the moment: trade, travel and the internet are knitting economies together, though the dot-com stock bubble bursts in March. The United States is the unchallenged superpower, but its November presidential election between George W. Bush and Al Gore ends in a disputed Florida recount settled by the Supreme Court. Vladimir Putin becomes president of Russia, pledging to restore order, and wages a second war in Chechnya. China is booming and preparing to join the World Trade Organization, and Europe has launched the euro. Democracy spreads, as Mexico's ruling party loses power after 71 years and Serbia's Slobodan Milosevic is ousted, but the Israeli-Palestinian peace process collapses into a new uprising. Wars continue in Congo, Sierra Leone and Afghanistan, AIDS is ravaging Africa, and the world's population has just passed six billion.

regions.southern-africa: Thabo Mbeki has succeeded Nelson Mandela as South Africa's president, while Zimbabwe's Robert Mugabe backs violent seizures of white-owned farms after losing a referendum in February. The Second Congo War (1998-2003) draws in armies from half a dozen nations against Laurent-Desire Kabila's government in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (still labelled Zaire on this map). Angola's civil war continues, devastating floods strike Mozambique, and Paul Kagame becomes president of Rwanda. HIV/AIDS is killing millions across the region.
regions.northern-africa: Ethiopia and Eritrea end a bloody border war with the Algiers Agreement in December. British troops intervene to save Sierra Leone's government from rebels in May. Nigeria has returned to civilian rule under Olusegun Obasanjo, Senegal sees its first peaceful change of party in power with Abdoulaye Wade, and Algeria's Abdelaziz Bouteflika works to end the civil war. Hosni Mubarak rules Egypt, Gaddafi rules Libya, King Mohammed VI has succeeded his father in Morocco, and Sudan's al-Bashir regime fights a long war in the south.
regions.europe: The European Union of 15 members launched the euro currency in 1999 and in December 2000 agrees the Treaty of Nice to prepare for expansion into Eastern Europe. In October, mass protests overthrow Slobodan Milosevic in Serbia, while Kosovo is under UN administration. Vladimir Putin becomes president of Russia, captures Grozny in the Second Chechen War, and faces criticism over the Kursk submarine disaster. Germany's government, under Gerhard Schroder, has moved to Berlin, Tony Blair leads Britain and Jacques Chirac France.
regions.middle-east-south-asia: Peace talks at Camp David collapse in July, and the Second Intifada erupts in September, while Israel withdraws from southern Lebanon in May. Syria's Hafez al-Assad dies and is succeeded by his son Bashar; al-Qaeda bombs the USS Cole in Aden in October; and Saddam Hussein's Iraq remains under sanctions. The Taliban control most of Afghanistan, sheltering Osama bin Laden. India, under Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee, passes a billion people, and General Pervez Musharraf rules Pakistan after a 1999 coup; both are now nuclear-armed.
regions.north-central-asia: Central Asia's authoritarian presidents are entrenched: Nazarbayev in Kazakhstan, Karimov in Uzbekistan, Niyazov (who has made himself president for life) in Turkmenistan, Akayev in Kyrgyzstan, and Rahmonov in Tajikistan after the civil war. Kazakhstan's oil boom is under way, with the giant Kashagan field discovered in 2000. Russia's Siberian oil and gas fund Putin's state, and Mongolia elects Nambaryn Enkhbayar as prime minister in July 2000.
regions.east-asia: China, under Jiang Zemin and Premier Zhu Rongji, has regained Hong Kong (1997) and Macau (1999) and is close to joining the World Trade Organization. In Taiwan, Chen Shui-bian's election ends half a century of Kuomintang rule. South Korea's Kim Dae-jung meets North Korea's Kim Jong-il in the first inter-Korean summit in June and wins the Nobel Peace Prize. Japan, under Emperor Akihito and Prime Minister Mori Yoshiro, is mired in economic stagnation.
regions.southeast-asia: East Timor, after voting for independence from Indonesia in 1999, is under UN administration and will become independent in 2002. Indonesia, democratic since Suharto's fall in 1998, is led by President Abdurrahman Wahid, and the Philippines' President Joseph Estrada is impeached in November and put on trial before the Senate in December. All ten Southeast Asian nations are now in ASEAN; Vietnam is visited by President Clinton in November, and Myanmar remains under military rule.
regions.northern-north-america: Canada, under Jean Chretien, re-elected in November 2000, is prosperous and closely tied to the US economy; former prime minister Pierre Trudeau dies in September. The Inuit territory of Nunavut was created in 1999. Greenland has home rule under Denmark, and Alaska is a US state.
regions.southern-north-america: Bill Clinton's last year in office is marked by economic prosperity, but the dot-com crash begins in March, and the November election between George W. Bush and Al Gore is decided by the Supreme Court in December. In Mexico, Vicente Fox of the National Action Party wins in July, ending 71 years of PRI rule. Panama took full control of its canal on 31 December 1999, and Fidel Castro still rules Cuba.
regions.northern-south-america: Hugo Chavez, re-elected in 2000 under a new constitution, is reshaping Venezuela with his 'Bolivarian Revolution'. Colombia, under Andres Pastrana, launches Plan Colombia with US aid against drug cartels and FARC guerrillas. In Peru, President Alberto Fujimori flees to Japan amid a corruption scandal and resigns by fax in November; Ecuador adopts the US dollar, a plan announced just before a January coup; and Brazil, under Fernando Henrique Cardoso, marks 500 years since the arrival of the Portuguese.
regions.southern-cone: Argentina, under Fernando de la Rua, is sliding into the recession that will explode into crisis in 2001. Chile elects socialist Ricardo Lagos, and former dictator Augusto Pinochet returns home after 16 months of detention in Britain. Uruguay is led by Jorge Batlle and Paraguay by Luis Gonzalez Macchi, and the Mercosur trade bloc links the region's economies.
regions.australasia: Sydney hosts the 2000 Olympic Games, and Australia, under Prime Minister John Howard, sees hundreds of thousands march for reconciliation with Aboriginal Australians after voters rejected becoming a republic in 1999. New Zealand is led by Helen Clark. Coups strike Fiji, where George Speight holds the government hostage in May, and the Solomon Islands, and Papua New Guinea works toward peace on Bougainville.

eras.title: The Great Crash
eras.overview: In 2008 the world suffers its worst financial crisis since the Great Depression. A boom in risky American home loans turns to bust, and on 15 September the Wall Street bank Lehman Brothers goes bankrupt, freezing credit around the globe. Governments spend vast sums rescuing banks, stock markets crash, and the world slides into a deep downturn soon called the Great Recession. Earlier in the year, soaring food prices set off protests and riots in dozens of poorer countries, and oil peaks at about $147 a barrel in July before collapsing to near $30 by December. The crisis hastens a shift in global power: in November the leaders of the G20, which includes China, India and Brazil, meet for the first time to steer the world economy. The United States, still at war in Iraq and Afghanistan after the attacks of 11 September 2001, elects Barack Obama as its first African American president. China hosts a spectacular Olympic Games in Beijing, Russia fights a short war with Georgia, Kosovo declares independence, a cyclone devastates Myanmar, an earthquake kills some 69,000 people in China, and in November gunmen attack Mumbai.

regions.southern-africa: South Africa's ruling ANC forces President Thabo Mbeki to resign in September, and Kgalema Motlanthe takes over until the 2009 election. Zimbabwe's economy has collapsed into hyperinflation; after a disputed election in March, opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai pulls out of a violent June run-off, leaving Robert Mugabe in power until a power-sharing deal is signed in September. In Kenya, violence after the disputed December 2007 election kills over a thousand people before Mwai Kibaki and Raila Odinga agree to share power. In the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, ruled by Joseph Kabila, Laurent Nkunda's rebels push towards the city of Goma late in the year.
regions.northern-africa: In Sudan, where the Darfur conflict has driven millions from their homes, the International Criminal Court's prosecutor asks in July for an arrest warrant against President Omar al-Bashir. Somalia's weak transitional government depends on Ethiopian troops against the Islamist al-Shabaab insurgency, while pirates off the Somali coast attack over a hundred ships during the year. Soaring food prices bring protests and riots to Egypt, ruled by Hosni Mubarak, and to Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Senegal and other countries. Military coups topple the governments of Mauritania in August and Guinea in December, the day after the death of its long-time ruler Lansana Conte. Muammar Gaddafi's Libya has restored full relations with the United States, and Umaru Yar'Adua is Nigeria's president.
regions.europe: Europe is hit hard by the crisis: Britain nationalises the bank Northern Rock in February and pours billions into its other banks in October, and in October all three of Iceland's big banks collapse, wrecking its economy. Kosovo declares independence from Serbia in February; it is recognised by many Western countries but not by Serbia or Russia. In August, Russia and Georgia fight a five-day war over South Ossetia, after which Russia recognises South Ossetia and Abkhazia as independent states. Dmitry Medvedev becomes Russia's president in May, with Vladimir Putin as his prime minister. Angela Merkel leads Germany, Nicolas Sarkozy France, Gordon Brown Britain, and Silvio Berlusconi returns to power in Italy.
regions.middle-east-south-asia: Violence in Iraq is falling after the 2007 US troop 'surge', and in November the two governments agree that US forces will leave by the end of 2011, while the Taliban insurgency grows against Hamid Karzai's government in Afghanistan. In Pakistan, Pervez Musharraf resigns in August and Asif Ali Zardari, widower of the assassinated Benazir Bhutto, becomes president. In November, ten gunmen from the Pakistan-based group Lashkar-e-Taiba attack Mumbai, killing 166 people and straining relations between India, led by Manmohan Singh, and Pakistan. Nepal abolishes its 240-year-old monarchy in May, Bhutan holds its first general election, Iran's President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad faces UN sanctions over its nuclear programme, and on 27 December Israel launches a major offensive against Hamas in Gaza.
regions.north-central-asia: Central Asia's oil and gas states ride high energy prices until the autumn crash: Nursultan Nazarbayev's Kazakhstan, Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedow's Turkmenistan, which he has ruled since Saparmurat Niyazov's death in 2006, and Islam Karimov's Uzbekistan. Kurmanbek Bakiyev rules Kyrgyzstan and Emomali Rahmon Tajikistan. In Mongolia, riots break out in July over alleged fraud in parliamentary elections. Siberia's oil and gas fund a resurgent Russia, but the oil price falls by about three-quarters between July and December.
regions.east-asia: China, under President Hu Jintao and Premier Wen Jiabao, has a turbulent year: protests against Chinese rule in Tibet in March are put down, and the Sichuan earthquake in May kills some 69,000 people. But the Beijing Olympic Games in August showcase China's rise, its astronauts make their first spacewalk in September, and as exports slump it announces a 4-trillion-yuan stimulus plan in November. In Taiwan, Ma Ying-jeou is elected president and opens direct flights to the mainland. South Korea's new president, Lee Myung-bak, faces huge protests over US beef imports, North Korea's Kim Jong-il is reported to have suffered a stroke, and Japan, under Emperor Akihito, changes prime minister from Fukuda Yasuo to Aso Taro in September.
regions.southeast-asia: Cyclone Nargis strikes Myanmar's Irrawaddy delta in May, killing at least 138,000 people, while the ruling generals at first restrict foreign aid and push through a new constitution in a referendum. Thailand is in turmoil: anti-government protesters occupy Government House and in late November shut Bangkok's airports, until a court dissolves the ruling party and Abhisit Vejjajiva becomes prime minister in December. Indonesia, led by Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono, sees its former dictator Suharto die in January. Malaysia's ruling coalition loses its two-thirds majority in parliament for the first time since 1969, and Gloria Macapagal Arroyo leads the Philippines.
regions.northern-north-america: Canada's Conservative Prime Minister Stephen Harper formally apologises in June for the residential schools that took Indigenous children from their families, and wins a second minority government in October. As the recession bites, opposition parties plan to bring him down, and in December he has Parliament suspended to avoid a confidence vote. In November, about three-quarters of Greenland's voters approve greater self-government within the Danish realm, to take effect in June 2009.
regions.southern-north-america: The US housing bubble bursts: the investment bank Bear Stearns is rescued in March, the government takes over the mortgage giants Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac in September, Lehman Brothers goes bankrupt on 15 September, and Congress approves a $700 billion bank rescue in October. In November, Democrat Barack Obama defeats John McCain to succeed George W. Bush. Mexico's President Felipe Calderon is waging war on the drug cartels, and more than 5,000 people are murdered in 2008 as violence escalates. Fidel Castro hands Cuba's presidency to his brother Raul in February, and Haiti is shaken by food riots.
regions.northern-south-america: Brazil, under Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, is riding a commodity boom, and huge oil fields have been found deep beneath its seabed. In March, Colombian forces under President Alvaro Uribe kill the FARC commander Raul Reyes in a raid inside Ecuador, and Ecuador and Venezuela move troops to the border; in July, Colombia frees the hostage Ingrid Betancourt and 14 others in a daring rescue. Ecuador's voters approve a new constitution backed by President Rafael Correa, Bolivia's Evo Morales faces violent protests in the eastern departments demanding autonomy, and Hugo Chavez rules Venezuela. In May, South American leaders found the Union of South American Nations (UNASUR).
regions.southern-cone: Argentina's President Cristina Fernandez de Kirchner, in office since December 2007, faces months of farmers' strikes and road blockades after raising export taxes on soybeans in March. In Paraguay, the former bishop Fernando Lugo wins the April election, ending 61 years of rule by the Colorado Party. Michelle Bachelet is Chile's first woman president, and Tabare Vazquez is president of Uruguay.
regions.australasia: Australia's new Labor prime minister, Kevin Rudd, makes a formal national apology on 13 February to the Stolen Generations of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children taken from their families. New Zealand elects John Key's National Party in November, ending Helen Clark's nine years in power. Fiji remains under the military government of Commodore Frank Bainimarama, who seized power in a 2006 coup, and Michael Somare leads Papua New Guinea.

eras.title: Pandemic and War
eras.overview: A new coronavirus, first identified in Wuhan, China, at the end of 2019, spreads around the world in early 2020. The World Health Organization declares COVID-19 a pandemic on 11 March; billions of people live under lockdowns, borders close, and the world economy suffers its worst recession since the Second World War. Vaccines developed at record speed are first given in December 2020. More than 7 million deaths are officially reported, and the WHO estimates that almost 15 million more people than usual died in 2020 and 2021 alone. The years to 2024 bring further shocks. The Taliban retake Afghanistan in 2021. Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 starts the largest war in Europe since 1945 and drives up energy and food prices worldwide. A Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 is followed by a devastating war in Gaza, and in December 2024 Syria's Bashar al-Assad is overthrown. The world's population passes eight billion in November 2022, and India overtakes China as the most populous country in 2023. Artificial-intelligence chatbots such as ChatGPT (2022) spread fast, rivalry between the United States and China sharpens, and 2024 is the warmest year on record.

regions.southern-africa: South Africa, under Cyril Ramaphosa, imposes one of the world's strictest lockdowns, and its scientists detect the Beta variant of the virus in 2020 and help identify Omicron in 2021. In 2024 the ANC loses the parliamentary majority it has held since 1994 and forms a coalition government. In the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, the M23 rebels, which UN experts say are backed by Rwanda, launch a new offensive in 2022, and an Islamist insurgency in northern Mozambique's Cabo Delgado province draws in Rwandan troops in 2021. Samia Suluhu Hassan becomes Tanzania's first woman president after John Magufuli's death in 2021, and Kenya elects William Ruto in 2022.
regions.northern-africa: In November 2020 war breaks out between Ethiopia's government, led by Abiy Ahmed, and the leaders of its Tigray region; by some estimates hundreds of thousands die before a peace deal is signed in Pretoria in November 2022. Sudan's transition after Omar al-Bashir's fall is ended by a coup in 2021, and in April 2023 war erupts between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, driving over ten million people from their homes. A wave of military coups sweeps the Sahel, in Mali (2020 and 2021), Guinea (2021), Burkina Faso (twice in 2022) and Niger (2023); the juntas of Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger send French troops home and form the Alliance of Sahel States. Abdel Fattah el-Sisi rules Egypt, Tunisia's President Kais Saied suspends parliament in 2021, and in September 2023 an earthquake kills nearly 3,000 people in Morocco and floods devastate Derna in Libya.
regions.europe: Italy is Europe's first coronavirus hotspot, and lockdowns spread across the continent; in July 2020 EU leaders agree a €750 billion recovery fund. Britain leaves the European Union on 31 January 2020. On 24 February 2022 Russia, which annexed Crimea in 2014, launches a full-scale invasion of Ukraine; Ukrainian forces under President Volodymyr Zelenskyy drive the invaders back from Kyiv, but fighting grinds on in the east and south, and millions of Ukrainians flee abroad. Finland (2023) and Sweden (2024) join NATO. In Belarus, Alexander Lukashenko crushes mass protests after a disputed 2020 election, and Azerbaijan regains much of Nagorno-Karabakh in a 2020 war and the rest in 2023, when almost all its Armenian population flees. Olaf Scholz succeeds Angela Merkel in Germany in 2021, Emmanuel Macron leads France, Britain has four prime ministers from Boris Johnson to Keir Starmer, and Queen Elizabeth II dies in September 2022.
regions.middle-east-south-asia: India, under Narendra Modi, suffers a devastating wave of the Delta variant in 2021, clashes with Chinese troops in the Galwan valley in 2020, lands a probe near the Moon's south pole in 2023, and in 2024 returns Modi for a third term at the head of a coalition. As US troops withdraw, the Taliban take Kabul on 15 August 2021. Floods put huge areas of Pakistan under water in 2022, economic collapse forces Sri Lanka's president from office the same year, and Bangladesh's Sheikh Hasina resigns and flees in August 2024 after student-led protests. In 2020 the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain establish relations with Israel. On 7 October 2023 a Hamas-led attack kills about 1,200 people in Israel and takes some 250 hostages; Israel's offensive in Gaza kills more than 40,000 Palestinians by late 2024, according to Gaza's health ministry, and fighting spreads to Lebanon and the Red Sea. Mass protests follow the death of Mahsa Amini in Iranian police custody in 2022, an earthquake kills more than 50,000 people in Turkey and Syria in February 2023, and Syria's Bashar al-Assad is overthrown in December 2024.
regions.north-central-asia: In Kyrgyzstan, protests after a disputed election in October 2020 bring Sadyr Japarov to power. In January 2022, deadly unrest in Kazakhstan leads President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev to call in troops from a Russian-led alliance and to remove his predecessor Nursultan Nazarbayev from his remaining post. Turkmenistan's Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedow hands the presidency to his son Serdar in 2022, Shavkat Mirziyoyev leads Uzbekistan, and Emomali Rahmon's Tajikistan fights deadly border clashes with Kyrgyzstan in 2021 and 2022. When Russia orders a military call-up in September 2022, hundreds of thousands of Russian men leave the country, many crossing into Kazakhstan.
regions.east-asia: China, under Xi Jinping, seals off Wuhan and then pursues a 'zero-COVID' policy of mass testing and lockdowns until it is abruptly dropped in December 2022, after rare street protests. A national security law imposed on Hong Kong in 2020 ends its protest movement, and Xi begins a third term as Communist Party leader in 2022. Taiwan, led by Tsai Ing-wen and from 2024 by Lai Ching-te, faces large Chinese military exercises. Japan, under Emperor Naruhito, holds the postponed Tokyo Olympics in 2021; Prime Minister Abe Shinzo resigns in 2020 and is assassinated in 2022. North Korea's Kim Jong Un seals his borders and steps up missile tests, and in December 2024 South Korea's President Yoon Suk Yeol briefly declares martial law and is impeached.
regions.southeast-asia: In Myanmar the army seizes power on 1 February 2021 and detains Aung San Suu Kyi; its crackdown on protests turns into a civil war in which armed resistance groups make large gains from late 2023. Ferdinand Marcos Jr., son of the former dictator, is elected president of the Philippines in 2022, succeeding Rodrigo Duterte. Indonesia's Joko Widodo, who begins building a new capital, Nusantara, on Borneo, is followed by Prabowo Subianto, elected in 2024. Thailand sees youth-led protests in 2020, and Anwar Ibrahim becomes Malaysia's prime minister in 2022 after years of political turmoil.
regions.northern-north-america: Canada, under Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, is shaken in 2021 by the discovery of possible unmarked graves at former residential schools for Indigenous children. Truckers protesting vaccine rules blockade Ottawa and border crossings in early 2022, and in 2023 wildfires burn a larger area than in any season on record. Greenland, self-governing within Denmark, draws growing interest as melting Arctic ice opens sea routes and access to minerals, and its 2021 election is fought over a planned rare-earth and uranium mine.
regions.southern-north-america: The United States records more than a million COVID-19 deaths, the most of any country. The murder of George Floyd by a Minneapolis police officer in May 2020 sparks nationwide protests, Joe Biden defeats Donald Trump in November 2020, and Trump's supporters storm the US Capitol on 6 January 2021; in November 2024 Trump is elected again. Mexico elects Claudia Sheinbaum as its first woman president in 2024. Haiti's President Jovenel Moise is assassinated in 2021, and armed gangs take over much of Port-au-Prince, while El Salvador's Nayib Bukele jails tens of thousands in a sweeping crackdown on gangs from 2022.
regions.northern-south-america: Brazil, under Jair Bolsonaro, records some 700,000 COVID-19 deaths, and Peru reports the world's highest death rate. Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva returns as Brazil's president in January 2023, a week before Bolsonaro's supporters storm government buildings in Brasilia. Peru's President Pedro Castillo is removed and arrested in December 2022 after trying to dissolve Congress. Nearly eight million Venezuelans have left their country, and Nicolas Maduro claims victory in a disputed July 2024 election. Colombia elects its first left-wing president, Gustavo Petro, in 2022, Ecuador's President Daniel Noboa declares war on drug gangs in January 2024, and an oil boom makes Guyana one of the world's fastest-growing economies.
regions.southern-cone: Argentina, battered by the pandemic and by inflation approaching 200 percent a year, elects the libertarian outsider Javier Milei, who takes office in December 2023 promising to slash the state; Argentina also wins the 2022 football World Cup. In Chile, Gabriel Boric is elected president in 2021 after mass protests, but voters reject two proposed new constitutions, in 2022 and 2023. Paraguay elects Santiago Pena in 2023, Uruguay elects Yamandu Orsi in November 2024, and in 2024 the worst floods in its history devastate Brazil's southern state of Rio Grande do Sul.
regions.australasia: Australia and New Zealand close their borders and keep COVID-19 deaths low through 2020 and 2021. New Zealand's Jacinda Ardern wins a landslide in 2020 and steps down in 2023, and Christopher Luxon becomes prime minister later that year. Under the AUKUS pact (2021), Australia is to gain nuclear-powered submarines with American and British help; Anthony Albanese becomes prime minister in 2022, and Australians reject an Indigenous Voice to Parliament in a 2023 referendum. The Hunga Tonga undersea volcano erupts with enormous force in January 2022, and deadly unrest breaks out in New Caledonia in 2024 over voting rules.

empires.name: Ancient Egypt
empires.capital: Memphis; later Thebes, Amarna, Pi-Ramesses and Sais

empires.summary: Around 3100 BCE the farming chiefdoms along the Nile were united into a single kingdom, traditionally by Narmer. The river's yearly flood fed a dense population ruled by a god-king, the pharaoh, through scribes, priests and provincial governors. Historians divide its long history into the Old Kingdom, when the great pyramids were built, the Middle Kingdom, and the New Kingdom, when warrior pharaohs built an empire stretching from Nubia into Syria. Periods of division and foreign rule, by Libyans, Kushites, Assyrians and Persians, alternated with revivals. After Alexander the Great's conquest in 332 BCE Egypt was ruled by the Greek Ptolemies, and its independence ended when Cleopatra VII died and Rome annexed the country in 30 BCE.
empires.legacy: Egypt gave the world monumental stone architecture, one of the first writing systems and a 365-day calendar, and its pyramids and mummies still fascinate people everywhere.

empires.summary: Sumer, in the marshy south of Mesopotamia (modern Iraq), was home to the world's first cities. Between about 3500 and 3000 BCE towns such as Uruk grew into cities of tens of thousands, organised around temples that managed irrigation, grain and trade. To keep records, Sumerian scribes invented cuneiform writing on clay tablets around 3200 BCE. Sumer was never one country: a dozen rival city-states, each with its own patron god and king, fought over water and fields. Sargon of Akkad conquered them around 2334 BCE, but after Akkad's fall the Third Dynasty of Ur reunited the region and built a centralised state with a vast bureaucracy. Ur fell to Elamite invaders in 2004 BCE, and Sumerian gradually died out as a spoken language.
empires.legacy: Sumer pioneered writing, early wheeled vehicles, the base-sixty counting behind our hours and minutes, and the first stories of Gilgamesh.

empires.name: Akkadian Empire
empires.capital: Akkad (Agade), whose site has not yet been found

peak.note: Under Naram-Sin, from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean and the Anatolian foothills; c. 0.8M km² (Taagepera 1978), though directly ruled land was smaller; c. 0.8M km² c. 2250 BCE (Taagepera 1978)

rulers.name: Sargon of Akkad
rulers.note: Founder; conquered the Sumerian city-states

rulers.name: Rimush
rulers.note: Crushed widespread revolts

rulers.name: Manishtushu
rulers.note: Campaigned across the Persian Gulf

rulers.name: Naram-Sin
rulers.note: Called himself king of the four quarters and a god

rulers.name: Shar-kali-sharri
rulers.note: Last strong king before the collapse

empires.summary: Often called the world's first empire, Akkad was founded by Sargon, a man of humble origins who rose to serve the king of Kish and then seized power around 2334 BCE. Sargon conquered the quarrelling Sumerian city-states and campaigned as far as Syria and western Iran, uniting speakers of Sumerian and the Semitic Akkadian language under one ruler. He installed loyal governors, standardised weights and measures, and made Akkadian a language of administration. His grandson Naram-Sin pushed the borders further and was the first Mesopotamian king to call himself a god. Revolts, pressure from the Gutian mountain peoples and possibly a severe drought broke the empire apart, and by about 2154 BCE it had collapsed.
empires.legacy: Akkad set the model of a multi-ethnic empire run from one capital, and Akkadian became the diplomatic language of the Near East for over a thousand years.

empires.summary: Babylon was a small town until an Amorite dynasty made it a capital around 1894 BCE. Its sixth king, Hammurabi, conquered all of southern Mesopotamia and is remembered for his law code carved on a stone pillar. Over the next thousand years Babylon was ruled by Kassites, native kings and, for long stretches, the Assyrians, yet it remained the region's religious and cultural heart, famous for its scholars and astronomers. In 626 BCE Nabopolassar, traditionally called a Chaldean, threw off Assyrian rule and, allied with the Medes, destroyed Assyria. His son Nebuchadnezzar II built a Neo-Babylonian empire, rebuilt Babylon with the Ishtar Gate and captured Jerusalem in 587 BCE. Cyrus the Great of Persia took the city without a fight in 539 BCE.
empires.legacy: Babylonian law, mathematics and astronomy, including the division of the circle into 360 degrees, shaped later Persian, Greek and Jewish thought.

empires.capital: Assur; later Nimrud, Dur-Sharrukin and Nineveh

peak.note: Under Esarhaddon, from Egypt to western Iran; c. 1.4M km² c. 670 BCE (Taagepera 1978); c. 1.4M km² c. 670 BCE (Taagepera 1978; Turchin, Adams & Hall 2006)

empires.summary: Assyria grew from the trading city of Assur on the upper Tigris, whose merchants ran caravans into Anatolia soon after 2000 BCE. After centuries as a regional kingdom it became a great power, and from the 9th century BCE its kings built the largest empire the world had yet seen. The Neo-Assyrian state had a professional standing army, iron weapons, siege engines and a road and messenger system, and it ruled through provinces under appointed governors. Rebellious peoples were deported en masse to break resistance. At its height Assyria controlled Mesopotamia, the Levant and, briefly, Egypt. Civil war after Ashurbanipal weakened it, and a coalition of Babylonians and Medes sacked Nineveh in 612 BCE; the last Assyrian army was defeated in 609 BCE.
empires.legacy: Assyria invented much of the machinery of imperial rule later copied by Persia, and Ashurbanipal's library preserved thousands of cuneiform texts, including the Epic of Gilgamesh.

peak.note: Under Suppiluliuma I and his successors, from central Anatolia to Syria; c. 0.45M km² c. 1250-1220 BCE (Taagepera 1978); c. 0.45M km² c. 1250 – 1220 BCE (Taagepera 1978)

empires.summary: The Hittites, speakers of the oldest recorded Indo-European language, built a kingdom in central Anatolia (modern Turkey) around 1650 BCE with its capital at Hattusa. An early king, Mursili I, raided as far as Babylon and sacked it in 1595 BCE. After a period of weakness, Suppiluliuma I made the Hittites a great power in the 14th century BCE, defeating the Mitanni and taking control of Syria, where he set up his sons as vassal kings. The Hittites were famed for their chariots and diplomacy, and after the Battle of Kadesh against Egypt they signed one of the earliest known peace treaties. Around 1180 BCE, amid the wider Bronze Age collapse, Hattusa was abandoned and the empire broke into small Syro-Hittite kingdoms.
empires.legacy: The Hittite-Egyptian treaty is a landmark of international diplomacy, and the Hittite archives revealed a lost civilisation known before only from brief mentions in the Bible and in Egyptian records.

empires.name: Indus Valley Civilisation
empires.capital: No known capital; major cities included Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Rakhigarhi, Ganweriwala and Dholavira

peak.note: Mature Harappan phase, across modern Pakistan and north-west India; the cultural zone is put at c. 1.2M km², while Taagepera (1978) estimated c. 0.3M km² c. 1800 BCE for any political unit

rulers.name: No rulers known
rulers.note: The Indus script is undeciphered and no royal names, palaces or tombs have been found

empires.summary: The Indus or Harappan civilisation flourished along the Indus river and its neighbours in what is now Pakistan and north-west India. Farming villages grew into planned cities after about 2600 BCE, the Mature Harappan phase. Mohenjo-daro and Harappa were laid out on grids, with baked-brick houses, covered drains, possible granaries and, at Mohenjo-daro, a Great Bath, and standard weights and seals were used across an area larger than Egypt and Mesopotamia combined. Indus merchants traded with Mesopotamia by sea. Strikingly, no palaces, royal tombs or images of kings have been found, and the Indus script remains undeciphered, so we do not know how the cities were governed. After about 1900 BCE the cities were gradually abandoned, probably because of climate change and shifting rivers, and people dispersed into smaller villages.
empires.legacy: The Indus cities set early standards in urban planning and sanitation, and many scholars trace continuities between Harappan crafts and later South Asian culture.

empires.name: Minoan civilisation

peak.note: Neopalatial period: Crete plus Aegean islands such as Thera

empires.summary: The Minoans, named by the archaeologist Arthur Evans after the legendary King Minos, created Europe's first advanced civilisation on the island of Crete. From about 1900 BCE they built large palace complexes at Knossos, Phaistos, Malia and Zakros, which acted as centres for religion, storage and craft production. Minoan ships traded across the eastern Mediterranean with Egypt and the Levant, and their colourful frescoes show bull-leaping, processions and sea life. They wrote in a script called Linear A, which is still undeciphered, so their rulers' names and language are unknown. After widespread destruction around 1450 BCE, possibly linked to earthquakes and the aftermath of the Thera eruption, Crete came under Mycenaean Greek control, and Minoan culture faded by about 1100 BCE.
empires.legacy: Minoan art, architecture and seafaring strongly influenced Mycenaean Greece and inspired the Greek myths of the Minotaur and the labyrinth.

empires.name: Greek city-states
empires.capital: No single capital; leading poleis included Athens, Sparta, Corinth, Thebes and Syracuse

peak.note: Mainland Greece, the Aegean and colonies from Spain to the Black Sea

rulers.name: Solon of Athens
rulers.note: Lawgiver who reformed Athenian society

rulers.name: Cleisthenes of Athens
rulers.note: Founded Athenian democracy

rulers.name: Leonidas I of Sparta

rulers.name: Epaminondas of Thebes
