empires.summary: The Mexica, a people who claimed to have migrated from a homeland called Aztlan, founded Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco around 1325. At first vassals of the Tepanec city of Azcapotzalco, in 1428 they formed the Triple Alliance with Texcoco and Tlacopan and overthrew their overlords. Under rulers such as Moctezuma I and Ahuitzotl, the alliance conquered much of central and southern Mexico, collecting tribute in maize, cotton, cacao, feathers and gold from hundreds of towns rather than governing them directly. Tenochtitlan, linked to the shore by causeways and fed by floating chinampa gardens, held perhaps 200,000 people. Warfare also supplied captives for human sacrifice. In 1519 Hernán Cortés arrived; allied with the Tlaxcalans and helped by smallpox, the Spanish captured Tenochtitlan in 1521.
empires.legacy: Mexico City stands on the ruins of Tenochtitlan, and the Aztec emblem of an eagle on a cactus appears on the Mexican flag.

sources.title: Taagepera (1997), Expansion and Contraction Patterns of Large Polities

empires.name: Tiwanaku

peak.note: Influence from the Titicaca basin into southern Peru, northern Chile and north-west Argentina (rough estimate)

rulers.name: Rulers unknown
rulers.note: Tiwanaku had no writing; its elite is known only from monuments such as the Gateway of the Sun

empires.summary: Tiwanaku grew near the southern shore of Lake Titicaca, about 3,850 metres above sea level in what is now Bolivia. Settled long before, it became a major city and ceremonial centre from about 500 CE, with stone temples such as the Akapana pyramid, the Kalasasaya enclosure and the carved Gateway of the Sun. Its farmers fed tens of thousands of people using raised fields separated by canals, which protected crops from frost, while herds of llamas and alpacas carried goods. Tiwanaku spread its influence through colonies, religion and trade across the southern Andes into Peru, Chile and Argentina, sharing a staff-god imagery with its northern neighbour Wari. After about 1000 a long drought undermined its farming, and the city was gradually abandoned.
empires.legacy: Tiwanaku is a symbol of indigenous Andean identity in Bolivia, and its raised-field farming has been revived by modern farmers.

empires.name: Wari Empire

peak.note: Much of the Peruvian highlands and coast (rough estimate)

rulers.name: Rulers unknown
rulers.note: Wari left no writing; its rulers' names are lost

empires.summary: The Wari state rose around 600 CE in the Ayacucho valley of the central Peruvian highlands, with its capital at Huari, a city covering several square kilometres. Many archaeologists see Wari as the first true empire of the Andes: it built planned administrative centres such as Pikillacta near Cusco and Viracochapampa in the north, linked by roads, and moved colonists to expand terrace farming. Wari officials probably kept records on khipus, knotted cords later used by the Inca. Wari shared religious imagery, notably a staff-holding god, with Tiwanaku to the south, and the two powers met but seem to have avoided major war. Around 1000 Wari collapsed, perhaps because of drought and internal unrest, leaving a patchwork of regional states.
empires.legacy: Wari pioneered the roads, administrative centres, terracing and record-keeping that the Inca later built into their own empire.

empires.name: Chimú Empire (Chimor)

peak.note: About 1,000 km of the north Peruvian coast (rough estimate)

rulers.name: Tacaynamo
rulers.note: Founder in Chimú tradition, said to have arrived by sea

rulers.name: Ñançenpinco
rulers.note: Remembered as the conqueror who expanded Chimor

empires.summary: The Chimú kingdom, called Chimor, arose around 900 in the Moche valley on Peru's desert north coast, where the Moche civilisation had flourished earlier. Its capital, Chan Chan, was the largest adobe city in the Americas, made up of walled royal compounds, each built by a king who was buried in it with his treasures. Chimú engineers dug long irrigation canals to water the desert, and its craftsmen were skilled goldsmiths and weavers. From the 14th century the Chimú conquered neighbouring valleys until they controlled about 1,000 kilometres of coast, from near the Ecuadorian border to near Lima. Around 1470 the Inca under Topa Inca Yupanqui conquered Chimor, reportedly by cutting its water supply, and carried its king and many artisans off to Cusco.
empires.legacy: Chan Chan is a World Heritage Site, and Chimú metalworkers shaped the gold-working traditions of the Inca court.

empires.name: Inca Empire (Tawantinsuyu)

peak.note: From southern Colombia to central Chile; c. 2.0M km² in 1527 (Taagepera 1997; Turchin, Adams & Hall 2006)

rulers.name: Manco Cápac
rulers.note: Legendary founder of Cusco

rulers.name: Pachacuti
rulers.note: Began the imperial expansion; rebuilt Cusco

rulers.name: Topa Inca Yupanqui
rulers.note: Conquered Chimor and pushed into Chile

rulers.name: Huayna Capac
rulers.note: Ruled at the empire's height; died in an epidemic, possibly smallpox

rulers.name: Atahualpa
rulers.note: Won the civil war, then was executed by Pizarro

empires.summary: The Inca were a small kingdom around Cusco in the Peruvian highlands, traditionally founded by Manco Cápac around 1200. In 1438 Pachacuti repelled an attack by the rival Chanka and began a series of conquests that his son Topa Inca and grandson Huayna Capac continued, creating Tawantinsuyu, the Land of the Four Quarters, the largest empire in the pre-Columbian Americas. The Inca ruled some 10 million people through a network of about 40,000 kilometres of roads with rope bridges and relay runners, state storehouses and a labour tax called mit'a, keeping records on knotted khipus. They resettled loyal colonists and spread the Quechua language. A civil war between Huáscar and Atahualpa had just ended when Francisco Pizarro arrived; he captured Atahualpa and executed him in 1533.
empires.legacy: Machu Picchu and the Inca roads are world-famous, and Quechua, the Inca state language, is still spoken by millions of Andean people.

sources.title: Taagepera (1997), Expansion and Contraction Patterns of Large Polities
Turchin, Adams & Hall (2006), East-West Orientation of Historical Empires

empires.name: Thule culture
empires.capital: None; small seasonal villages across the Arctic

peak.note: From Alaska across Arctic Canada to Greenland (rough estimate)

rulers.name: No rulers
rulers.note: Thule society was organised in kin-based groups led by experienced whaling captains (umialik)

empires.summary: The Thule people, ancestors of today's Inuit, developed in coastal Alaska around 1000 CE. Using sophisticated technology, including large skin boats called umiaks, kayaks, toggling harpoons, dog sleds and snow houses, they hunted bowhead whales, seals and walrus. From about 1200, perhaps encouraged by warmer conditions and the search for iron and new hunting grounds, they spread rapidly eastward across Arctic Canada to Greenland in just a few generations, replacing the earlier Dorset people. In Greenland they met Norse settlers, whose colonies later vanished. Thule communities were small and mobile, without states or kings, but linked by trade networks stretching thousands of kilometres. As the Little Ice Age cooled the Arctic after about 1400, whaling declined and Thule culture evolved into the regional Inuit cultures met by Europeans.
empires.legacy: The Thule migration created the Inuit world of Alaska, Canada and Greenland, whose inventions such as the kayak are now used worldwide.

sources.title: Historical Climatology: What made the Thule move? (on Friesen & Arnold 2008)

rulers.note: First Tuʻi Tonga, said to be the son of the god Tangaloa

rulers.name: Tuʻitātui

empires.summary: According to Tongan tradition, the line of sacred kings called Tuʻi Tonga began around 950 with ʻAhoʻeitu, son of the sky god Tangaloa and a mortal woman. From Tongatapu, the Tuʻi Tonga built a maritime chiefdom whose influence, through voyaging canoes, marriage alliances and tribute, extended at its height in the 12th and 13th centuries across Samoa, ʻUvea (Wallis), Futuna and parts of Fiji. The royal centre at Muʻa has great stone-faced tombs called langi, and the Haʻamonga ʻa Maui trilithon is attributed to the king Tuʻitātui. After several Tuʻi Tonga were assassinated, around the 15th century they handed political power to a new line, the Tuʻi Haʻatakalaua, and later the Tuʻi Kanokupolu, keeping a sacred role. The title lapsed when Laufilitonga died in 1865, as George Tupou I unified Tonga as a modern kingdom.
empires.legacy: The Tuʻi Tonga tradition underpins the modern Kingdom of Tonga, the only Pacific island monarchy never formally colonised.

empires.name: Pallava dynasty

rulers.name: Simhavishnu

rulers.name: Mahendravarman I
rulers.note: Pioneered Pallava rock-cut temples and wrote the Sanskrit satire Mattavilasa Prahasana; lost his northern provinces to the Chalukya Pulakeshin II

rulers.name: Narasimhavarman I (Mamalla)
rulers.note: Defeated and killed Pulakeshin II and sacked Vatapi in 642; Mamallapuram is named after him

rulers.name: Paramesvaravarman I
rulers.note: Fought off a renewed Chalukya invasion under Vikramaditya I

rulers.name: Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha)
rulers.note: Built the Shore Temple at Mamallapuram and the Kailasanathar temple at Kanchipuram; sent embassies to Tang China

rulers.name: Nandivarman II (Pallavamalla)
rulers.note: Chosen as a boy from a collateral branch; Kanchipuram was taken by the Chalukya Vikramaditya II, and he built the Vaikuntha Perumal temple

rulers.name: Nandivarman III
rulers.note: Defeated the Pandyas at Tellaru and kept a strong navy trading with South-east Asia

rulers.name: Aparajita
rulers.note: Last Pallava king, defeated and killed by the Chola Aditya I

empires.summary: The Pallavas first appear in 4th-century copper-plate grants issued from Kanchipuram, and probably began as feudatories of the Satavahanas before ruling the region around Kanchi in their own right. After a period of eclipse under the Kalabhra invasions, Simhavishnu revived the dynasty in the later 6th century and the Tamil country was divided between the Pallavas in the north and the Pandyas in the south. A struggle with the Chalukyas of Vatapi lasted more than two centuries: Pulakeshin II took Mahendravarman I's northern provinces, but Narasimhavarman I killed him and sacked Vatapi in 642, and the Chalukyas later captured Kanchipuram in their turn. The Pallava court patronised Sanskrit and Tamil literature, the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang visited Kanchipuram in about 640, and Narasimhavarman II sent an embassy to Tang China. Squeezed between the Pandyas, Rashtrakutas and a reviving Chola dynasty, the Pallavas declined in the 9th century, and the Chola Aditya I defeated and killed the last king, Aparajita, in about 897.
empires.legacy: The Pallavas moved southern Indian architecture from rock-cut caves to free-standing stone temples, leaving the Pancha Rathas and Shore Temple at Mamallapuram (a UNESCO World Heritage Site) and the Kailasanathar temple at Kanchipuram, and their script, carried by traders, priests and monks, became the ancestor of Grantha and Tamil and of many South-east Asian scripts such as Khmer.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram

empires.name: Kalabhra dynasty
empires.capital: Unknown (Kaveripattinam in the Chola country is sometimes proposed)

peak.note: Rough: the map's c. 0.14M km² (Cliopatria, 353–591) assumes rule over the whole Tamil plain from just south of Kanchipuram to Kanyakumari. No estimate by Taagepera or Turchin exists, and how much of this the Kalabhras held, and when, is unknown; the year is a mid-point near Achyuta Vikranta, the one attested king

rulers.name: Achyuta Vikranta (Accutavikkanta)
rulers.note: Named in the Pali works of the Buddhist monk Buddhadatta as ruler of the Chola country 'of the Kalamba family'; later Tamil tradition says he held the Chera, Chola and Pandya kings captive, and the 10th-century Jain grammarian Amitasagara quotes verses about him

empires.summary: The Kalabhras are known almost only from what their enemies said about them. The Velvikudi copper plates of the Pandya Nedunjadaiyan (c. 770) say that a 'Kali king' called Kalabhran drove out numberless great kings and seized brahmin land grants before the Pandya Kadungon ended his rule, and the Kasakudi plates of the Pallava Nandivarman II list the Kalabhras among the kings defeated by Simhavishnu. Nilakanta Sastri placed their incursion about 300 or a little later; Upinder Singh notes that 4th-century Pallava charters show they did not then rule near the Penner and Vellar rivers, and Schwartzberg's atlas dates their conquests to the late 4th century with a query. The only named king, Achyuta Vikranta, appears in the works of the 5th-century Buddhist monk Buddhadatta, who wrote in monasteries on the Kaveri while Achyuta ruled the Chola country. The Pallankoil plates, a mid-6th-century grant by a Pallava Simhavarman to a Jain teacher at Kanchi, show Pallava kings still ruling at Kanchipuram before the Kalabhras fell. Their origin is unknown: they have been seen as hill tribes, as Karnatas from the north-west, as the Kallar or Kalappalar of the Tamil country, or as linked to the Muttaraiyar, and they are thought to have favoured Jainism or Buddhism. The period was long called a 'dark age' of Tamil history, but critics point out that the label rests on hostile records written centuries later, and some scholars dismiss the Kalabhra interregnum as practically a myth. Their rule ended in the last quarter of the 6th century, when the Pallava Simhavishnu (c. 575–600) took the country up to the Kaveri and Kadungon (c. 590–620 in Sastri's dating, c. 560–590 in others) revived the Pandya kingdom at Madurai.
empires.legacy: Much of the post-Sangam Tamil literature, including the Tirukkural and the epics Silappatikaram (Jain) and Manimekalai (Buddhist), is commonly dated to these centuries, and some scholars credit Kalabhra patronage of Jain and Buddhist learning for it, though both the dating and the attribution are contested; the Pandya and Pallava kings who followed presented themselves as restorers of the brahmin and Shaiva-Vaishnava order the Kalabhras were said to have overturned.

sources.title: K. A. Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India (1958), pp. 3, 139-140, 144-146 (Internet Archive)
Kasakudi plates of Nandivarman Pallavamalla, SII 2.73 (DHARMA edition)
Jaina Inscriptions in Tamilnadu: Pallankovil plates (jainqq.org)

peak.note: c. 13.7M km² (Taagepera 1997), including vast claimed but thinly settled lands in North and South America, plus the Philippines; c. 13.7M km² (Taagepera 1997)

empires.summary: Spain's empire grew from the union of Castile and Aragon under Isabella and Ferdinand, who in 1492 conquered Granada and sponsored Columbus's first voyage. Within two generations conquistadors toppled the Aztec and Inca empires, and silver from Potosí and Zacatecas paid for Habsburg wars across Europe, where Charles V and Philip II also ruled the Netherlands, much of Italy and, from 1580 to 1640, Portugal. The Americas were run through viceroyalties, royal courts and the Catholic Church, with Indigenous labour forced through the encomienda and mita systems and enslaved Africans shipped in. After Napoleon invaded Spain in 1808, the mainland American colonies won independence by 1825. Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Philippines were lost to the United States in 1898, and the last African holdings were given up by 1976.
empires.legacy: Spanish is now the first language of nearly 500 million people, and Catholic churches, grid-plan towns and legal traditions across the Americas and the Philippines trace back to Spanish rule.

empires.name: Portuguese Empire

peak.note: Nominal extent, mostly Brazil, shortly before its independence in 1822 (10.4M km², Brzezinski 2012); Taagepera (1997), counting only effectively controlled land, gives c. 5.5M km² for 1820

rulers.name: John I

rulers.name: Manuel I
rulers.note: Vasco da Gama reached India and Cabral reached Brazil in his reign

rulers.name: John III
rulers.note: Began the colonisation of Brazil; trade reached Japan

rulers.name: John IV

rulers.name: John VI

rulers.name: António de Oliveira Salazar
rulers.note: Dictator who fought to keep the African colonies

empires.summary: Portugal, a small Atlantic kingdom, began Europe's age of overseas empire when it captured Ceuta in Morocco in 1415. Encouraged by Prince Henry the Navigator, its sailors crept down the African coast until Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498. Rather than conquering large lands, Portugal first built a chain of fortified trading posts from Elmina and Mozambique to Goa, Malacca and Macau, controlling the spice trade with naval power. Brazil, claimed in 1500, became the heart of the empire through sugar, gold and the labour of millions of enslaved Africans. The royal court fled to Rio de Janeiro in 1808, and Brazil became independent in 1822. Portugal clung to Angola, Mozambique and Guinea until a revolution at home in 1974 ended long colonial wars; Macau was returned to China in 1999.
empires.legacy: Portuguese is spoken by some 250 million people on four continents, and the empire's Atlantic slave trade reshaped the populations of Brazil and Africa.

empires.name: British Empire
aliases: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

peak.note: c. 35.5M km² (Taagepera 1997); about a quarter of the world's land and a quarter of its people

rulers.name: Elizabeth I
rulers.note: Her reign saw the first English colonial ventures and the East India Company's charter

rulers.name: George III
rulers.note: Won Canada and India from France but lost the American colonies

rulers.name: Victoria
rulers.note: Empress of India from 1876

rulers.name: George V
rulers.note: Reigned as the empire reached its greatest size

rulers.name: Winston Churchill
rulers.note: Prime minister who led the empire through the Second World War

rulers.name: Elizabeth II
rulers.note: Oversaw decolonisation and the modern Commonwealth

empires.summary: England's overseas expansion began with Atlantic claims and colonies in Virginia, New England and the Caribbean, built by chartered companies, sugar plantations and the slave trade. After union with Scotland in 1707, Britain beat France for North America and India in the Seven Years' War, then lost thirteen colonies in the American Revolution. It rebuilt in Asia, Africa and the Pacific: the East India Company conquered India, convicts and settlers founded Australia, and in the scramble for Africa Britain took Egypt, Nigeria, Kenya and lands from the Cape towards Cairo. Rule ranged from self-governing settler dominions to direct rule and indirect rule through princes and chiefs, all guarded by the Royal Navy. Two world wars drained its strength; India's independence in 1947 began rapid decolonisation, and Hong Kong's return to China in 1997 is often taken as the end.
empires.legacy: English became a global language, and parliamentary government, common law and railways spread with the empire, as did lasting scars from conquest, famine and partition. Most former colonies remain linked through the Commonwealth.

empires.name: French Colonial Empire
clio: French Mandate for Syria and Lebanon

peak.note: c. 11.5M km² (Taagepera 1997); most of it in North, West and Central Africa

rulers.name: Louis XIV
rulers.note: His minister Colbert built up New France, the Caribbean colonies and overseas trade

rulers.name: Louis XV
rulers.note: Lost Canada and most of India to Britain in 1763

rulers.name: Napoleon I
rulers.note: Failed to restore slavery in Saint-Domingue and sold Louisiana in 1803

rulers.note: Prime minister who drove expansion into Tunisia, Indochina and Africa

rulers.name: Charles de Gaulle
rulers.note: President who ended the Algerian War and granted African independence

empires.summary: France's first colonial empire began with Jacques Cartier's voyages to the St Lawrence in 1534 and grew into New France, a vast fur-trading realm reaching down the Mississippi to Louisiana, plus rich sugar islands such as Saint-Domingue worked by enslaved Africans. Defeat by Britain in 1763 cost Canada and most of India, the Haitian Revolution freed Saint-Domingue, and Napoleon sold Louisiana in 1803. A second empire began with the invasion of Algeria in 1830 and spread across West and Equatorial Africa, Madagascar, Indochina and, after 1919, Syria and Lebanon. Paris governed centrally, claiming a civilising mission and assimilating a small educated elite. After the Second World War, defeat in Vietnam in 1954 and a brutal war in Algeria, independent in 1962, brought most colonies to independence; some islands remain parts of France today.
empires.legacy: French is still widely spoken across West and Central Africa, and overseas departments such as Martinique, Guadeloupe and Réunion remain part of France.

empires.name: Dutch Republic and Dutch Colonial Empire
clio: Sovereign Principality of the United Netherlands
empires.capital: Amsterdam (government at The Hague); Batavia in the East Indies

peak.note: c. 2.1M km² (Oxford figure cited in Wikipedia's list; not covered by Taagepera); mostly the Netherlands Indies, today's Indonesia, plus Suriname

rulers.name: Maurice of Nassau
rulers.note: Stadtholder and army reformer during the war with Spain

empires.summary: The Dutch Republic was born when seven northern provinces of the Habsburg Netherlands revolted against Philip II of Spain and renounced his rule in 1581. Its merchants built the most advanced commercial economy of the 17th century, and two chartered firms, the Dutch East India Company (VOC, 1602) and the West India Company (1621), carved out an empire of trade. The VOC seized the Spice Islands from Portugal, founded Batavia (Jakarta) in 1619 and held Ceylon, the Cape and a post at Nagasaki, while the West India Company briefly held northeastern Brazil and New Amsterdam, later New York. After the VOC collapsed in 1799, the Netherlands, a kingdom from 1815, ruled the East Indies directly and forced farmers to grow export crops. Indonesia won independence in 1949 after a war, and Suriname left in 1975.
empires.legacy: Afrikaans, Dutch place names from New York to South Africa, and modern financial tools such as the stock exchange all trace back to the Dutch golden age.

sources.title: World History Encyclopedia: Dutch East India Company

empires.name: Belgium and the Belgian Congo

empires.summary: Belgium broke away from the Netherlands in 1830 and became a constitutional kingdom under Leopold I. His son Leopold II, eager for a colony, used explorers and a front of humanitarian societies to win international recognition at the Berlin Conference of 1884–85 for the Congo Free State, which he owned personally. Its rubber and ivory profits were extracted through forced labour, hostage-taking and mutilation, and millions died from violence, famine and disease. International outrage forced Belgium to annex the territory as the Belgian Congo in 1908. The state, the Catholic Church and mining companies then ran it as a paternalist colony that allowed Africans almost no higher education. After the First World War Belgium also governed Ruanda-Urundi. Congo became independent in 1960, and Rwanda and Burundi in 1962.
empires.legacy: The Congo Free State became a worldwide symbol of colonial atrocity, and its exploitation shaped the troubled history of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

empires.name: Habsburg Monarchy (Austrian Empire, Austria-Hungary)

peak.note: c.; Austria-Hungary was c. 622,000 km² in 1905 (Encyclopaedia Britannica 1911), plus Bosnia-Herzegovina (c. 51,000 km²), annexed in 1908

rulers.note: Gained Bohemia and Hungary after Mohács; Holy Roman Emperor from 1556

empires.summary: The Austrian Habsburgs, Holy Roman Emperors almost continuously since 1438, became a great power when Archduke Ferdinand I inherited the crowns of Bohemia and Hungary after the Battle of Mohács in 1526. Their multinational realm, ruled from Vienna, held off the Ottomans at the sieges of 1529 and 1683 and then reconquered Hungary. Maria Theresa and her son Joseph II reformed the army, taxes and schools, while wars with Prussia cost them Silesia. Francis I declared an Austrian Empire in 1804 and dissolved the Holy Roman Empire in 1806. Defeat by Prussia in 1866 led to the Compromise of 1867, creating Austria-Hungary, a dual monarchy of two governments under one emperor. Rising nationalism among Czechs, Poles, Serbs and others strained it, and after defeat in the First World War it broke apart in 1918.
empires.legacy: Vienna's music and architecture flowered under the Habsburgs, and the successor states of Central Europe, from Czechoslovakia to Yugoslavia, were drawn from the empire's ruins.

empires.name: Tsardom of Russia and Russian Empire

peak.note: c. 22.8M km² (Taagepera 1997; Turchin, Adams & Hall 2006), after the conquest of Central Asia; Alaska had been sold in 1867

rulers.name: Ivan IV, the Terrible
rulers.note: First crowned tsar; conquered Kazan and Astrakhan

rulers.name: Michael I
rulers.note: First Romanov tsar, after the Time of Troubles

rulers.name: Peter I, the Great
rulers.note: Westernised the state and proclaimed the Russian Empire in 1721

rulers.name: Catherine II, the Great
rulers.note: Annexed Crimea and much of Poland

rulers.name: Alexander I
rulers.note: Defeated Napoleon's invasion of 1812

rulers.name: Alexander II
rulers.note: Freed the serfs in 1861; assassinated

rulers.name: Nicholas II
rulers.note: Last tsar, forced to abdicate in 1917

empires.summary: Moscow's grand princes threw off Mongol overlordship and gathered the Russian lands, and in 1547 Ivan IV, the Terrible, was crowned the first Tsar of All Russia. His conquest of Kazan and Astrakhan opened the Volga, and Cossacks and fur traders crossed Siberia to reach the Pacific by 1639. After the chaotic Time of Troubles, the Romanov dynasty took power in 1613. Peter the Great built a modern army and navy, founded St Petersburg and proclaimed the Russian Empire in 1721; Catherine the Great added Crimea, the Black Sea steppe and much of Poland. In the 19th century Russia took Finland, the Caucasus and Central Asia. The tsars ruled as autocrats over a peasant majority, most of them serfs until 1861. Defeats and hardship in the First World War led to revolution in 1917 and the end of the monarchy.
empires.legacy: Russia became the largest country on Earth, and the expansion that brought dozens of peoples under Moscow's rule still shapes politics from the Baltic to the Pacific.

empires.name: Soviet Union (USSR)

peak.note: About one-sixth of the world's land surface; official area 22.4M km²; Taagepera (1997) gives c. 22.3M km² for 1945

rulers.name: Vladimir Lenin
rulers.note: Led the Bolshevik Revolution and headed the Soviet government from 1917

rulers.name: Joseph Stalin
rulers.note: Dictator of forced collectivisation, purges and victory over Nazi Germany

rulers.name: Nikita Khrushchev
rulers.note: Denounced Stalin; Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962

rulers.name: Leonid Brezhnev
rulers.note: Era of stability and later stagnation

rulers.name: Mikhail Gorbachev
rulers.note: His reforms, glasnost and perestroika, preceded the union's collapse

empires.summary: The Soviet Union grew out of the October Revolution of 1917, when Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power in Petrograd and then won a brutal civil war. In 1922 Russia, Ukraine, Belarus and the Transcaucasian republics formed the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, a one-party state run by the Communist Party from Moscow. Under Stalin it forced peasants into collective farms, industrialised at terrible human cost and sent millions to Gulag labour camps. Invaded by Nazi Germany in 1941, it lost around 27 million people but drove on to Berlin, then dominated Eastern Europe through allied communist regimes. It rivalled the United States in the Cold War, launching the first satellite and the first human into space. Economic stagnation, Gorbachev's reforms and nationalist movements led to its breakup into fifteen independent states in December 1991.
empires.legacy: The Cold War rivalry it led divided the world for four decades, and Russian remains a common language across its fifteen successor states.

empires.name: Russian Federation

peak.note: The largest country on Earth; c. 17.1M km² (Taagepera 1997)

rulers.name: Boris Yeltsin
rulers.note: First president; led the shift to a market economy

rulers.name: Vladimir Putin
rulers.note: Recentralised power; prime minister 2008–2012

rulers.name: Dmitry Medvedev
rulers.note: President while Putin served as prime minister

empires.summary: The Russian Federation emerged as the main successor of the Soviet Union when it dissolved in December 1991, inheriting its seat on the UN Security Council, its nuclear arsenal and about three-quarters of its territory. Under Boris Yeltsin the country moved rapidly toward a market economy, but hasty privatisation enriched a small group of oligarchs while many people lost savings and jobs; a financial crisis struck in 1998, and wars were fought against separatists in Chechnya. Vladimir Putin, president from 2000, used high oil and gas revenues to restore central control, curbing independent media and political opposition. Russia fought Georgia in 2008, annexed Crimea from Ukraine in 2014 and launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, provoking sweeping Western sanctions.
empires.legacy: Still the largest country on Earth, spanning eleven time zones, Russia remains a major energy exporter and nuclear power.

empires.name: Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth

peak.note: c. 1.0M km² after the Truce of Deulino with Russia (1618–19); Taagepera (1997) gives c. 1.1M km² for 1650

empires.summary: The Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania had shared monarchs since 1386, and in 1569 the Union of Lublin merged them into a single Commonwealth with one parliament, the Sejm. It was unusual for its time: kings were elected by the whole nobility, the szlachta, who made up nearly a tenth of the population, and the Warsaw Confederation of 1573 guaranteed religious toleration. At its height it stretched from the Baltic almost to the Black Sea, and its army occupied Moscow in 1610. But the liberum veto, which let a single deputy block legislation, paralysed government, and the wars of the mid-17th century, known as the Deluge, devastated it. Weakened, it was carved up by Russia, Prussia and Austria in three partitions in 1772, 1793 and 1795, despite the reforming Constitution of 3 May 1791.
empires.legacy: Its 1791 constitution is often called the first modern written constitution in Europe, and memories of the Commonwealth inspired later Polish and Lithuanian nationalism.

empires.summary: Sweden left the Danish-led Kalmar Union under Gustav Vasa in 1523, and his heirs built a strong, Lutheran, centralised state rich in iron and copper. Gustavus Adolphus turned it into a great power: his reformed army won stunning victories in the Thirty Years' War, and by the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 Sweden held lands around the Baltic in Finland, Estonia, Livonia, Pomerania and Bremen. Charles X Gustav took Scania and other provinces from Denmark in 1658, and Sweden briefly had a colony on the Delaware River. With a small population stretched thin, the empire could not survive a coalition of Russia, Denmark and Saxony in the Great Northern War; Charles XII was crushed at Poltava in 1709, and the Treaty of Nystad in 1721 ended Swedish dominance. Finland was lost to Russia in 1809.
empires.legacy: Sweden's century as a great power left an efficient state administration, and after losing its empire it turned toward the neutrality and prosperity it later became known for.

empires.summary: When the Kalmar Union fell apart after Sweden broke away in 1523, Denmark kept Norway, and in 1537 Christian III made Norway a dependency ruled from Copenhagen, along with Iceland, the Faroe Islands and claims to Greenland. The twin realms controlled the Sound, the narrow strait into the Baltic, and collected rich tolls from passing ships. Christian IV built towns and fortresses but lost wars to Sweden, and in 1658 Denmark gave up Scania, Halland and Blekinge for good. In 1660 Frederick III became an absolute hereditary monarch. Denmark-Norway also held trading posts in India and on the Gold Coast, and the Danish West Indies, where enslaved Africans grew sugar. Siding with Napoleon proved disastrous: after his defeat, the Treaty of Kiel in 1814 handed Norway to Sweden.
empires.legacy: Greenland and the Faroe Islands are still linked to Denmark, and written Norwegian long remained close to Danish.

empires.summary: Prussia became a duchy in 1525, when Albert of Hohenzollern, Grand Master of the Teutonic Knights, turned Lutheran and secularised their lands. In 1618 it passed to his relatives, the electors of Brandenburg, and Frederick William the Great Elector forged their scattered territories into a disciplined state with a standing army. His son crowned himself King in Prussia in 1701. Frederick William I enlarged the army further, and Frederick the Great seized Silesia from Austria, survived the Seven Years' War and took a share of partitioned Poland. Crushed by Napoleon in 1806, Prussia reformed and gained the Rhineland in 1815. Under Bismarck it defeated Denmark, Austria and France, and in 1871 its king became German Emperor. Prussia lived on as the largest German state until the Allies abolished it in 1947.
empires.legacy: Prussia's efficient bureaucracy, compulsory schooling and general staff were widely copied, though its militarism is often blamed for Germany's path to war.

empires.summary: The German Empire was proclaimed at Versailles in January 1871, after Prussia under Otto von Bismarck defeated France and united the German states except Austria. It quickly became Europe's leading industrial and scientific power and gained colonies in Africa and the Pacific, where a rising in German South West Africa was crushed in the genocide of the Herero and Nama. Kaiser Wilhelm II's ambitions helped bring on the First World War, and defeat in 1918 brought the Weimar Republic. Economic crisis let Adolf Hitler's Nazis take power in 1933; their dictatorship murdered six million Jews in the Holocaust and launched the Second World War, which ended in total defeat in 1945. Germany was split into four occupation zones, then into West and East Germany in 1949, and was peacefully reunited in 1990.
empires.legacy: Reunited Germany is Europe's largest economy and a founding member of the European Union, and its reckoning with the Nazi past is often cited as a model of remembrance.

empires.summary: For centuries Italy was divided among rival states and foreign powers. In the Risorgimento, or resurgence, the Kingdom of Sardinia, ruled by the House of Savoy from Turin, led unification: its prime minister Cavour allied with France against Austria in 1859, Garibaldi's volunteers conquered the south in 1860, and Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed King of Italy in 1861. Venice followed in 1866 and Rome in 1870, becoming the capital. Italy took colonies in Eritrea, Somalia and Libya and gained Trieste and South Tyrol after the First World War. Benito Mussolini's Fascists ruled from 1922, conquered Ethiopia in 1936 and joined Hitler in the Second World War, which ended in defeat and the loss of all colonies. A referendum in 1946 abolished the monarchy and created the Italian Republic.
empires.legacy: Italy became a founding member of the European Community and one of the world's largest economies, though the gap between its industrial north and poorer south dates back to unification.

empires.summary: The Republic of Turkey rose from the ruins of the Ottoman Empire after the First World War. When the Allies occupied Istanbul and planned to partition Anatolia, Mustafa Kemal led a nationalist war of independence from Ankara, defeating Greek, Armenian and French forces. The Treaty of Lausanne in 1923 recognised Turkey's borders, followed by a vast population exchange with Greece, and the republic was proclaimed that October. Kemal, later named Atatürk, abolished the sultanate and caliphate, replaced Islamic law with European-style codes, adopted the Latin alphabet and gave women the vote. A one-party state until 1950, Turkey then became a multiparty democracy, interrupted by military coups in 1960, 1971 and 1980. It joined NATO in 1952 and became a regional power bridging Europe and the Middle East.
empires.legacy: Atatürk's secular reforms reshaped Turkish society, and the tension between secular nationalism and religious politics still defines Turkish public life.

empires.name: Mughal Empire
empires.capital: Agra, Fatehpur Sikri, Lahore and Delhi at different times

empires.summary: Babur, a Central Asian prince descended from both Timur and Genghis Khan, invaded India and defeated the Delhi Sultanate at Panipat in 1526. His son Humayun lost the throne to Sher Shah Suri but regained it in 1555. Humayun's son Akbar built a lasting empire through conquest and alliances with Rajput kings, a ranked nobility of mansabdars and a revenue system based on surveyed land, and he promoted dialogue among religions. Under Jahangir and Shah Jahan, who built the Taj Mahal, the court was among the richest in the world. Aurangzeb pushed the empire to its greatest size in the Deccan but exhausted it in endless wars. After his death in 1707 provincial governors, Marathas, Sikhs and the British carved it up, and the British deposed the last emperor after the rebellion of 1857.
empires.legacy: Mughal architecture, painting, cuisine and the Urdu language left a deep mark on South Asian culture, from the Taj Mahal to Delhi's Red Fort.

empires.summary: The Safavids began as leaders of a Sufi order in Ardabil whose Turkmen followers, the Qizilbash or red heads, revered them. In 1501 the young Ismail I captured Tabriz and declared himself shah, and he made Twelver Shia Islam the state religion, gradually converting a largely Sunni Iran. Defeat by the Ottomans at Chaldiran in 1514 began a long frontier rivalry. Shah Abbas the Great rebuilt the state, creating an army of slave soldiers loyal to the crown, recovering lands from the Ottomans and Uzbeks, and making Isfahan a magnificent capital of mosques, bridges and bazaars that traded silk with Europe and India. Later shahs were weaker and more secluded, and in 1722 Afghan invaders captured Isfahan. The general Nader, who drove the Afghans out, ended the dynasty by crowning himself shah in 1736.
empires.legacy: The Safavids gave Iran its Shia identity and much of its modern territory, and Isfahan's Naqsh-e Jahan Square remains a masterpiece of Islamic architecture.

empires.summary: After the Safavids fell, the general Nader crowned himself shah in 1736 and briefly built a vast empire, sacking Delhi in 1739, but it fell apart after his murder in 1747, and Karim Khan Zand then ruled most of Iran from Shiraz. Agha Mohammad Khan, chief of the Turkic Qajar tribe, then defeated his rivals, made Tehran his capital in 1786 and was crowned shah in 1796. His successors lost Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan to Russia by 1828, while Britain and Russia competed for influence and concessions. The Constitutional Revolution of 1905–1911 created Iran's first parliament. In 1925 the army officer Reza Khan founded the Pahlavi dynasty, modernising the country by force, and in 1935 Persia officially became Iran abroad. His son Mohammad Reza Shah, backed by the West and oil wealth, was overthrown in the Islamic Revolution of 1979.
empires.legacy: Iran's modern borders, its capital at Tehran and its tradition of popular protest against foreign influence took shape under these two dynasties.

empires.capital: Raigad, then Satara; Pune under the Peshwas

empires.summary: The Marathas, Marathi-speaking warriors of the western Deccan hills, rose under Shivaji, who used hill forts and swift guerrilla raids to carve a kingdom out of the Bijapur sultanate and the Mughal Empire, crowning himself Chhatrapati in 1674. They survived Aurangzeb's long war against them, and from 1713 real power passed to hereditary chief ministers, the Peshwas, ruling from Pune. Peshwa Baji Rao I led cavalry far into the north, and by the 1750s Maratha armies collected tribute from Delhi to Bengal and the far south. Their advance was checked by the Afghan Ahmad Shah Durrani at the third battle of Panipat in 1761. The realm then became a confederacy of powerful chiefs, the Scindias, Holkars, Gaekwads and Bhonsles, who fought the British East India Company in three wars and were finally defeated in 1818.
empires.legacy: The Marathas ended Mughal supremacy and were India's last great indigenous power before British rule; Shivaji remains a hero in Maharashtra.

empires.summary: The Sikh faith, founded by Guru Nanak in Punjab around 1500, was forged into a martial brotherhood, the Khalsa, by Guru Gobind Singh in 1699. As Mughal power collapsed in the 18th century, Sikh bands fought both the Mughals and Afghan invaders and divided Punjab among a dozen confederacies called misls. Ranjit Singh, leader of the Sukerchakia misl, captured Lahore in 1799 and was proclaimed Maharaja of Punjab in 1801. He united the misls, built a modern army trained partly by European officers, and conquered Multan, Kashmir and Peshawar, ruling Sikhs, Muslims and Hindus with notable tolerance. After his death in 1839, court intrigue and a rapid succession of rulers weakened the state. The British East India Company defeated it in two Anglo-Sikh wars and annexed Punjab in 1849.
empires.legacy: Ranjit Singh's kingdom is remembered as a golden age of Sikh power, and the Koh-i-Noor diamond, taken by the British in 1849, is still claimed by several countries.

empires.summary: When Nader Shah of Iran was assassinated in 1747, Ahmad Khan Abdali, a commander of his Afghan cavalry, was chosen king by a tribal council near Kandahar and took the title Durr-i-Durran, Pearl of Pearls. Uniting the Pashtun tribes, he built an empire stretching from Mashhad to Kashmir and Punjab, raiding Mughal India repeatedly and crushing the Marathas at Panipat in 1761. His son Timur Shah moved the capital to Kabul. Rivalry among Ahmad Shah's grandsons broke the empire apart in the early 1800s, as the Sikhs took Punjab and Kashmir, and power passed to the Barakzai family under Dost Mohammad Khan. Afghanistan survived two wars with Britain and became a buffer between the British and Russian empires, which fixed its borders in the 1880s and 1890s.
empires.legacy: Ahmad Shah Durrani is honoured as the father of modern Afghanistan, and his empire defined the Pashtun-led state that followed.

empires.summary: The English East India Company began as a trading firm with posts at Surat, Madras, Bombay and Calcutta. As Mughal power waned, its victory at Plassey in 1757 made it master of Bengal, and over the next century it conquered or subordinated most of the subcontinent, ruling through armies of Indian sepoys and alliances with princes. The great rebellion of 1857 led the British Crown to take direct control in 1858, and Queen Victoria became Empress of India in 1876. The Raj, governed by a viceroy and the Indian Civil Service, built railways and universities but drained wealth and presided over deadly famines. The Indian National Congress, and from the 1920s Gandhi's mass non-violent campaigns, pressed for self-rule. In 1947 Britain withdrew, partitioning the Raj into India and Pakistan amid terrible violence.
empires.legacy: Railways, the English language and parliamentary institutions remain from the Raj, as does the bitter legacy of partition between India and Pakistan.

empires.summary: Independent India was born at midnight on 15 August 1947, when British rule ended and the subcontinent was partitioned, displacing some 15 million people. Jawaharlal Nehru became prime minister, while Vallabhbhai Patel persuaded or forced over 500 princely states to join the new nation. The constitution of 1950, drafted under B. R. Ambedkar, created a secular, federal parliamentary democracy with universal suffrage. India fought wars with Pakistan and China, absorbed Goa from Portugal in 1961 and Sikkim in 1975, and followed a planned, largely state-led economy and a foreign policy of non-alignment. Democracy was suspended only once, during Indira Gandhi's Emergency of 1975–77. Economic liberalisation from 1991 brought rapid growth, and India tested nuclear weapons in 1974 and 1998.
empires.legacy: India is the world's most populous country and largest democracy, with nearly a billion eligible voters.

empires.summary: Pakistan was created on 14 August 1947 as a homeland for the Muslims of British India, the goal of Muhammad Ali Jinnah and the Muslim League. It began in two wings, West and East Pakistan, separated by about 1,600 km of Indian territory, and partition brought mass migration and violence. War with India over Kashmir broke out at once and recurred in 1965. Pakistan became an Islamic republic in 1956 but was often ruled by the army, under Ayub Khan, Yahya Khan and later Zia-ul-Haq. Resentment in the Bengali-speaking east over political and economic domination led to a brutal war in 1971 and, with Indian help, the independence of Bangladesh. Zulfikar Ali Bhutto and later his daughter Benazir led civilian governments between periods of military rule.
empires.legacy: Pakistan became a nuclear power in 1998, and its unresolved dispute with India over Kashmir remains one of the world's most dangerous rivalries.

sources.title: Majumdar (ed.), The History and Culture of the Indian People, vol. XI: Struggle for Freedom (Internet Archive)

empires.name: Saudi State (Diriyah, Nejd, Saudi Arabia)

peak.note: c. 2.15M km²; about four-fifths of the Arabian Peninsula

empires.summary: In 1744 the emir of the oasis town of Diriyah, Muhammad bin Saud, allied with the reforming preacher Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab, joining political power to a strict form of Sunni Islam. This First Saudi State conquered most of Arabia, including Mecca and Medina, until an Egyptian army sent on behalf of the Ottomans destroyed Diriyah in 1818. A smaller Second Saudi State ruled from Riyadh from 1824 until its rivals, the Rashidis, took over in 1891. In 1902 the young Abdulaziz ibn Saud recaptured Riyadh, then conquered Nejd, the Hasa coast, the Rashidi lands and, in 1924–25, the Hejaz with the holy cities. In 1932 he renamed his realm the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. Oil, found in 1938, made it one of the world's richest states, an absolute monarchy ruled by his sons.
empires.legacy: As guardian of Mecca and Medina and holder of vast oil reserves, Saudi Arabia wields great influence over the Muslim world and global energy markets.

empires.name: Kazakh Khanate

peak.note: Rough estimate under Kasym Khan, when the Kazakhs controlled nearly the whole eastern steppe; steppe borders were fluid and no scholarly area figure was found

empires.summary: Around 1465 the Chinggisid princes Kerei and Janibek led their followers away from the Uzbek khan Abu'l-Khayr and settled in the Chu valley; these nomads became known as Kazakhs, roughly meaning free wanderers. Under Kasym Khan in the early 1500s the khanate grew into a powerful steppe confederation stretching from the Syr Darya towards the Irtysh, its herders moving seasonally with sheep, horses and camels. It later divided into three hordes, or zhuz: the Senior, Middle and Junior. Devastating invasions by the Dzungars in the early 18th century, remembered as the Years of Great Disaster, led the Junior and then the Middle horde to accept Russian protection from 1731. Russia abolished the khans' powers between the 1820s and 1840s, and the last khan, Kenesary, died fighting in 1847.
empires.legacy: The khanate is regarded as the foundation of Kazakh nationhood, and independent Kazakhstan celebrated its 550th anniversary in 2015.

empires.summary: The Crimean Khanate broke away from the disintegrating Golden Horde in 1441 under Hacı Giray, founder of a dynasty descended from Genghis Khan that ruled for over three centuries from Bakhchysarai. In 1475 it became a vassal of the Ottoman Empire, which held the southern coast, yet the khans kept wide freedom and a powerful cavalry. For two centuries Crimean raiders swept into Poland-Lithuania and Russia, carrying off hundreds of thousands of captives for the slave markets of Kaffa and Istanbul, and in 1571 Devlet Giray burned Moscow. As Russia grew stronger it pushed south, and the Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca in 1774 made the khanate independent of the Ottomans, in practice a Russian client. Catherine the Great annexed it in 1783.
empires.legacy: The Crimean Tatars are the khanate's descendants; deported en masse by Stalin in 1944, they were able to return only after 1989.

empires.summary: In 1500 the Uzbek leader Muhammad Shaybani, a descendant of Genghis Khan, swept down from the steppe and conquered Timurid Transoxiana, taking Samarkand and Bukhara. His Shaybanid heirs made Bukhara their capital, and under Abdullah Khan II in the late 1500s the khanate reached Herat, Mashhad and Badakhshan. Power passed to the Janid, or Ashtarkhanid, dynasty around 1600, and later to the Manghit family, whose rulers took the Islamic title of emir in 1785. Bukhara was a great centre of Islamic learning, with scores of madrasas, and a hub of the caravan trade, though it competed constantly with Khiva, Kokand and Iran. Russian armies defeated it in 1868, making it a protectorate, and the Red Army overthrew the last emir in 1920.
empires.legacy: Bukhara's old city, rich in mosques and madrasas, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the khanate's lands form the core of modern Uzbekistan.

empires.capital: Nizwa and Rustaq under the Yaruba imams; Muscat from 1792; Zanzibar became the sultan's main seat in the 1830s–1840

empires.summary: In 1650 Imam Sultan bin Saif of the Yaruba dynasty drove the Portuguese out of Muscat, and Omani fleets went on to seize Portuguese strongholds on the East African coast, taking Fort Jesus at Mombasa in 1698. Under the Al Said dynasty, founded by Ahmad bin Said in 1744, Oman built a maritime trading empire across the western Indian Ocean. Said bin Sultan moved his main court to Zanzibar around 1840, where clove plantations worked by enslaved Africans and the caravan trade in ivory and slaves made the island rich. After his death in 1856 his sons split the realm into the Sultanate of Zanzibar and the Sultanate of Muscat and Oman, both increasingly under British influence. Zanzibar's sultan was overthrown in a revolution in 1964, while the Al Said dynasty continued to rule Oman.
empires.legacy: Swahili coastal culture still bears Omani influence, and the Al Said dynasty rules Oman to this day.

empires.summary: When the Qing dynasty collapsed in 1911, Mongol princes in Urga declared independence and made the Buddhist leader Jebtsundamba Khutuktu their ruler, the Bogd Khan. Chinese troops reoccupied the country in 1919, but in February 1921 the White Russian warlord Baron Ungern-Sternberg drove them from Urga, and Mongolian revolutionaries led by Damdin Sükhbaatar, aided by the Soviet Red Army, then expelled him and entered Urga in July. After the Bogd Khan died, the Mongolian People's Republic was declared in 1924, the world's second communist state. Under Khorloogiin Choibalsan, purges in the late 1930s killed tens of thousands of people, including many Buddhist monks, and most monasteries were destroyed. Mongolia remained a close Soviet ally, and China recognised its independence in 1946. Peaceful protests in 1990 brought multiparty democracy and a market economy.
empires.legacy: Mongolia built one of Asia's most stable post-communist democracies and has revived Genghis Khan as a national symbol.

empires.summary: The Qing were founded by the Manchus, Jurchen peoples of the northeast united by Nurhaci, whose son Hong Taiji proclaimed the Qing dynasty in 1636. When rebels toppled the Ming in 1644, Manchu armies entered Beijing and went on to conquer all of China, forcing Chinese men to adopt the Manchu queue hairstyle. The Kangxi, Yongzheng and Qianlong emperors ruled for over a century of prosperity, roughly doubling the empire's size by conquering Taiwan, Mongolia, Xinjiang and Tibet, and the population soared past 300 million. In the 19th century the empire was battered by the Opium Wars with Britain, the Taiping Rebellion, which killed perhaps 20 million people, and defeat by Japan in 1895. Reforms came too late: the 1911 revolution forced the child emperor Puyi to abdicate in 1912, ending over two thousand years of imperial rule.
empires.legacy: The borders of modern China, including Tibet, Xinjiang and Inner Mongolia, largely follow those the Qing conquered.

empires.summary: The Republic of China was founded on 1 January 1912 after the revolution against the Qing, with Sun Yat-sen as provisional president. Power soon passed to the general Yuan Shikai, and after his death in 1916 China fragmented among rival warlords. Sun's Nationalist Party, the Kuomintang, rebuilt in the south, and in 1926–28 Chiang Kai-shek's Northern Expedition reunited much of the country under a government in Nanjing. Chiang fought both the Communists and, from 1937, a full-scale Japanese invasion that killed millions. After Japan's defeat the civil war resumed, and in 1949 the Communists won the mainland. Chiang's government retreated to Taiwan, which it ruled under martial law until 1987. Under Chiang Ching-kuo and Lee Teng-hui, Taiwan became a prosperous democracy.
empires.legacy: The Republic of China survives on Taiwan, a high-tech economy whose status remains one of the most sensitive questions in world politics.

empires.summary: Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic of China in Beijing on 1 October 1949, after the Communist Party won the civil war. The new state took control of Tibet in 1950–51, fought the United States in Korea and carried out land reform and Soviet-style planning. Mao's Great Leap Forward of 1958–62 caused a famine that killed tens of millions, and his Cultural Revolution of 1966–76 unleashed a decade of persecution and chaos. After his death, Deng Xiaoping began reform and opening in 1978, allowing family farming, foreign investment and markets while keeping one-party rule, which was violently reasserted at Tiananmen Square in 1989. Hong Kong and Macau returned to Chinese rule in 1997 and 1999. Decades of rapid growth lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty and made China the world's second-largest economy.
empires.legacy: China is once again a great power, a manufacturing centre for the world and a rival to the United States in technology and influence.

empires.capital: Edo (Tokyo); the emperor stayed in Kyoto

empires.summary: After a century of civil war in the Sengoku, or Warring States, period, Japan was reunited by Oda Nobunaga and Toyotomi Hideyoshi. When Hideyoshi died, Tokugawa Ieyasu defeated his rivals at Sekigahara in 1600, and in 1603 the emperor named him shogun. From Edo, the Tokugawa shoguns ruled through about 260 domain lords, the daimyo, who had to spend alternate years in Edo, while the emperor remained a figurehead in Kyoto. Christianity was banned, and from the 1630s foreign trade was restricted to the Dutch and Chinese at Nagasaki. Two and a half centuries of peace brought growing cities, a wealthy merchant class and arts such as kabuki and woodblock prints. The arrival of Commodore Perry's American warships in 1853 forced Japan open, and in 1867–68 the last shogun surrendered power to the emperor.
empires.legacy: The long Tokugawa peace created the urban, literate society that let Japan modernise so rapidly after 1868.

empires.name: Empire of Japan

empires.summary: In the Meiji Restoration of 1868, reformers overthrew the shogunate in the name of Emperor Meiji and set out to modernise Japan so it could resist the Western powers. They abolished the samurai class, built railways, factories and a conscript army, and adopted a constitution in 1889. Japan defeated China in 1895, taking Taiwan, and stunned the world by defeating Russia in 1905; it annexed Korea in 1910. Militarists gained control in the 1930s, seizing Manchuria in 1931 and invading China in 1937. After attacking Pearl Harbor in December 1941, Japan overran Southeast Asia and the western Pacific, committing widespread atrocities. Following the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, Japan surrendered in 1945. Under American occupation a new constitution in 1947 made the emperor a symbol and renounced war.
empires.legacy: Postwar Japan rebuilt into one of the world's largest economies, while memories of its wartime empire still strain relations with China and Korea.

empires.summary: After Ayutthaya fell in 1767, the general Taksin drove out the Burmese and ruled from Thonburi. In 1782 his general Chao Phraya Chakri took the throne as Rama I, founding the Chakri dynasty and a new capital at Bangkok across the river; the period is named Rattanakosin after its royal island. The kingdom extended its rule over Laos, western Cambodia and northern Malay sultanates. Kings Mongkut and Chulalongkorn modernised Siam, signing trade treaties, abolishing slavery and building railways and ministries, and skilfully played Britain and France against each other, so that Siam alone in Southeast Asia escaped colonisation, though it ceded outlying lands. A revolution in 1932 ended absolute monarchy, and the country was renamed Thailand in 1939. Military governments alternated with elected ones, while King Bhumibol reigned for seventy years.
empires.legacy: Thailand is the only Southeast Asian country never colonised by a European power, and the Chakri dynasty still reigns.

empires.summary: The Toungoo dynasty began in the small principality of Taungoo, which grew strong as refugees fled wars elsewhere in Burma. King Tabinshwehti, from 1530, united Upper and Lower Burma and took the Mon port of Pegu, using Portuguese mercenaries and firearms. His brother-in-law Bayinnaung built the largest empire in the history of Southeast Asia, subduing the Shan states, Manipur, Lan Na, Lan Xang and Ayutthaya, which he took in 1569. It was held together by personal loyalty and could not survive him: under Nanda Bayin it collapsed by 1599. Anaukpetlun and Thalun rebuilt a smaller, sturdier kingdom, and the capital moved to Ava in 1635. Weakened by Manipuri raids and a Mon rebellion, the restored kingdom fell when the Mons captured Ava in 1752.
empires.legacy: The Toungoo kings laid the foundations of a unified Burmese state, and Bayinnaung is still celebrated as one of Myanmar's greatest rulers.

sources.title: D. G. E. Hall, A History of South-East Asia, 4th ed. (1981), archive.org

empires.summary: When Mon forces sacked Ava in 1752, a village chief named Aung Zeya rallied resistance, took the royal name Alaungpaya and reunified Burma within a decade. His sons were formidable conquerors: Hsinbyushin destroyed Ayutthaya in 1767 and beat back four Qing invasions, and Bodawpaya annexed Arakan in 1785, after which Burmese armies pushed into Manipur and Assam. That advance brought Burma into conflict with British India. Three Anglo-Burmese wars followed; in 1826 Burma lost Assam, Arakan and Tenasserim, and in 1852 Lower Burma with Rangoon. King Mindon tried to modernise from his new capital at Mandalay, but in 1885 Britain seized the rest of the kingdom and exiled King Thibaw to India. Burma was ruled as part of British India until 1937 and became independent in 1948.
empires.legacy: The Konbaung kings unified the lands that make up modern Myanmar, and Mandalay's royal city remains a symbol of Burmese independence.

sources.title: D. G. E. Hall, A History of South-East Asia, 4th ed. (1981), archive.org

empires.summary: Malacca was founded around 1400 by Parameswara, a prince from Palembang in Sumatra, who settled at a fishing village on the strait between Sumatra and the Malay peninsula. By seeking the protection of Ming China, whose admiral Zheng He visited several times, the young port escaped Siamese control. Its rulers converted to Islam, and Malacca became the busiest trading hub in Southeast Asia, where merchants from Gujarat, China, Java and the Spice Islands exchanged cloth, spices and porcelain under efficient harbour officials. Under the long-serving chief minister Tun Perak the sultanate expanded along both shores of the strait. Its wealth drew the Portuguese, who captured the city in 1511; Sultan Mahmud Shah fled, and his heirs founded the sultanates of Johor and Perak.
empires.legacy: Malacca helped spread Islam and the Malay language across maritime Southeast Asia, and its court is remembered as the model of classical Malay kingship.

sources.title: D. G. E. Hall, A History of South-East Asia, 4th ed. (1981), archive.org

empires.summary: Indonesian nationalists Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta declared independence on 17 August 1945, two days after Japan surrendered and ended its wartime occupation of the Dutch East Indies. The Netherlands fought to return, but after four years of war and diplomacy, and American pressure, it transferred sovereignty in 1949; western New Guinea followed in 1963. Sukarno led a turbulent young nation of thousands of islands and hundreds of ethnic groups, united by the Indonesian language and the state philosophy of Pancasila. After a failed coup in 1965, the army under Suharto oversaw the killing of hundreds of thousands of alleged communists and took power. Suharto's New Order brought economic growth but also corruption and the invasion of East Timor in 1975. The Asian financial crisis toppled him in 1998, opening the way to democracy.
empires.legacy: Indonesia is the world's largest Muslim-majority country and its third-largest democracy.

empires.summary: The Songhai people had long been based around Gao on the Niger River, for a time as tributaries of the Mali Empire. Sonni Ali, ruling from 1464, broke free and conquered Timbuktu in 1468 and then Djenné with powerful cavalry and a river fleet, building one of the largest empires in African history. His successor Askia Muhammad, a devout Muslim, seized the throne in 1493, made the pilgrimage to Mecca and organised provinces under appointed governors, with a professional army and standard weights and measures. Timbuktu flourished as a centre of Islamic scholarship and of the trans-Saharan trade in gold, salt and slaves. Succession struggles weakened the Askias, and in 1591 an army sent by the Moroccan sultan Ahmad al-Mansur, armed with guns, defeated Songhai at the battle of Tondibi. Songhai remnants held out to the south.
empires.legacy: The manuscripts and mosques of Timbuktu and Gao recall a golden age of African scholarship, and the Songhai language is still spoken along the middle Niger.

empires.name: Sokoto Caliphate

peak.note: About; a federation of some 30 emirates. Estimates range from c. 400,000 km² (Wesseling) to c. 488,500 km² (Wikipedia, 1900)

empires.summary: In 1804 Usman dan Fodio, a Fulani Islamic scholar who preached against the corruption of the Hausa kings, declared a jihad in what is now northern Nigeria. His followers overthrew most Hausa states within a few years, creating a vast caliphate of emirates such as Kano, Zaria and Adamawa. His son Muhammad Bello founded Sokoto as the capital in 1809 and ruled as caliph, while Usman's daughter Nana Asma'u, a poet and teacher, spread education among women. Each emirate was governed by an emir loyal to the caliph, sending tribute and troops. The caliphate fostered Islamic learning but also relied heavily on slave raiding and slave plantations. In 1903 British forces under Frederick Lugard captured Kano and Sokoto, and Britain then ruled the emirates indirectly through their emirs within the Protectorate of Northern Nigeria.
empires.legacy: The Sultan of Sokoto remains the spiritual leader of Nigeria's Muslims, and the emirate system still shapes northern Nigerian society.

empires.name: Zulu Kingdom

peak.note: c.; the core kingdom under Shaka, whose influence reached much further: Gluckman (1960) put the area he dominated by 1822 at about 80,000 sq mi (c. 207,000 km²)

empires.summary: The Zulu were a small Nguni chiefdom until Shaka seized power in 1816 with the backing of the Mthethwa leader Dingiswayo. He reorganised fighting men into disciplined age-grade regiments armed with short stabbing spears and large shields, and used encircling horns of the buffalo tactics to absorb neighbouring peoples, amid the wars and migrations known as the Mfecane. Shaka was assassinated in 1828 by his half-brother Dingane, who clashed with Voortrekker Boers and lost the battle of Blood River in 1838. Under Mpande the kingdom recovered, but Britain demanded its submission, and in the Anglo-Zulu War of 1879 Cetshwayo's army won a famous victory at Isandlwana before being defeated at Ulundi. Britain divided Zululand, annexed it in 1887 and joined it to the colony of Natal in 1897.
empires.legacy: Isandlwana remains a celebrated symbol of African resistance, and the Zulu king is still a revered traditional leader in South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal.

peak.note: c. 259,000 km² ("over 250,000", Iliffe 1995), including tributary states, most of present-day Ghana

empires.summary: The Akan states of the Gold Coast forest were united around 1700 by Osei Tutu, ruler of Kumasi, with the priest Okomfo Anokye, who according to tradition called down the Golden Stool from the sky as the symbol of Asante unity. After defeating its overlord Denkyira in 1701, Asante grew into the dominant power of the region, trading gold, kola nuts and enslaved captives to European forts on the coast for guns and cloth. Its kings, the Asantehene, ruled through a sophisticated bureaucracy and a network of great roads radiating from Kumasi. Asante fought a series of wars with Britain in the 19th century; the British burned Kumasi in 1874 and exiled King Prempeh I in 1896, and after the War of the Golden Stool, led by Yaa Asantewaa, they annexed Asante in 1902.
empires.legacy: The Asantehene still reigns as a traditional king in Ghana, and Asante kente cloth and goldwork are famous worldwide.

empires.name: Kingdom of Mutapa
empires.capital: Royal towns in the northern Zimbabwe plateau and Zambezi valley

peak.note: Rough estimate; borders were fluid and many chiefs only paid tribute. Wikipedia gives a disputed c. 700,000 km² for the 16th century

empires.summary: According to tradition, the Mutapa state was founded around 1430 by Nyatsimba Mutota, a Shona prince who moved north from the region of Great Zimbabwe to the Zambezi valley, perhaps seeking salt and new trade. His son Matope extended Mutapa rule over much of the plateau between the Zambezi and Limpopo rivers. The ruler's title, Mwenemutapa, is usually translated as lord of the conquered lands. The kingdom grew rich by exporting gold and ivory through Swahili and later Portuguese traders on the Indian Ocean coast. Portuguese adventurers coveted its gold, and after civil wars a king accepted Portuguese overlordship in 1629. In the 1690s the rising Rozvi state drove the Portuguese from the plateau, and the Mutapa kingdom shrank to a small realm in the Zambezi valley.
empires.legacy: Under the spelling Monomotapa, the kingdom appeared on European maps for centuries as a legendary African land of gold.

empires.summary: The Merina people of Madagascar's central highlands built small rival kingdoms around Antananarivo from the 1500s. Around 1785 Andrianampoinimerina began reuniting Imerina, expanding rice terraces and declaring that the sea would be the border of his rice field. His son Radama I allied with Britain, which helped him build a modern army, end the export slave trade and write the Malagasy language in the Latin alphabet with the help of missionaries. By the 1820s the Merina controlled about two-thirds of the island. Queen Ranavalona I resisted foreign influence and persecuted Christians, while her successors, guided by Prime Minister Rainilaiarivony, converted to Protestantism and modernised. France invaded in 1895, and in 1897 it abolished the monarchy and exiled Queen Ranavalona III.
empires.legacy: The Merina kingdom unified much of Madagascar and shaped its written language, and Antananarivo remains the national capital.

empires.summary: Morocco has been ruled since the 1500s by sharifian dynasties claiming descent from the Prophet Muhammad. The Saadians rose in the south leading resistance to Portuguese coastal forts, displaced the Wattasid sultans and took Fez in 1549. Ahmad al-Mansur, who took the throne when his brother Abd al-Malik died during the victory over Portugal at the Battle of the Three Kings in 1578, grew rich on sugar and Saharan gold and sent an army that conquered Songhai in 1591. After civil war, the Alaouite dynasty took power in the 1660s; Moulay Ismail built a huge army of enslaved Black soldiers and a palace city at Meknes. Morocco avoided Ottoman rule, but European pressure grew, and in 1912 it was divided into French and Spanish protectorates. Sultan Mohammed V led the country to independence in 1956 and took the title of king.
empires.legacy: The Alaouite dynasty, ruling since the 1660s, is one of the oldest reigning royal houses in the world.

sources.title: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (ed. B. A. Ogot, 1992)

empires.name: Union and Republic of South Africa

peak.note: 1,221,000 km²; roughly unchanged since union; South West Africa was also ruled from 1915 to 1990

empires.summary: The Union of South Africa was formed in 1910 from four British colonies, the Cape, Natal, Transvaal and Orange River, eight years after the Boer War. It was a self-governing dominion of the British Empire, but only white men, with limited exceptions in the Cape, could vote, and the Natives Land Act of 1913 confined Africans to a small share of the land. Under Louis Botha and Jan Smuts it fought for Britain in both world wars. In 1948 the National Party won power and imposed apartheid, a rigid system of racial segregation enforced by pass laws, forced removals and violence against protest, such as the Sharpeville massacre of 1960. South Africa became a republic in 1961. Resistance and sanctions led F. W. de Klerk to free Nelson Mandela in 1990, and democratic elections in 1994 ended apartheid.
empires.legacy: South Africa's peaceful transition to democracy and its 1996 constitution made Mandela a global symbol of reconciliation.

empires.name: Boer Republics (Transvaal and Orange Free State)

peak.note: Rough combined total, sources differ: the Transvaal about 190,000–290,000 km² and the Orange Free State about 130,000–180,000 km²

empires.summary: Dutch-speaking settlers at the Cape, known as Boers or Afrikaners, resented British rule and its abolition of slavery, and from 1835 thousands left on the Great Trek into the interior. After Britain annexed their short-lived republic of Natalia, they founded two independent states that Britain recognised: the South African Republic, or Transvaal, in 1852, and the Orange Free State in 1854. Both had elected presidents and parliaments, but citizenship and land were reserved for white men, and African peoples were conquered or pushed off their lands. The Transvaal threw off a British annexation in the First Boer War of 1880–81, but the discovery of gold on the Witwatersrand in 1886 drew a flood of foreigners and British ambitions. Britain won the Second Boer War of 1899–1902 and annexed both republics.
empires.legacy: The war's concentration camps, where many Boer and African civilians died, left deep bitterness, and Afrikaner nationalism later shaped apartheid.

empires.summary: Liberia began in 1822 as a settlement founded by the American Colonization Society for freed African Americans, who were later joined by Africans freed from slave ships. In 1847 the colonists declared the independent Republic of Liberia, with a constitution modelled on that of the United States, and Joseph Jenkins Roberts became its first president. The Americo-Liberian minority dominated politics and the economy through the True Whig Party for over a century, while Indigenous Africans were largely excluded. Liberia kept its independence during the scramble for Africa but lost claimed territory to Britain and France, and in 1926 the Firestone company leased vast lands for rubber. William Tubman's long presidency brought foreign investment. A coup by Samuel Doe in 1980 ended Americo-Liberian rule, and civil wars from 1989 to 2003 devastated the country.
empires.legacy: Liberia was Africa's first independent republic, and in 2006 Ellen Johnson Sirleaf became the continent's first elected woman head of state.

empires.summary: Thirteen British colonies along the Atlantic coast declared independence on 4 July 1776 and won it in the Revolutionary War with French help. The Constitution of 1787 created a federal republic with an elected president, Congress and courts, and George Washington became the first president in 1789. The young nation expanded westward through the Louisiana Purchase in 1803, war with Mexico in 1846–48 and the acquisition of Oregon and Alaska, displacing Native American nations by force and treaty. Disputes over slavery led to the Civil War of 1861–65, in which the Union's victory abolished slavery. Rapid industrialisation and mass immigration made it the world's largest economy by the 1890s. After the world wars the United States emerged as a superpower, leading the West in the Cold War against the Soviet Union.
empires.legacy: The United States became the world's leading economic, military and cultural power, and its constitution, the oldest written national constitution still in use, inspired republics worldwide.

peak.note: The First Mexican Empire: c. 4.43M km² plus c. 446,000 km² of Central America (Rodríguez & Vincent 1997)

empires.summary: Mexico's war of independence began with the priest Miguel Hidalgo's call to revolt in 1810 and ended in 1821, when the royalist officer Agustín de Iturbide joined the rebels; he briefly reigned as emperor, and Central America broke away in 1823. The young republic was unstable, and under the strongman Santa Anna it lost Texas in 1836 and, after war with the United States in 1846–48, about half its territory. Benito Juárez's liberal reforms provoked civil war and a French invasion that installed the Austrian archduke Maximilian as emperor, executed in 1867. Porfirio Díaz then ruled for over three decades, building railways but concentrating land and wealth. The Mexican Revolution of 1910–20 overthrew him, and the party later called the Institutional Revolutionary Party governed from 1929 until the elections of 2000.
empires.legacy: Mexico is the world's most populous Spanish-speaking country, and its revolution's land reform and nationalised oil industry became models for Latin America.

empires.name: Gran Colombia

peak.note: Approximate: the combined area of present-day Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama; with claimed Amazon lands now in Brazil and Peru, Wikipedia gives c. 3.06M km²

empires.summary: Gran Colombia was the republic created by Simón Bolívar's independence campaigns in northern South America; historians use the name to distinguish it from today's Colombia. After his victory at Boyacá in 1819, the Congress of Angostura proclaimed the Republic of Colombia, joining the former Viceroyalty of New Granada and the Captaincy General of Venezuela, and the Congress of Cúcuta gave it a constitution in 1821. Victories at Carabobo in 1821 and Pichincha in 1822 added Venezuela's heartland and Quito, and Panama joined after breaking from Spain. Bolívar was president but was often away leading campaigns in Peru, leaving Vice President Santander to govern from Bogotá. The country was huge, with poor communications, and regional leaders in Venezuela and Quito resented central rule. Venezuela and Ecuador seceded in 1830, the year Bolívar died, and the union dissolved in 1831.
empires.legacy: Its successors are Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama, and Bolívar's dream of a united Spanish America still inspires politicians across the region.

empires.summary: When Napoleon invaded Portugal in 1807, the Portuguese royal family fled to Rio de Janeiro, which became the capital of the whole empire. After King João VI returned to Lisbon, his son Pedro declared Brazil independent in 1822 and became its emperor. Unlike its Spanish-speaking neighbours, Brazil stayed united as a constitutional monarchy, and Pedro II's long reign from 1831 brought stability and coffee wealth, though the economy depended on slavery. Brazil fought Paraguay in the devastating war of 1864–70. Slavery was abolished only in 1888, the last in the Americas, and the next year the army proclaimed a republic. Getúlio Vargas ruled from 1930 to 1945 and again in the 1950s, and the new capital Brasília opened in 1960. A military dictatorship from 1964 to 1985 gave way to democracy.
empires.legacy: Brazil is the largest country in Latin America and the world's biggest Portuguese-speaking nation, home to most of the Amazon rainforest.

empires.summary: Buenos Aires deposed its Spanish viceroy in the May Revolution of 1810, and the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata declared independence at Tucumán in 1816. José de San Martín led armies across the Andes to free Chile and Peru, while Paraguay, Bolivia and Uruguay went their own ways. Decades of conflict between Buenos Aires and the provinces followed, dominated by the caudillo Juan Manuel de Rosas, until a national constitution was adopted in 1853. Presidents Mitre, Sarmiento and Roca built a modern state, and the Conquest of the Desert in 1878–85 seized Patagonia from Indigenous peoples. Millions of European immigrants and exports of beef and grain made Argentina one of the richest countries by 1900. The 20th century brought Peronism, repeated coups, a brutal dictatorship from 1976 and defeat in the Falklands War of 1982.
empires.legacy: Argentina's immigrant culture produced the tango, and its trials of the dictatorship's leaders made it a pioneer of human rights justice.

empires.summary: French and British colonies along the St Lawrence and the Atlantic coast were united under British rule after 1763. In 1867 the Province of Canada, which became Ontario and Quebec, joined Nova Scotia and New Brunswick in Confederation to form the Dominion of Canada, led by Prime Minister John A. Macdonald. The new country acquired the vast Hudson's Bay Company lands in 1870, added Manitoba, British Columbia and Prince Edward Island, and completed a transcontinental railway in 1885, often at the expense of First Nations and Métis peoples. Canadian troops fought in both world wars, and the Statute of Westminster in 1931 confirmed its legislative independence. Newfoundland joined in 1949. Canada built a welfare state, adopted official bilingualism and multiculturalism, and in 1982 brought home its constitution with a Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
empires.legacy: Canada is known for its bilingual federal democracy, though reconciliation with Indigenous peoples remains unfinished.
