empires.summary: The French colony of Saint-Domingue was the richest in the Caribbean, producing sugar and coffee with the labour of about half a million enslaved Africans. In 1791 they rose in revolt, and under the formerly enslaved Toussaint Louverture they ended slavery and fought off Spanish, British and French armies. When Napoleon tried to restore slavery, Jean-Jacques Dessalines led the final war and on 1 January 1804 declared independence, naming the country Haiti. It was the first free Black republic and the only nation born from a successful slave revolt. Haiti was split for years between Henri Christophe's northern kingdom and a southern republic, then united under Jean-Pierre Boyer, who also ruled the whole island from 1822 to 1844. A crushing indemnity demanded by France in 1825, foreign interventions and dictatorships kept it poor.
empires.legacy: The Haitian Revolution inspired enslaved people and independence movements across the Americas and helped push Napoleon to sell Louisiana.

empires.summary: Polynesian voyagers settled the Hawaiian islands many centuries ago, and by the 18th century they were divided among rival chiefdoms. Kamehameha I, a chief from the island of Hawaii, used European ships and guns to conquer Maui, Oahu and the others, winning the decisive battle of Nuʻuanu in 1795; Kauai submitted peacefully in 1810. His successors abolished the old kapu religious laws in 1819, and American missionaries brought Christianity and literacy. Kamehameha III issued a constitution in 1840 and carried out the Great Mahele land reform, which let foreigners buy land. Sugar plantations owned by Americans grew powerful while new diseases cut the native population sharply. In 1893 American businessmen, backed by US Marines, overthrew Queen Liliʻuokalani, and the United States annexed the islands in 1898. Hawaii became the 50th US state in 1959.
empires.legacy: The Hawaiian language and hula traditions have revived since the 1970s, and in 1993 the US Congress formally apologised for the overthrow.

empires.summary: Britain founded a convict colony at Sydney in 1788, claiming the land despite more than 50,000 years of Aboriginal occupation. Six separate colonies grew, driven by wool, wheat and the gold rushes of the 1850s, while frontier violence and disease devastated Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. On 1 January 1901 the colonies federated as the Commonwealth of Australia, a self-governing dominion with a parliament modelled partly on Britain's and partly on that of the United States. One of its first laws began the White Australia policy restricting non-European immigration. Australians fought in both world wars, notably at Gallipoli in 1915, and from 1942 the country turned to the United States as its main ally. Mass immigration from Europe and later Asia transformed the country, and the White Australia policy was dismantled by 1973.
empires.legacy: Australia is a prosperous, multicultural federation that remains a constitutional monarchy under the British Crown, while recognition of Indigenous Australians is still a central national debate.

empires.name: New Zealand
empires.capital: Okiato (Old Russell) 1840–1841, then Auckland, then Wellington from 1865

peak.note: The main islands; it also governed Western Samoa (1920–1962) and the Cook Islands

rulers.name: Richard Seddon
rulers.note: Premier of social reform; women won the vote in 1893 despite his opposition

rulers.name: Michael Joseph Savage
rulers.note: First Labour prime minister; built the welfare state

rulers.name: Peter Fraser
rulers.note: Wartime prime minister

rulers.name: Keith Holyoake
rulers.note: Long-serving National Party leader

rulers.name: David Lange
rulers.note: Made New Zealand nuclear-free

empires.summary: Māori settled New Zealand around 1300, making it one of the last major land masses to be peopled. British colonisation began in earnest after the Treaty of Waitangi in 1840, signed by representatives of the British Crown and many Māori chiefs, though its English and Māori versions differed on sovereignty. Disputes over land led to the New Zealand Wars of the 1840s to 1870s and large confiscations of Māori land. Settlers built a farming economy exporting wool, meat and butter to Britain. New Zealand became a self-governing colony and, in 1893, the first country to give women the vote in national elections. It became a dominion in 1907 and fought for Britain in both world wars. Full independence was adopted in 1947, and from the 1970s the country revived Māori rights and adopted a nuclear-free policy.
empires.legacy: New Zealand is known for pioneering social reforms, and te reo Māori is an official language alongside English and New Zealand Sign Language.

moments.title: Farming begins
moments.place: Jericho and the Fertile Crescent (southern Levant)
moments.summary: In the Fertile Crescent, people began cultivating wild cereals such as barley around 9500 BCE and settled in permanent villages like Jericho, founded beside a spring between about 9500 and 9000 BCE. Over the following one to two thousand years emmer and einkorn wheat, barley, lentils, peas, chickpeas, bitter vetch and flax became fully domesticated crops, and the region's wild sheep, goats, cattle and pigs became farm animals.
moments.why: Farming fed far more people from the same land than hunting and gathering, making possible permanent villages, food surpluses, growing populations and, in time, towns, specialists and states.
moments.also: Farming was invented independently in several other places: rice and millet in China (rice domesticated between about 13,500 and 8,200 years ago), taro and yams at Kuk in New Guinea (perhaps from 8000 BCE), squash and maize in Mesoamerica (maize from about 7000 BCE), potatoes and manioc in South America, sorghum and pearl millet in Africa, and sunflowers and other seed plants in eastern North America (c. 2500 BCE).

moments.title: Çatalhöyük, an early proto-city
moments.summary: On the Konya plain of Anatolia, farmers built a tightly packed settlement of mudbrick houses with no streets: people walked across the rooftops and climbed down into their homes by ladder. Houses were plastered and decorated with wall paintings and bull horns, and the dead were buried beneath the floors. Older estimates put its population at 5,000 or more; recent excavations suggest perhaps 600–800 people in a typical year of its middle phase.
moments.why: Çatalhöyük shows early farmers living together in large numbers for some 2,000 years without palaces, temples or obvious rulers, making it a key site for understanding the step from village life towards towns.

moments.title: Copper smelting begins
moments.place: Belovode, near Petrovac na Mlavi (eastern Serbia)
moments.summary: At Belovode, a village of the Vinča culture in the Balkans, copper slag dated to about 5000 BCE is the oldest securely dated evidence of smelting copper from ore at high temperature. Within a few centuries metal was spreading across south-eastern Europe: the cemetery at Varna on the Black Sea coast (c. 4600–4300 BCE) held copper tools and some 3,000 gold objects, often called the oldest gold treasure in the world.
moments.why: Smelting turned rock into tools, ornaments and portable wealth, opening the Copper Age, and rich graves like those at Varna show metal sharpening the divide between elites and everyone else.
moments.also: Early copper-working is also documented in the Near East, and around the North American Great Lakes people of the Old Copper complex cold-hammered native copper from about 6500 BCE, though without smelting it.

sources.title: Radivojević, Archaeometallurgy of the Vinča culture: Belovode in eastern Serbia (Historical Metallurgy 47)

moments.title: The wheel and the plough
moments.summary: Wheeled vehicles appear almost at once across a wide area in the second half of the 4th millennium BCE: a pot from Bronocice in Poland (c. 3600–3400 BCE) is incised with a four-wheeled wagon, pictographs from Uruk show wagons around 3500–3350 BCE, and the oldest surviving wooden wheel, from the Ljubljana Marshes in Slovenia, dates to about 3340–3030 BCE. In the same era farmers in the Near East harnessed oxen to the ard, a simple scratch plough, part of a wider shift to using animals for pulling, milk and wool.
moments.why: Animal power multiplied the land a farming family could work and the loads it could move, opening up new land and making heavy overland transport practical.
moments.also: In Mesoamerica the wheel was invented independently but was used only on small wheeled toys, never for transport before the 16th century.

moments.title: Writing is invented
moments.summary: In the temple district of Uruk, scribes began pressing signs into clay tablets around 3300 BCE to keep accounts of grain, animals and labour, a system that grew out of older clay accounting tokens. This proto-cuneiform developed into cuneiform, used for Sumerian, Akkadian and many other languages for some 3,000 years. In Egypt, labels from tomb U-j at Abydos (c. 3400–3200 BCE) show the beginnings of hieroglyphs, usually counted as a separate invention.
moments.why: Writing let people store information beyond human memory, run large states and economies, and record laws, letters and literature; it marks the line between prehistory and history.
moments.also: Writing was invented independently at least twice more: in Shang China (oracle-bone inscriptions, c. 1250 BCE) and in Mesoamerica, where Maya inscriptions date from the 3rd century BCE and possible earlier Olmec writing is debated.

moments.title: Uruk, the first great city
moments.summary: In the Late Uruk period, Uruk grew to some 250 hectares and perhaps 25,000–50,000 people, with tens of thousands more in its surrounding territory, the largest urban area in the world at the time. Its walled Eanna temple district had monumental temples, administrators using cylinder seals and tablets, and mass-produced ration bowls, and Uruk-style outposts spread from western Iran to south-eastern Anatolia.
moments.why: Uruk is the earliest clear example of a city-state, with social classes, full-time specialists, temples and bureaucrats, a pattern of urban life soon repeated across Mesopotamia.

moments.title: Egypt is unified
moments.summary: Kings from Upper (southern) Egypt took control of the Nile Delta, completing a unification begun by earlier rulers. The Narmer Palette, found at Nekhen, shows King Narmer, usually identified with the legendary Menes, wearing the crowns of both Upper and Lower Egypt. The First Dynasty ruled from Memphis, where the Nile valley meets the delta.
moments.why: Unification created a single kingdom along the Nile under one king, with writing and a bureaucracy, and pharaonic rule endured, with interruptions, for about 3,000 years.

moments.title: Bronze comes into wide use
moments.place: Anatolia and Mesopotamia (Kestel tin mine, southern Türkiye)
moments.summary: Metalworkers found that adding arsenic or, better, tin to copper made a harder alloy, bronze. Arsenical bronze came first (the Maykop culture of the North Caucasus used it by the mid-4th millennium BCE), and by about 3000 BCE the Bronze Age had begun across much of the Old World, from Mesopotamia and Egypt to the Indus. Because tin is rare, bronze depended on long-distance trade; Kestel in southern Türkiye was mined for tin from about 3250 BCE.
moments.why: Bronze tools and weapons were tougher than copper ones, and the hunt for tin and copper tied distant regions together in the first long-distance metal trade networks.
moments.also: A tin-bronze foil from Pločnik in Serbia may date to c. 4650 BCE, though its dating is disputed. In China bronze-working took hold later, with early centres in the north-west by c. 2500–2300 BCE and large-scale casting at Erlitou.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Tin sources and trade in ancient times

moments.title: Caral, first cities of the Americas
moments.summary: On Peru's dry north-central coast, the Caral–Supe (Norte Chico) civilisation built the earliest known monumental centres in the Americas, with large-scale construction from about 3200 BCE. Caral itself, inhabited from about 2600 to 2000 BCE, had six monumental complexes each built around a pyramid, sunken circular plazas and around 3,000 residents. Its people irrigated cotton for fishing nets and textiles, ate fish and shellfish as well as crops, and made no pottery.
moments.why: Caral shows that cities and monumental architecture arose in the Americas entirely independently, and almost as early as in Egypt and Mesopotamia.

moments.title: Indus Valley cities flourish
moments.summary: In its mature phase the Indus civilisation built planned cities such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, each with perhaps 30,000–60,000 people, laid out on grids with baked-brick houses and covered street drains. Spread over more than 1,000 settlements from Afghanistan and Balochistan to Gujarat, it covered a larger area than Egypt and Mesopotamia combined, yet no clear palaces or temples have been found and its script is still undeciphered.
moments.why: The Indus cities were among the world's first urban societies, with some of the earliest known city sanitation, and show that early urban life could flourish without obvious palaces or royal monuments.

moments.title: The Great Pyramid rises
moments.summary: For the Fourth Dynasty pharaoh Khufu, Egyptians built the Great Pyramid at Giza, originally about 146.6 m tall, over roughly 26 years. Excavated workers' camps point to organised, conscripted labour rather than slaves, perhaps 13,000 on average and up to about 40,000 at peak, and the papyrus diary of an official named Merer records limestone being shipped to the site in Khufu's 27th year.
moments.why: It was the tallest human-made structure on Earth for more than 3,700 years and shows how far an early state could organise labour, food supply and engineering.

moments.title: Sargon builds the first empire
moments.summary: Sargon, who in later legend began as cupbearer to the king of Kish, defeated Lugal-zage-si of Uruk around 2300 BCE, took control of Sumer to the Persian Gulf, and campaigned from Elam in Iran to Mari and Syria. He ruled from Akkad, a city whose site has never been found, and at its height around 2250 BCE his dynasty's empire reached from the Mediterranean to Iran.
moments.why: Often called the world's first empire (historians debate the label), Akkad set the pattern of one king ruling many conquered cities and peoples, with a professional army and Akkadian as a shared language of government.

moments.title: Horses and war chariots
moments.summary: Ancient DNA shows that the ancestors of nearly all modern domestic horses were domesticated around 2200 BCE in the Volga–Don region of the western Eurasian steppe. Soon after, people of the Sintashta culture east of the Urals, who built fortified settlements such as Arkaim, buried light chariots with spoked wheels, the oldest known, in graves dated to around 2000 BCE, often together with these horses.
moments.why: Fast horses and chariots transformed warfare, travel and communication: within about 500 years chariots appeared in Greece, Egypt and Mesopotamia, and they reached Shang China around 1200 BCE.

moments.title: Code of Hammurabi
moments.summary: Late in his reign (c. 1792–1750 BCE), King Hammurabi of Babylon had about 282 laws carved on a 2.25 m basalt stele crowned by an image of the sun god Shamash. The laws cover trade, wages, family and property, set penalties that differed by social class, and include the principle of an eye for an eye. Centuries later the stele was carried off to Susa in Iran as plunder; it was found there in 1901 and is now in the Louvre.
moments.why: It is the best-known early law collection, a ruler's public statement of fixed rules for justice, and it made the idea of written, displayed law famous across the ages.
moments.also: It was not the first: the earlier Mesopotamian law collections of Ur-Nammu, Lipit-Ishtar and Eshnunna are known.

sources.title: Louvre: Law Code of Hammurabi, King of Babylon

moments.title: The Vedas are composed
moments.summary: In the north-west of the Indian subcontinent, poets composed the Rigveda, 1,028 hymns in Vedic Sanskrit, most likely between about 1500 and 1000 BCE, and it was gathered into a fixed collection around 1200–1000 BCE. Passed down orally with remarkable precision for many centuries before being written down, it was followed by the other Vedas and, from roughly the 7th–6th centuries BCE (dates are debated), by the philosophical Upanishads.
moments.why: The Vedas are the oldest scriptures of Hinduism, and the Upanishads' ideas of brahman, atman and karma became central to Indian religion and philosophy.

moments.title: Shang bronzes and oracle bones
moments.summary: At Yin, the last capital of the Shang dynasty near modern Anyang, kings consulted their ancestors by cracking turtle shells and ox shoulder blades with heat and carving the questions and answers onto them. These oracle-bone inscriptions, beginning in the reign of Wu Ding around 1250 BCE, are the earliest substantial body of Chinese writing, with around 5,000 different characters. The same court cast magnificent bronze ritual vessels, like those in the tomb of Fu Hao, Wu Ding's consort and a war leader.
moments.why: The oracle-bone script is the ancestor of the Chinese characters still in use today, making Chinese one of the world's longest continuously used writing systems.

moments.title: Olmec civilisation flourishes
moments.summary: In the tropical lowlands of Mexico's Gulf Coast, the Olmecs built San Lorenzo, the largest city in Mesoamerica from about 1200 to 900 BCE, before La Venta became their leading centre (c. 900–400 BCE). They carved colossal stone heads up to about 3 m tall and weighing many tonnes, probably portraits of rulers, and buried rich offerings of jade and serpentine.
moments.why: Often called the mother culture of Mesoamerica (a debated label), the Olmecs pioneered monumental art and possibly ideas such as the ballgame and the Long Count calendar that shaped later civilisations like the Maya.

moments.title: Late Bronze Age collapse
moments.summary: Within a few decades around 1200 BCE, the interconnected palace kingdoms of the eastern Mediterranean fell apart. The Hittite Empire broke up, the Mycenaean palaces of Greece were abandoned, and the port of Ugarit was destroyed around 1190–1185 BCE, its last letters warning of enemy ships; Egypt and Assyria survived but were weakened. Recent studies suggest fewer cities were destroyed than once believed.
moments.why: The collapse ended an age of palace-run kingdoms and long-distance trade and cleared the way for the Iron Age world of new peoples, iron tools and the alphabet; its causes probably combined drought, earthquakes, migrations including the Sea Peoples, and fragile, over-centralised states.

moments.title: Iron working spreads
moments.summary: Iron had long been known in small amounts, from meteorites and occasional smelting, but around 1300–1200 BCE smiths in Anatolia and neighbouring regions mastered smelting iron ore, which needs far higher temperatures than bronze. In the 12th and 11th centuries BCE ironworking spread across the eastern Mediterranean, and smiths learned to harden iron into steel by heating it in charcoal and quenching it. The old idea that the Hittites guarded the secret of iron is no longer accepted.
moments.why: Iron ore is far more common than tin, so once smelting was mastered, iron tools and weapons became cheap and widespread, transforming farming and warfare.
moments.also: Iron was worked early, and probably independently, elsewhere: in India's Ganges plain from about 1800–1200 BCE, in sub-Saharan Africa (see Nok), and in China, which was making cast iron by the 5th century BCE.

moments.title: The Phoenician alphabet
moments.summary: Phoenician scribes in coastal cities such as Byblos used a script of just 22 letters, each standing for a consonant, developed from the earlier Proto-Sinaitic script, which was itself derived from Egyptian hieroglyphs. Its conventional starting date is c. 1050 BCE, and the inscription on the sarcophagus of King Ahiram of Byblos, usually dated to around 1000 BCE, is the earliest known example of the fully developed alphabet.
moments.why: Carried by Phoenician traders around the Mediterranean, it became the ancestor of the Greek and Latin alphabets and, through Aramaic, of the Hebrew and Arabic scripts; a couple of dozen letters made reading and writing far easier to learn than systems with hundreds of signs.
moments.also: At Ugarit, scribes had earlier used a 30-letter alphabet written in cuneiform wedges (c. 1400 BCE), whose letter order resembles the Phoenician.

moments.title: Lapita voyagers reach Polynesia
moments.summary: The Lapita people, Austronesian-speaking seafarers known for their pottery decorated with toothed stamps, had settled the Bismarck Archipelago off New Guinea by about 1600–1200 BCE. After 1200 BCE they sailed east into previously uninhabited islands, reaching Vanuatu, New Caledonia and Fiji, and high-precision dating puts their founding settlement at Nukuleka in Tonga, the first landfall in Polynesia, at about 890 BCE.
moments.why: Crossing hundreds of kilometres of open ocean in outrigger canoes, the Lapita began the human settlement of Remote Oceania, which their Polynesian descendants would later carry across the Pacific.

sources.title: Burley, Weisler & Zhao (2012), High Precision U/Th Dating of First Polynesian Settlement, PLoS ONE

moments.title: First Olympic Games
moments.summary: According to tradition, the first Olympic Games were held in 776 BCE at the sanctuary of Zeus at Olympia, with a single footrace, the stadion, won by Koroibos of Elis; archaeology suggests major games began nearer 700 BCE. Held every four years for free-born Greek men, the games were protected by a sacred truce for travellers and continued until the late 4th century CE or a little later.
moments.why: The four-year Olympiad became a common Greek way of dating events, the games gave rival Greek city-states a shared festival and identity, and they inspired the modern Olympic Games.

moments.title: Iron smelting in West Africa
moments.summary: The Nok culture of central Nigeria, famous for its hollow, near life-sized terracotta sculptures, was smelting iron in bloomery furnaces by about 550 BCE and perhaps from 750 BCE or earlier. Excavations at Taruga uncovered iron slag, clay furnace pipes and wrought iron, helping to show that the Nok people lived in an Iron Age.
moments.why: Early dates at Nok and other sites match or predate known ironworking at Carthage and Meroë, so many archaeologists now argue that iron smelting was invented independently south of the Sahara, though the evidence is still debated.
moments.also: Even earlier smelting dates claimed for sites in Niger (Termit, c. 1500 BCE) and Nigeria (Lejja) remain disputed.

moments.title: First coins in Lydia
moments.summary: In Lydia and the neighbouring Greek cities of Ionia, the first coins, small lumps of electrum (a natural gold–silver alloy) stamped with a design, were struck in the late 7th century BCE; the electrum coin of Phanes from Ephesus dates to about 625–600 BCE. Around 550 BCE King Croesus issued the first coins of refined gold and silver, and workshops for separating electrum into pure gold and silver have been excavated at the Lydian capital, Sardis.
moments.why: Coins of guaranteed weight and purity made trade, taxes and paying soldiers far simpler, and coinage soon spread through the Greek and Persian worlds.
moments.also: In China, shovel-shaped bronze coins were cast at a mint in Henan between about 640 and 550 BCE, a separate tradition; India's punch-marked coins followed by the 4th century BCE, possibly earlier.

moments.title: Cyrus founds the Persian Empire
moments.summary: Cyrus II, king of Anshan in Persis, overthrew his Median overlord Astyages around 550 BCE and built his capital, Pasargadae, near the site of his victory. He went on to conquer Lydia (546 BCE) and Babylon (539 BCE), where the Cyrus Cylinder presents him as a restorer of temples and of displaced peoples; the Bible credits him with letting exiled Jews return to Jerusalem.
moments.why: By his death in 530 BCE the Achaemenid Persian Empire stretched from Asia Minor to the Indus, the largest empire the world had yet seen, uniting many peoples, languages and religions under one king.

moments.title: Democracy in Athens
moments.summary: The reformer Cleisthenes reorganised the citizens of Athens into ten tribes based on where they lived rather than on family, created a Council of 500 chosen by lot, and strengthened the Assembly, where any adult male citizen could speak and vote. He called the system isonomia, equality before the law.
moments.why: Athens became the best-known early democracy, where ordinary citizens debated and decided policy directly, though women, slaves and foreign residents were excluded, so voters were a minority of adults.

moments.title: The Axial Age thinkers
moments.place: Bodh Gaya (Bihar, India) and across Eurasia
moments.summary: Within a few centuries, thinkers across Eurasia laid the foundations of lasting religions and philosophies: the Buddha (enlightened at Bodh Gaya; his dates are debated, c. 563–483 or c. 480–400 BCE) and Mahavira in India, Confucius (traditionally 551–479 BCE) and, according to tradition, Laozi in China, the Hebrew prophets in Israel, and Greek philosophers from Heraclitus and Parmenides to Plato. In 1949 the philosopher Karl Jaspers named this period, roughly the 8th to 3rd centuries BCE, the Axial Age.
moments.why: Buddhism, Jainism, Confucianism, Daoism, the prophetic tradition of Judaism and Greek philosophy still shape the ethics and beliefs of billions of people; scholars debate whether this was one connected shift or a convenient label for separate developments.

moments.title: The Persian Wars
moments.summary: After Athens helped the Ionian Greeks revolt against Persia, King Darius sent an expedition that the Athenians and Plataeans defeated at Marathon in 490 BCE. In 480 BCE Xerxes invaded with a far larger force, won at Thermopylae and sacked an evacuated Athens, but lost the sea battle of Salamis; Greek victories at Plataea and Mycale in 479 BCE ended the invasion.
moments.why: Greek independence survived, Athens rose as a naval power at the head of the Delian League, and its classical age followed; Herodotus' account of the wars earned him the title Father of History.

moments.title: Alexander's conquests
moments.summary: Alexander III of Macedon crossed into Asia in 334 BCE, beat the Persians at the Granicus, Issus (333) and Gaugamela (331), took Egypt, where he founded Alexandria, and overthrew the Achaemenid Empire. He pushed on to the Indus, defeating King Porus at the Hydaspes in 326 BCE, until his army refused to go further; he died at Babylon in 323 BCE, aged 32.
moments.why: His conquests and the kingdoms of his successors spread Greek language and culture from Egypt to north-western India, opening the Hellenistic age in which Greek became a shared language across the region and cultures mixed, from Greco-Buddhist art to Alexandrian science.

moments.title: Euclid and the Library of Alexandria
moments.summary: In Alexandria, Ptolemy I founded the Mouseion, a research institute whose great library, probably established under Ptolemy II (r. 285–246 BCE), gathered somewhere between tens and hundreds of thousands of scrolls. Working in the city around 300 BCE, Euclid wrote the Elements, 13 books that build geometry and number theory step by step from definitions and postulates; later scholars there included Eratosthenes, who calculated the Earth's circumference.
moments.why: The Elements was the core of mathematics teaching for some 2,000 years and has appeared in more than 1,000 printed editions, while the library became a lasting symbol of the ambition to collect all knowledge in one place.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Euclid

moments.title: Ashoka turns from war
moments.summary: In about the eighth year of his reign, the Mauryan emperor Ashoka conquered Kalinga on India's east coast; his own Rock Edict 13 records 100,000 killed and 150,000 carried off, and expresses deep remorse. He turned to dhamma, a moral code of non-violence and right conduct not tied to a single religion, proclaimed it in edicts carved on rocks and pillars across his empire, and became a lay follower and patron of Buddhism.
moments.why: Ashoka is remembered as a ruler who renounced conquest by war, and the missionaries he is credited with sending, including his son Mahinda to Sri Lanka, helped Buddhism spread beyond India.

moments.title: Qin unifies China
moments.summary: After conquering the last of the rival Warring States, King Ying Zheng of Qin proclaimed himself Shi Huangdi, the First Emperor, in 221 BCE. He replaced hereditary lords with appointed officials in 36 commanderies and standardised the script, coins, weights, measures and even cart axle widths, while linking northern walls, building roads and ordering the burning of books from rival schools of thought.
moments.why: Although the Qin dynasty fell in 206 BCE, after only 15 years, it created the centralised imperial system and common written script that held China together under emperors until 1911.

moments.title: The Han dynasty begins
moments.summary: Liu Bang, born into a peasant family, rose from minor Qin official to rebel leader, defeated his rival Xiang Yu at Gaixia and became emperor in 202 BCE, remembered as Emperor Gaozu of Han. Keeping much of the Qin's centralised system but easing its harsh laws and taxes, the Han ruled from Chang'an and, after a brief break (9–23 CE), from Luoyang until 220 CE.
moments.why: Under the Han, Confucianism became the state ideology and a census of 2 CE counted some 57.7 million people; the dynasty became so central to Chinese identity that China's majority still call themselves the Han people and their writing Han characters.

moments.title: Paper is invented in China
moments.summary: The oldest surviving fragment of paper, apparently part of a map, was found at Fangmatan in Gansu and dates to about 179–141 BCE. Early paper made from plant fibres was used mostly for wrapping and padding, for example around bronze mirrors, and only later for writing. In 105 CE the court official Cai Lun refined papermaking using bark, hemp, rags and old fishing nets, which is why he was long credited with inventing it.
moments.why: Cheap, light paper gradually replaced bamboo, silk and parchment, reaching the Islamic world and then Europe by the 11th century, and made books and records far more widely available.

moments.title: Rome destroys Carthage and Corinth
moments.summary: In early 146 BCE, after a three-year siege in the Third Punic War, Roman troops under Scipio Aemilianus stormed Carthage, destroyed the city and sold some 50,000 survivors into slavery; its lands became the Roman province of Africa. In the same year Lucius Mummius defeated the Achaean League and sacked Corinth, bringing mainland Greece under direct Roman control.
moments.why: With its great rival gone and Greece subdued, Rome became the unchallenged power of the Mediterranean, and the flood of Greek art and learning into Rome reshaped Roman culture.

moments.title: The Silk Road opens
moments.summary: Around 138 BCE Emperor Wu of Han sent the envoy Zhang Qian west to seek allies against the Xiongnu. After years as a Xiongnu captive he reached Dayuan (Ferghana), the Yuezhi and Bactria, and returned to Chang'an in 125 BCE with reports of rich states to the west. Han embassies, campaigns and trade followed, and by around 114 BCE a network of routes linked China with Central Asia and, in time, the Roman world.
moments.why: For some 1,500 years the Silk Road carried silk, horses, paper and ideas across more than 6,400 km of Eurasia, linking civilisations that had known little of one another.

moments.title: From Caesar to Augustus
moments.summary: On 15 March 44 BCE, about 60 senators led by Brutus and Cassius stabbed Julius Caesar, recently named dictator for life, in the Curia of Pompey in Rome. His heir Octavian joined Mark Antony and Lepidus in the Second Triumvirate, then defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BCE; in 27 BCE the Senate gave him the name Augustus.
moments.why: Augustus became Rome's first emperor, ending the Republic and founding the Principate, a system of one-man rule behind republican forms that opened a long era of relative peace known as the Pax Romana.

moments.title: Birth of Jesus
moments.summary: Jesus of Nazareth was probably born between about 6 and 4 BCE, since the Gospels place his birth in the reign of King Herod, whose death is usually dated to 4 BCE. The Gospels of Matthew and Luke set his birth in Bethlehem, though many historians think he was more likely born in Nazareth in Galilee, where he grew up.
moments.why: Christianity, which grew from his life and teachings, became one of the world's largest religions, and the Anno Domini year count devised by Dionysius Exiguus in 525 CE, which placed his birth a few years too late, underlies today's common calendar era.

moments.title: Christianity spreads beyond Judea
moments.summary: After Jesus was crucified in Jerusalem, around 33 CE, his followers formed communities that spread quickly to Damascus and Antioch, where, according to the Book of Acts, they were first called Christians. From the mid-40s to the mid-50s CE the apostle Paul travelled through Cyprus, Asia Minor and Greece, founding churches among non-Jews, before dying in Rome around 64–65 CE, about the time Nero blamed the city's Christians for the Great Fire of 64.
moments.why: Opening the movement to non-Jews turned a small Jewish sect into a religion that could travel along the Roman Empire's roads and sea lanes, and from there around the world.

moments.title: Buddhism reaches China
moments.summary: Buddhism reached China along the Silk Road in the 1st century CE. Tradition says Emperor Ming of the Eastern Han dreamed of a golden figure, sent envoys west and in 68 CE founded the White Horse Temple at Luoyang for two Indian monks, though many scholars treat the story as a pious legend. Firmer evidence comes in the 2nd century, when Central Asian monks such as the Parthian An Shigao (from 148 CE) and the Kushan Lokakṣema began translating Buddhist texts into Chinese at Luoyang.
moments.why: The translation work begun at Luoyang carried Indian religious and philosophical ideas into the Chinese language, starting a transmission that made Buddhism a lasting part of Chinese life.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Silk Road transmission of Buddhism

moments.title: Teotihuacan, metropolis of Mesoamerica
moments.summary: Teotihuacan grew explosively in the first centuries CE into the largest city in Mesoamerica, laid out along the Avenue of the Dead with the Pyramid of the Sun, about 65 m high, completed by around 100 CE. At its height around 450 CE it may have housed about 100,000 people, though estimates range from 25,000 to well over that. Its ruling-class buildings were burned around 550 CE and the city declined; the Aztecs, who revered its ruins centuries later, gave it the Nahuatl name by which we know it.
moments.why: Teotihuacan's power reached far beyond central Mexico: in 378 CE a warlord linked to the city took over the Maya city of Tikal and installed a new king, showing how one metropolis could shape politics across Mesoamerica.

moments.title: Cai Lun improves papermaking
moments.summary: In 105 CE Cai Lun, an official at the Eastern Han court, presented Emperor He with an improved way of making paper from tree bark, hemp waste, old rags and fishing nets. Paper already existed in China (the oldest surviving fragment, from Fangmatan in Gansu, dates to about 179–141 BCE), so historians see his work as improving and standardising an existing craft rather than inventing it, but his improvements led to paper's widespread use.
moments.why: Cheaper and lighter than silk or heavy bamboo strips, paper gradually replaced them, letting whole books circulate and be carried by hand; Cai Lun came to be honoured as the traditional inventor of paper.

moments.title: The Pax Romana and Rome at its height
moments.summary: The Pax Romana, the roughly two centuries from Augustus (27 BCE) to the death of Marcus Aurelius (180 CE), was a time of relative peace and prosperity inside the Roman Empire, though not free of revolts and frontier wars. Under Trajan, who conquered Dacia and briefly annexed Armenia and Mesopotamia, the empire reached its greatest extent at his death in 117 CE. Its population is estimated to have peaked at about 70 million.
moments.why: Long internal peace let trade flourish across the Mediterranean and beyond, and because it overlapped with Han China's own era of stability it stimulated travel and commerce right across Eurasia.

moments.title: Kanishka and the Kushan crossroads
moments.summary: The Kushan Empire, which ruled from Central Asia to northern India between about 30 and 375 CE, reached its peak under Kanishka, who reigned from about 127 to 150 CE from Purushapura (Peshawar) and Mathura. It linked Silk Road caravan routes with Indian Ocean sea trade, and Kanishka, though not himself a convert, patronised Buddhism and both the Gandhara and Mathura schools of Buddhist art.
moments.why: Kushan control of the routes between India, Iran and China helped carry Buddhism, especially Mahayana Buddhism, into Central Asia and China.

moments.title: Constantine, Christianity and a new Rome
moments.summary: After defeating his rival Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge near Rome in 312, Constantine began favouring Christianity, and in 313 he and his co-emperor Licinius agreed at Milan to grant religious freedom and return confiscated church property. In 325 he summoned the Council of Nicaea, which produced the Nicene Creed, and on 11 May 330 he consecrated a new capital, Constantinople, on the site of Byzantium.
moments.why: A persecuted faith became the emperor's favoured religion, and in 380 Theodosius I made it the empire's official one; Constantinople remained a Christian imperial capital until 1453.

moments.title: The Gupta age in India
moments.summary: From Pataliputra, Chandragupta I (crowned c. 320), his son Samudragupta and grandson Chandragupta II built an empire across northern India. The period is often called India's golden age, a label some historians dispute; the poet Kalidasa, the astronomer Aryabhata and the visiting Chinese monk Faxian, who praised its mild government, all belong to it. Hun invasions from the late 490s and rising regional rulers broke the empire up by the mid-6th century.
moments.why: Gupta-era scholars produced lasting works of Sanskrit literature and science: Aryabhata, writing around 500, used place-value notation and gave π as about 3.1416, part of the tradition that produced modern numerals.

moments.title: Aksum becomes a Christian kingdom
moments.summary: Aksum, in today's northern Ethiopia and Eritrea, grew rich on Red Sea trade through its port of Adulis, exporting ivory, gold and tortoiseshell and minting its own coins; in the 3rd century the prophet Mani counted it among the world's four great powers with Rome, Persia and China. King Ezana, taught by Frumentius, a Christian from the Roman east, became its first Christian ruler, around 325–330 by most estimates, and his coins replaced the pagan disc and crescent with the cross.
moments.why: Aksum became one of the earliest states anywhere to adopt Christianity, and Ezana made its Ge'ez script and language official alongside Greek, rooting a Christian, literate tradition in the Horn of Africa.

moments.title: The Western Roman Empire falls
moments.summary: On 4 September 476 the Germanic general Odoacer took Ravenna, deposed the young emperor Romulus Augustulus and sent the imperial regalia to the Eastern emperor Zeno in Constantinople instead of naming a new Western emperor. It capped a long decline that included mass migrations from 376, the sack of Rome in 410, civil wars and financial strain; historians also point to epidemics and climate change, and some prefer other end dates such as 480.
moments.why: Western Europe passed to Germanic kingdoms while the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire carried on for nearly a thousand years more; 476 is often used to mark the end of antiquity.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Fall of the Western Roman Empire

moments.title: Justinian's law code and reconquests
moments.summary: The Eastern Roman emperor Justinian I (r. 527–565) had a commission led by Tribonian gather centuries of Roman law into the Code (529, revised 534), the Digest and the Institutes (533), later called the Corpus Juris Civilis. After the Nika riots of 532 burned the old church, he rebuilt Hagia Sophia, completed in 537, and his generals retook North Africa from the Vandals (533–534), Italy from the Ostrogoths (535–554) and part of southern Spain. From 541 plague, caused by the same bacterium as the later Black Death, swept the Mediterranean.
moments.why: Recovered in Italy around 1070 and taught at Bologna, Justinian's law books became the foundation of the civil-law systems used across continental Europe and far beyond.

moments.title: The Tang dynasty
moments.summary: The Tang dynasty, founded in 618 after the collapse of the Sui, ruled China for nearly three centuries from Chang'an, a walled grid city of about 78 km² whose population inside the walls is estimated at 800,000 to 1 million. Merchants, monks and envoys from Central Asia, Persia, India and Arabia filled its markets, and the era is counted the greatest age of Chinese poetry, the age of Li Bai and Du Fu. The An Lushan rebellion (755–763) badly weakened the dynasty, which ended in 907.
moments.why: Tang China was one of the most cosmopolitan societies of its time, and Chang'an's grid plan was copied for Japan's capitals at Nara and Kyoto and for Silla Korea's capital at Gyeongju.

moments.title: Muhammad's Hijra to Medina
moments.summary: Muhammad, born in Mecca around 570, began around 610 to report revelations that Muslims believe were delivered by the angel Gabriel and that form the Quran. Facing hostility from Mecca's ruling Quraysh, in 622 he and his followers migrated to Medina, then called Yathrib, where he became the community's leader and judge. Mecca surrendered to him in 629–630, and by his death in 632 most of the Arabian Peninsula had converted to Islam.
moments.why: The Hijra marks the founding of the first Muslim community, and the caliph Umar later made it year one of the Islamic calendar, which Muslims still use.

moments.title: Zero becomes a number
moments.summary: Indian mathematicians had been writing numbers with base-10 place value for centuries (the earliest leaves of the Bakhshali manuscript are dated to about 224–383 CE), and around 500 Aryabhata marked empty places with the word kha, 'emptiness'. In 628 Brahmagupta, a native of Bhillamala, completed his Brahmasphutasiddhanta, the earliest known text to treat zero as a number in its own right, with rules for adding, subtracting and multiplying with zero and negative numbers.
moments.why: Translated into Arabic at the Abbasid court, spread by al-Khwarizmi's book on Hindu numerals (c. 825) and brought into Europe from the 12th century, Indian place-value numerals with zero became the digits the whole world uses today.

moments.title: The Arab Muslim conquests
moments.summary: Within a few years of Muhammad's death, Arab Muslim armies defeated the Byzantines at Yarmuk and the Sasanian Persians at al-Qadisiyya (both 636), taking Syria, Iraq, Jerusalem (638) and Egypt (639–642); Persian resistance was broken at Nahavand in 642 and the last shah was killed in 651. Under the Umayyad caliphs, ruling from Damascus from 661, the conquests reached Spain and Sindh in 711, until the Franks defeated a raid near Tours in 732.
moments.why: By 750 Muslim rulers governed, by various estimates, 11–15 million km² from Iberia to the Indus, and Arabic, made the language of government under the Umayyads, became a shared language of religion, law and learning across this vast area.

moments.title: Vikings raid Lindisfarne
moments.summary: In 793 Norse raiders plundered the island monastery of Lindisfarne, killing or enslaving many monks; the scholar Alcuin wrote that such terror had never before appeared in Britain. Over the next two and a half centuries Scandinavians raided, traded and settled from Ireland to the Russian rivers, where Rurik's successors founded Kievan Rus', served the Byzantine emperors, received Normandy in 911 and settled Iceland and Greenland. The age is traditionally closed by Harald Hardrada's death at Stamford Bridge in 1066.
moments.why: Viking raiding, trading and settlement reshaped early medieval Europe, founding new states and linking the North Atlantic and the Baltic to Constantinople.
moments.also: Around 1021 Norse Greenlanders were at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, a date fixed by tree rings; excavated by Helge and Anne Stine Ingstad from 1961, it is the only confirmed Norse site in North America outside Greenland, almost five centuries before Columbus.

moments.title: Charlemagne crowned emperor
moments.summary: Charlemagne, king of the Franks from 768 and of the Lombards from 774, conquered Saxony, Bavaria, northern Italy and part of northern Spain, uniting most of Western and Central Europe. On Christmas Day 800 Pope Leo III crowned him emperor in Rome. From his palace at Aachen he sponsored a revival of learning, the Carolingian Renaissance, led by scholars such as Alcuin of York, whose scribes spread the clear Carolingian minuscule handwriting.
moments.why: Carolingian copyists made the earliest surviving copies of many Latin classics, including Cicero, Horace and Lucretius, and Charlemagne's lasting influence on the continent has earned him the title 'Father of Europe'.

moments.title: The Classic Maya collapse
moments.summary: In the 8th and 9th centuries the great Maya city-states of the southern lowlands broke down: dated monuments fell from about 40 a year around 750 to none by 900, and monumental building in the central area stopped after 830. Tikal, which may once have held tens of thousands of people, raised its last monument in 869 and was largely deserted by the end of the 10th century. Drought is now the leading explanation among more than 80 theories, alongside warfare, environmental damage and the collapse of trade routes.
moments.why: The collapse shows how large, sophisticated societies can unravel, yet Maya civilization continued in northern Yucatán at cities such as Chichén Itzá and Mayapán, and independent Maya rule lasted until 1697.

moments.title: Baghdad's House of Wisdom
moments.summary: After the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur founded Baghdad in 762, the city became a centre of learning, and under al-Ma'mun (r. 813–833) a royal library known as the House of Wisdom became a hub for scholars translating Greek, Persian, Syriac and Indian works into Arabic. Hunayn ibn Ishaq translated Galen and Hippocrates, and al-Khwarizmi, who worked there around 820, wrote the book on al-jabr that gave us the word 'algebra'. Some historians doubt it was a formal academy, seeing the name as covering a library and Baghdad's wider community of scholars.
moments.why: The translation movement preserved and built on ancient science and philosophy, and Arabic works such as al-Khwarizmi's later reached Europe in Latin; his Latinised name gave us the word 'algorithm'.

moments.title: The Diamond Sutra, oldest dated printed book
moments.summary: In Tang China printers carved whole pages into wooden blocks, inked them and pressed them onto paper. A printed scroll of the Buddhist Diamond Sutra, dated 11 May 868 and made 'for universal free distribution', was sealed in a cave library at Dunhuang, found there in 1900 and acquired by Aurel Stein in 1907; it is now in the British Library. It is the oldest surviving printed book that carries a date, though earlier undated prints exist.
moments.why: Printing let texts be copied quickly and cheaply, and in the 1040s Bi Sheng took the next step in China with movable type made of baked clay, one character per piece.

moments.title: Polynesians settle the remote Pacific
moments.summary: Sailing double-hulled canoes and steering by the rising and setting points of stars and by ocean swells, Polynesian voyagers spread across thousands of kilometres of open Pacific. High-precision radiocarbon dating suggests the Society Islands were settled around 1025–1120 CE and that, in one rapid pulse around 1190–1290, voyagers reached the remaining islands of East Polynesia, including Hawaii, Rapa Nui (Easter Island) and Aotearoa New Zealand.
moments.why: Without instruments or charts, Polynesian navigators settled the last large habitable islands on the map of the Pacific, spreading related languages and cultures from Hawaii to New Zealand and Rapa Nui.
moments.also: Sweet potatoes, native to South America, were growing in the Cook Islands by about 1000 CE, which many researchers take as a sign that Polynesian voyagers reached the Americas and came back, though natural drift has also been proposed.

sources.title: Wilmshurst et al. 2011, PNAS: High-precision radiocarbon dating of East Polynesian colonization

moments.title: Song China: gunpowder, compass and paper money
moments.summary: Under the Song dynasty (960–1279), whose northern capital was Kaifeng, China's population roughly doubled and its economy boomed. In 1023–1024 the government took over the jiaozi notes first issued by Sichuan merchants, usually regarded as the first government paper money; the military manual Wujing Zongyao (compiled c. 1040–1044) holds the earliest known written formulas for gunpowder; and by 1088 Shen Kuo described the magnetic compass in use for navigation.
moments.why: Gunpowder weapons and the compass, first recorded in Europe around 1190, later transformed warfare and sea travel worldwide, while state-backed paper money pointed the way to modern currency.

moments.title: Cahokia, city of the Mississippians
moments.summary: Around 1050 a sudden building boom beside the Mississippi, across the river from today's St. Louis, created Cahokia, the dominant centre of the maize-farming Mississippian culture. At its peak around 1100 it held perhaps 10,000–20,000 people, and its Monks Mound, about 30 m high and 290 m long, is the largest earthen mound north of Mexico. The city declined over the following centuries and was abandoned by about 1350.
moments.why: Cahokia was the largest and most complex settlement north of the great cities of Mexico, showing that North America had its own urban societies long before Europeans arrived.

moments.title: The East–West Schism
moments.summary: On 16 July 1054 papal legates led by Cardinal Humbert laid a document excommunicating Patriarch Michael Cerularius on the altar of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople; days later the patriarch's synod excommunicated the legates in return. The quarrel capped centuries of disputes over the pope's authority, the filioque wording of the Nicene Creed and whether the Eucharist should use leavened or unleavened bread.
moments.why: The break, hardened when crusaders sacked Constantinople in 1204, divided Christianity into a Roman Catholic West and an Eastern Orthodox East; the mutual excommunications were lifted only in 1965.

moments.title: The First Crusade takes Jerusalem
moments.summary: Answering a Byzantine appeal for help against the Seljuk Turks, Pope Urban II called at Clermont in November 1095 for an armed pilgrimage to Jerusalem. Crusaders set out in 1096, some bands massacring Jewish communities in the Rhineland on the way, took Antioch in 1098 and stormed Jerusalem on 15 July 1099, killing much of its population. They founded four crusader states: the Kingdom of Jerusalem, the County of Edessa, the Principality of Antioch and the County of Tripoli.
moments.why: The crusade opened two centuries of holy war between Latin Christians and Muslim rulers in the Levant, and the crusading idea was later turned on Muslim Spain, the pagan Baltic and even Christian Constantinople.

moments.title: Angkor Wat and the Khmer Empire
moments.summary: The Khmer kings who ruled from Angkor from 802 built a vast 'hydraulic city' of reservoirs and canals; a 2007 survey found it was the largest pre-industrial city by area, with infrastructure spread over at least 1,000 km². King Suryavarman II (r. 1113–c. 1150) built Angkor Wat, a temple to Vishnu that is the largest religious complex in the world, and from 1181 Jayavarman VII added the walled city of Angkor Thom and made Mahayana Buddhism the state religion.
moments.why: Angkor shows the scale a tropical rice-farming civilization could reach; it remained the Khmer capital until Ayutthaya sacked it in 1431 and much of its population moved south.

moments.title: Genghis Khan unites the Mongols
moments.place: Source of the Onon River, Khentii (Mongolia)
moments.summary: In 1206 an assembly (kurultai) at the source of the Onon River proclaimed the Mongol chief Temüjin Genghis Khan, ruler of the united steppe peoples. He went on to force the Western Xia to submit, captured the Jin capital Zhongdu (modern Beijing) in 1215 and destroyed the Khwarazmian Empire in Central Asia from 1219, dying on campaign in 1227.
moments.why: His heirs built the largest contiguous land empire in history, about 23.5 million km² by 1294, whose 'Pax Mongolica' carried goods, technologies and ideas across Eurasia.

moments.title: Magna Carta
moments.summary: Facing a rebellion by his barons, King John set his seal to a charter of liberties in the meadow at Runnymede, between Windsor and Staines, on 15 June 1215. It declared the English Church free and set limits on the king's demands, but Pope Innocent III declared it void within weeks and civil war followed. It was reissued in 1216, 1217 and 1225, and three of its clauses remain law in England and Wales.
moments.why: Magna Carta came to stand for the principle that even the king is bound by law: later jurists and the American colonists invoked it, though it began as a settlement between the crown and the barons.

moments.title: Great Zimbabwe
moments.summary: Ancestors of today's Shona people began building in stone at Great Zimbabwe in the 11th century, and in the 13th and 14th centuries raised the Great Enclosure, whose mortarless walls stand up to 11 m high. The city was the capital of a kingdom that controlled the flow of gold from the Zimbabwean plateau to Swahili ports such as Sofala, and Chinese porcelain and glass beads found there show its links to Indian Ocean trade. Decline set in from the 15th century as power shifted to the Mutapa and Butua kingdoms.
moments.why: Colonial-era writers credited the ruins to Phoenicians or the Queen of Sheba and Rhodesian authorities pressured archaeologists to deny African builders; only in the 1950s did its African origin become the scholarly consensus, making it a lasting symbol of pre-colonial African achievement.

moments.title: The Mongols sack Baghdad
moments.summary: In late January 1258 a Mongol army under Hulagu, a grandson of Genghis Khan, besieged Baghdad; the caliph al-Musta'sim surrendered on 10 February, the city was sacked and the caliph was put to death. Later writers claimed 800,000 or more dead, figures historians regard as inflated, though the true toll is unknown.
moments.why: The sack ended the Abbasid caliphate in Baghdad after about 500 years and is traditionally seen as closing the Islamic Golden Age, although historians now see Baghdad's decline as more gradual and note that its libraries partly recovered within a few years.

moments.title: The fall of Acre ends the crusader states
moments.summary: In 1187 Saladin destroyed the crusader armies at Hattin and Jerusalem was lost, and later crusades, including the Fourth Crusade that sacked Christian Constantinople in 1204, failed to restore the crusader states. On 18 May 1291, after a six-week siege, the Mamluk sultan al-Ashraf Khalil captured Acre, the crusaders' last major stronghold, and their remaining mainland strongholds were lost the same year.
moments.why: Acre's fall ended two centuries of crusader rule on the Levantine mainland; the crusades had deepened the split between Catholic and Orthodox Christians and helped Italian merchants come to dominate Mediterranean trade.

moments.title: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage
moments.summary: Mansa Musa, ruler of the Mali Empire (c. 1312–1337), crossed the Sahara on pilgrimage to Mecca, reaching Cairo in July 1324 with a vast retinue; later Arabic accounts tell of thousands of attendants and camels laden with gold, numbers historians treat as rhetorical rather than measured. The Cairo official al-Umari reported that Musa's spending lowered the value of gold there for at least twelve years. On his return Musa commissioned the Djinguereber Mosque in Timbuktu, around 1327.
moments.why: Mali supplied almost half the Old World's gold in the early 14th century, and Musa's journey made West Africa's wealth famous in the Islamic world and Europe, where the Catalan Atlas of 1375 depicts him.

moments.title: Tenochtitlan is founded
moments.summary: According to their tradition, the Mexica settled where they saw an eagle with a snake in its beak perched on a cactus, on a swampy island in Lake Texcoco, traditionally in 1325. They enlarged the island with chinampa farm plots and joined it to the mainland with causeways, and after defeating Azcapotzalco in 1428 Tenochtitlan allied with Texcoco and Tlacopan in the Triple Alliance. By 1519 the city had over 200,000 people, and the empire it dominated covered most of central Mexico.
moments.why: Tenochtitlan was the heart of the Aztec Empire until Spanish and Tlaxcalan forces besieged and destroyed it in 1521, and today's Mexico City stands on its ruins.

moments.title: The Black Death
moments.summary: Plague caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, probably originating in Central Asia, reached the Black Sea in the mid-1340s, when the Golden Horde was besieging the Genoese port of Caffa in Crimea; the famous story of plague corpses catapulted over its walls comes from a single, doubtful source. Genoese ships carried the disease to Constantinople and, in October 1347, to Sicily, and by 1353 it had swept Europe, the Middle East and North Africa, killing an estimated 25–60 percent of Europe's people and more than a third of Cairo's.
moments.why: One of the deadliest pandemics in history, it left labour so scarce that wages rose in many places, while frightened communities turned on scapegoats: by 1351 some 210 Jewish communities had been destroyed.

moments.title: Zheng He's treasure voyages
moments.summary: Between 1405 and 1433 the Ming court eunuch Zheng He led seven great voyages into the Indian Ocean for the Yongle and Xuande emperors; the first had 317 ships and almost 28,000 men. Built largely at the Longjiang shipyard in Nanjing, the fleets called at Champa, Java, Malacca, Ceylon and Calicut, and later voyages reached Hormuz, Aden, Mogadishu and Malindi, returning with foreign envoys and gifts such as a giraffe.
moments.why: The voyages displayed Ming power and drew distant states into China's tributary system, but the court abandoned them after 1433 amid high costs and Mongol threats in the north, decades before Portuguese ships entered the Indian Ocean.

moments.title: Pachacuti builds the Inca Empire
moments.summary: In the standard chronology, the Inca ruler Pachacuti came to power in 1438 after the Chanka attack on Cusco and began turning his small kingdom into an empire, Tawantinsuyu. He rebuilt Cusco as an imperial capital and probably built Machu Picchu as a royal estate, and his son Topa Inca pushed conquests north into Ecuador. By the early 1500s the empire stretched along the Andes from Colombia to Chile, tied together by the Qhapaq Ñan road network and run with quipu knotted-cord records.
moments.why: It became the largest empire of the pre-Columbian Americas, governing perhaps 6–14 million people, before the Spanish conquest that began in 1532.

moments.title: Gutenberg's printing press
moments.summary: Around 1440 the German goldsmith Johannes Gutenberg developed a printing system that combined movable metal type cast in a hand mould, an oil-based ink and an adapted screw press. His Mainz workshop finished the 42-line Bible in 1454 or 1455, in an edition of perhaps 160–185 copies. Printing spread fast: by 1500 about 270 European cities had presses, which had turned out more than 20 million copies.
moments.why: Cheap printed books spread literacy, scholarship and new ideas across Europe and helped make the Protestant Reformation possible, when Martin Luther became Europe's most published author.
moments.also: Metal movable type had already been used in Korea, where the Jikji of 1377 is the oldest surviving book printed with it.

moments.title: The fall of Constantinople
moments.summary: On 6 April 1453 the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II laid siege to Constantinople with perhaps 50,000–80,000 troops and about 70 cannon, including a giant bombard cast by the engineer Orban, against some 7,000–8,000 defenders. After 53 days his forces broke through the 5th-century Theodosian Walls on 29 May; the last emperor, Constantine XI, died in the fighting, and Mehmed made the city his new capital.
moments.why: The conquest ended the Byzantine Empire, the last remnant of the Roman Empire after nearly 1,500 years, showed that gunpowder artillery could breach the strongest walls, and is often taken to mark the end of the Middle Ages.

moments.title: Columbus crosses the Atlantic
moments.summary: Sponsored by Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain, Christopher Columbus sailed from Palos on 3 August 1492 with the Santa María, Pinta and Niña, hoping to reach Asia by sailing west. On 12 October he landed on an island its people called Guanahani, probably today's San Salvador in the Bahamas, then explored Cuba and Hispaniola. He made four voyages in all (1492–1504) and maintained that he had reached the Indies.
moments.why: His voyages began lasting contact between the Americas and Afro-Eurasia: the Columbian exchange of crops, animals and diseases, and European conquest and colonization, as Old World diseases contributed to an estimated 80–95 percent fall in Native American populations within 100–150 years.

moments.title: Vasco da Gama reaches India by sea
moments.summary: Following Bartolomeu Dias, who had rounded the Cape of Good Hope in 1488, Vasco da Gama left Lisbon on 8 July 1497 with four ships, sailed around southern Africa and, with a pilot hired at Malindi on the Swahili coast, crossed the Indian Ocean on the monsoon winds. He landed near Calicut in May 1498, but talks with its ruler, the Zamorin, went badly, and only about 55 of his men survived the voyage home in 1499.
moments.why: It opened the first sea route from Europe to Asia, breaking Venice's hold on the spice trade and launching Portugal's maritime empire in the Indian Ocean; with Columbus's voyages it marks the start of the Age of Exploration.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Portuguese discovery of the sea route to India

moments.title: The Columbian Exchange
moments.summary: After Columbus's 1492 voyage, plants, animals and diseases crossed the Atlantic in both directions. American crops such as maize, potatoes, tomatoes, cassava, chili peppers and tobacco spread across Afro-Eurasia, while wheat, rice, sugar cane, horses, cattle, pigs and sheep transformed the Americas. Old World diseases such as smallpox, first recorded in the Americas in 1518, together with war, enslavement and exploitation, cut the Indigenous population of the Americas (perhaps around 50 million before contact, though estimates vary widely) by an estimated 80 to 95 percent.
moments.why: The exchange reshaped diets, farming and populations across the world: cassava became Africa's most important food crop, while maize, potatoes and sweet potatoes fed population growth in Asia and Europe, while the peoples of the Americas suffered a demographic catastrophe.
moments.also: Silver flowed the other way: the Cerro Rico at Potosí (in today's Bolivia), discovered in 1545 and worked by Indigenous forced labour under the mita system, was the Spanish Empire's main source of silver until the 18th century, and some of it crossed the Pacific on the Manila galleons to buy Asian goods.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Population history of the Indigenous peoples of the Americas

moments.title: Luther's Ninety-five Theses and the Reformation
moments.summary: On 31 October 1517 the theologian Martin Luther sent his Ninety-five Theses, an attack on the sale of indulgences, to the Archbishop of Mainz; by tradition he also posted them on the door of All Saints' Church in Wittenberg. Several hundred printed copies circulated in Germany that year, and Luther's challenge to papal authority grew into the Protestant Reformation, carried further by reformers such as Huldrych Zwingli and John Calvin and, in England, under Henry VIII.
moments.why: The Reformation split Western Christianity into Catholic and Protestant churches, used the printing press to spread religious writing in everyday languages, and fed the European wars of religion, which killed an estimated 7 to 17 million people.

moments.title: First circumnavigation of the Earth
moments.place: Sanlúcar de Barrameda, Spain (departure and return port)
moments.summary: Five ships and about 270 men left Spain on 20 September 1519 under the Portuguese navigator Ferdinand Magellan, seeking a western route to the Spice Islands (the Moluccas). The fleet entered the strait now named after Magellan on 1 November 1520 and crossed the Pacific in 98 days, but Magellan was killed fighting Lapu-Lapu's forces at Mactan in the Philippines in April 1521. Juan Sebastián Elcano brought the last ship, the Victoria, home around Africa on 6 September 1522 with just 18 of the original crew aboard.
moments.why: The voyage, the first by Europeans across the Pacific, revealed the vast size of that ocean and proved that ships could sail around the world by a western sea route.

moments.title: Suleiman the Magnificent and the Ottoman zenith
moments.summary: Suleiman I, sultan from 1520 to 1566, had the longest reign of any Ottoman ruler. He took Belgrade in 1521 and Rhodes in 1522, broke the Kingdom of Hungary at Mohács in 1526, besieged Vienna in 1529, annexed Iraq in wars with Safavid Iran, and built a fleet that dominated the seas from the Mediterranean to the Persian Gulf. His chief architect, Mimar Sinan, is credited with over 300 buildings, including the Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul.
moments.why: His reign marked the peak of Ottoman power and culture, ruling at least 25 million subjects, while the failed siege of Vienna set the limit of the empire's advance into central Europe.

moments.title: Fall of Tenochtitlan
moments.summary: Hernán Cortés reached the Aztec (Mexica) capital Tenochtitlan in November 1519 with a small Spanish force and a far larger army of Indigenous allies, above all Tlaxcaltec warriors. After the Spaniards were driven from the city in 1520, smallpox killed an estimated 40 percent of its roughly 200,000 people, and the Spanish-led coalition besieged the island city until it surrendered on 13 August 1521 and its last ruler, Cuauhtémoc, was captured.
moments.why: The fall of the most powerful state in Mesoamerica founded New Spain, governed from Mexico City on the site of Tenochtitlan, and opened the way to Spanish rule over much of the Americas.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire

moments.title: Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire
moments.summary: On 16 November 1532, 168 Spanish soldiers under Francisco Pizarro, with Indigenous auxiliaries, ambushed the Sapa Inca Atahualpa in the main square of Cajamarca, killing thousands of his unarmed attendants and taking him prisoner. The Inca Empire, by far the largest of the great pre-Columbian civilisations, had already been weakened by epidemics and by a civil war between Atahualpa and his brother Huáscar. Atahualpa paid a ransom but was executed in July 1533, and Inca resistance continued until 1572.
moments.why: The conquest brought the Andes under Spanish rule as the Viceroyalty of Peru and launched further Spanish campaigns into present-day Chile and Colombia.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire

moments.title: Copernicus puts the Sun at the centre
moments.place: Frombork, Royal Prussia (now Poland), where Copernicus is buried
moments.summary: In 1543, shortly before his death on 24 May, the astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus published De revolutionibus orbium coelestium (On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres), printed in Nuremberg. The book replaced Ptolemy's Earth-centred system, accepted since ancient times, with a model that placed the Sun at the centre of the universe.
moments.why: It began the Copernican Revolution: once Johannes Kepler and Galileo Galilei supplied supporting evidence half a century later, the Sun-centred model became a cornerstone of the Scientific Revolution.
moments.also: Acceptance was slow: by one count, sixty years after publication only about 15 astronomers in all of Europe supported Copernicus's system.

moments.title: Akbar and the Mughal high point
moments.summary: The Mughal Empire was founded in 1526, when Babur, a Timurid prince from Central Asia, defeated Sultan Ibrahim Lodi of Delhi at the First Battle of Panipat. Babur's grandson Akbar, emperor from 1556 to 1605, extended it over much of the Indian subcontinent, built a centralised administration, won the support of non-Muslim subjects by abolishing the sectarian jizya tax, and drew scholars, poets and holy men of many faiths to his courts, including his new capital at Fatehpur Sikri (1571–1585).
moments.why: Mughal India was one of the world's great manufacturing economies, producing about a quarter of world industrial output until 1750, and its architecture culminated in the Taj Mahal under Akbar's grandson Shah Jahan.
moments.also: The empire reached its greatest extent under Aurangzeb (d. 1707), then broke up, and was formally dissolved by the British after the Indian Rebellion of 1857.

moments.title: The Atlantic slave trade
moments.place: Atlantic coast of West and Central Africa (pin: Luanda, Angola)
moments.summary: From the 16th century until well into the 19th, European and American traders bought captives from West and Central African merchants and states and shipped them across the Atlantic on the 'Middle Passage' to be sold into slavery in Brazil, the Caribbean and the rest of the Americas. An estimated 12.5 million people were carried off from Africa, of whom about 10.7 million survived the voyage.
moments.why: In the first three centuries after Columbus far more Africans than Europeans crossed to the Americas, and the trade and the slavery it fed shaped the populations, economies and societies of the Atlantic world.
moments.also: Queen Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba (in present-day Angola) fought Portuguese expansion in the 17th century. Britain banned its slave trade in 1807 and the United States soon followed, but slavery itself lasted in Brazil until 1888.

moments.title: The Qing take Beijing
moments.summary: In April 1644 Beijing fell to the rebel army of Li Zicheng, and the last Ming emperor, the Chongzhen Emperor, hanged himself in the imperial garden outside the Forbidden City. Manchu forces, aided by the defecting Ming general Wu Sangui, defeated Li at Shanhai Pass and entered Beijing in June 1644, beginning the Qing dynasty's rule over China; Ming loyalists held out in the south and on Taiwan until 1683.
moments.why: The Qing, China's last imperial dynasty, ruled until 1912, controlled more territory than any earlier Chinese dynasty and assembled the territorial base of modern China.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Transition from Ming to Qing

moments.title: Thirty Years' War and the Peace of Westphalia
moments.summary: Rooted in the religious divisions of the Holy Roman Empire that followed the Reformation, and in disputes over imperial authority, the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648) drew in Austria, Spain, Sweden, France and many German states. An estimated 4.5 to 8 million soldiers and civilians died from battle, famine or disease, and parts of Germany lost more than half their population. Treaties signed at Münster and Osnabrück in October 1648, together called the Peace of Westphalia, ended the war; earlier that year Spain and the Dutch Republic had made peace at Münster, ending the Eighty Years' War.
moments.why: Many international-relations scholars trace the principle of sovereign states that do not interfere in one another's internal affairs ('Westphalian sovereignty') to this settlement, though some historians argue that reading was a later invention.

moments.title: Newton's Principia
moments.place: London (published under the Royal Society's imprimatur)
moments.summary: Isaac Newton's Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica (Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy), approved by the Royal Society in July 1686 and published in 1687, set out his laws of motion and his law of universal gravitation. With one set of mathematical principles Newton explained Kepler's laws of planetary motion, the paths of comets, the tides and irregularities in the Moon's motion.
moments.why: The Principia became the mathematical foundation of classical mechanics and is generally considered one of the most important works in the history of science; the Enlightenment is sometimes dated from its publication.

moments.title: Glorious Revolution and the Bill of Rights
moments.summary: In November 1688 the Catholic King James II of England was deposed after an invasion by his Dutch nephew and son-in-law, William of Orange, who then ruled jointly with James's daughter Mary II. The Bill of Rights, given royal assent on 16 December 1689, barred Catholics from the throne, forbade taxation or a peacetime standing army without Parliament's consent, and set out rights including free elections, regular parliaments, freedom of debate in Parliament and protection from cruel and unusual punishment.
moments.why: It established that the Crown must govern with the consent of Parliament, and the Bill became one of the models for the United States Bill of Rights, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the European Convention on Human Rights.

moments.title: The Enlightenment and the Encyclopédie
moments.summary: The Enlightenment, an intellectual movement that emerged in Western and Central Europe in the late 17th century and peaked in the 18th, championed reason, evidence and the scientific method, and promoted individual liberty, religious tolerance, progress and natural rights. Its landmark was the Encyclopédie, edited by Denis Diderot (with Jean le Rond d'Alembert until 1759) and published in France from 1751 to 1772: 28 volumes with some 71,818 articles, which Diderot hoped would 'change the way people think'.
moments.why: Enlightenment arguments for constitutional government, natural rights and the separation of church and state were a key inspiration for the American and French revolutions and remain foundations of modern democracy.
moments.also: Leading figures included John Locke, Voltaire, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, David Hume, Adam Smith, Benjamin Franklin and Immanuel Kant.

moments.title: The Seven Years' War
moments.summary: Fought mainly between Britain and Prussia on one side and France and Austria, with Russia, Spain, Sweden and others, on the other, the Seven Years' War spread from Europe to North America, the Caribbean, West Africa, India and the Philippines. Britain's victories included Plassey in Bengal (23 June 1757) and the Plains of Abraham outside Quebec (13 September 1759); in the 1763 Treaty of Paris France ceded Canada and its other North American lands east of the Mississippi to Britain, and Louisiana to Spain. By one compilation of national estimates, the armies of the main belligerents lost roughly 900,000 dead.
moments.why: The war made Britain the leading colonial power in North America and India, where the East India Company's victory at Plassey began its rule over Bengal.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Battle of the Plains of Abraham

moments.title: Watt's steam engine and the Industrial Revolution
moments.summary: Beginning in Great Britain around 1760, the Industrial Revolution moved production from hand methods to machines driven by water and steam, and brought the mechanised factory system, first in textiles: Richard Arkwright patented his water frame in 1769. That year James Watt also patented a separate condenser that made steam engines far more efficient than Thomas Newcomen's 1712 design; built commercially by Watt and Matthew Boulton from 1776, his engines used about half as much coal for the same power, and from 1781 could turn machinery with rotary motion.
moments.why: Economic historians regard the Industrial Revolution as one of the most important events in human history, comparable to the adoption of farming: it set off an unprecedented rise in output and population and had spread to continental Europe and the United States by about 1840.

moments.title: American Revolution and independence
moments.summary: Quarrels between Britain and its Thirteen Colonies turned to war in April 1775. On 4 July 1776 the Second Continental Congress, meeting in Philadelphia, adopted the Declaration of Independence, drafted chiefly by Thomas Jefferson, which proclaimed that 'all men are created equal'. With French, Spanish and Dutch support, George Washington's Continental Army won a decisive victory at Yorktown in 1781, and Britain recognised American independence in the Treaty of Paris of 3 September 1783.
moments.why: The revolution created the United States as a republic founded on Enlightenment ideas of natural rights and government by consent, and its Declaration has become one of the most circulated, reprinted and influential documents in history.

sources.title: Wikipedia: United States Declaration of Independence
US National Archives: Declaration of Independence

moments.title: The First Fleet reaches Australia
moments.summary: Eleven British ships under Captain Arthur Phillip, carrying over 1,400 convicts, marines, sailors and officials, reached Botany Bay in January 1788 and settled instead at Sydney Cove in Port Jackson on 26 January, founding the penal Colony of New South Wales. Aboriginal Australians had lived on the continent for 50,000 to 65,000 years; the local Eora people met the newcomers with curiosity and suspicion, and an outbreak of smallpox in April 1789 killed about half the Aboriginal population of the Sydney region.
moments.why: It began the British colonisation of Australia, which brought disease, violent conflict and the dispossession of Aboriginal peoples from their lands; 26 January is still marked as Australia Day.
moments.also: In New Zealand, the Treaty of Waitangi between the British Crown and Māori chiefs (rangatira), first signed on 6 February 1840, is increasingly recognised as a founding document of the country; its English and Māori texts differ, and their meaning is still debated.

moments.title: The French Revolution
