moments.summary: Amid financial crisis and widespread distress, the Estates General met in May 1789 for the first time since 1614; the Third Estate broke away to form a National Assembly, and on 14 July crowds in Paris stormed the Bastille fortress. The Assembly abolished feudalism and issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen; the monarchy was replaced by a republic in September 1792, Louis XVI was executed in January 1793, and after the Reign of Terror the Revolution ended when Napoleon Bonaparte seized power on 9 November 1799.
moments.why: Many of its ideas are considered fundamental principles of liberal democracy, and the wars that grew out of it reshaped Europe.

moments.title: The Haitian Revolution
moments.summary: On 21 August 1791 enslaved Africans rose in revolt in Saint-Domingue, France's most profitable colony, which in 1789 produced 60 percent of the world's coffee. Through 13 years of war and shifting alliances, including British and Spanish interventions and a large French expedition sent by Napoleon in 1802, the rebels prevailed; their foremost general, the formerly enslaved Toussaint Louverture, died in a French prison in 1803, and Jean-Jacques Dessalines, who led the final campaign, declared Haiti independent at Gonaïves on 1 January 1804.
moments.why: Haiti became the first independent nation in Latin America and the first post-colonial state founded and ruled by formerly enslaved people, and its revolution's effects on slavery were felt throughout the Americas.

moments.title: Jenner's smallpox vaccine: the first vaccination
moments.summary: Edward Jenner, a country doctor in Berkeley, Gloucestershire, suspected that the pus from cowpox blisters, a mild disease caught from cows, protected people against smallpox. On 14 May 1796 he scraped material from the cowpox blisters of a milkmaid, Sarah Nelmes, into two small cuts on the arm of James Phipps, the eight-year-old son of his gardener; when Jenner later exposed the boy to smallpox matter, he did not fall ill. Jenner published his results in 1798, and his Latin name for cowpox, variolae vaccinae, gave us the words vaccine and vaccination.
moments.why: Smallpox killed about 30 percent of the people it infected and is estimated to have killed up to 300 million people in the 20th century alone; vaccination campaigns, finished by a WHO global programme, wiped it out, and in 1980 smallpox became the only human disease ever eradicated. Jenner's idea of training the body's defences in advance grew into the vaccines that, by a 2024 WHO-led estimate, have saved at least 154 million lives in the past 50 years, 101 million of them infants.
moments.also: An older and riskier method, variolation (infecting people with material from a mild case of smallpox itself), had been practised in China from around the 1500s and reached Europe from Asia in the early 18th century; Jenner himself was variolated as a schoolboy.

sources.title: World Health Organization: Global immunization efforts have saved at least 154 million lives over the past 50 years (2024)

moments.title: Napoleonic Wars and Waterloo
moments.summary: From 1803 Napoleon's France fought a series of coalitions of European powers and dominated most of the continent, until the failed invasion of Russia in 1812 and defeat in 1814 sent him into exile on Elba. Returning to power in March 1815, he was beaten for the last time on 18 June 1815 near Waterloo by the Duke of Wellington's British-led army and Gebhard von Blücher's Prussians, and abdicated four days later. Estimates of military deaths across the wars run from at least 2.8 million to as many as 5 million, alongside many civilian victims.
moments.why: The Congress of Vienna redrew Europe's borders, and Britain emerged as the world's foremost naval and economic power for the rest of the 19th century.

moments.title: Latin American independence
moments.summary: Napoleon's invasion of Spain in 1808 broke the authority of the Spanish Crown, and from 1810 juntas and revolts across Spanish America turned into wars of independence. Simón Bolívar led what are now Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Panama, Peru and Bolivia to independence and José de San Martín led the armies of the south, until Antonio José de Sucre's victory at Ayacucho on 9 December 1824 secured the independence of Peru and the rest of Spanish South America. Mexico's war (1810–1821) ended in independence, and Brazil declared independence from Portugal on 7 September 1822.
moments.why: By 1826 Spain had lost its mainland American empire, keeping only Cuba and Puerto Rico until 1898, and new independent states took shape from Mexico to Argentina and Chile.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Spanish American wars of independence

moments.title: The first inter-city railway
moments.summary: The Liverpool and Manchester Railway, built by George Stephenson and opened on 15 September 1830, was the world's first inter-city railway and the first to rely entirely on steam locomotives, with double track, signalling and timetabled services. Its engines were chosen at the 1829 Rainhill trials, where the Stephensons' Rocket was the only locomotive to complete the course, and its opening day was marred when the MP William Huskisson was killed on the line.
moments.why: Its financial success set off railway building across Britain in the 1830s, and from the 1840s railways largely replaced canals, carrying people and goods faster and cheaper than ever before.

moments.title: The Opium Wars
moments.summary: When the Qing official Lin Zexu forced British merchants at Guangzhou to hand over some 1,420 tonnes of opium and destroyed it at Humen in June 1839, Britain went to war to win compensation and open China to trade. British victories forced the Treaty of Nanjing (29 August 1842), which ceded Hong Kong Island, opened five treaty ports and imposed an indemnity; in the Second Opium War (1856–1860) Britain and France captured Beijing, burned the Old Summer Palace and forced the legalisation of the opium trade.
moments.why: Chinese nationalists later counted 1839 as the start of a 'century of humiliation' under unequal treaties, and many historians date modern Chinese history from it.
moments.also: The weakened Qing also faced the Taiping Rebellion (1850–1864), the deadliest civil war in history, in which an estimated 20 to 30 million people died.

moments.title: The electric telegraph: "What hath God wrought"
moments.summary: With $30,000 from the US Congress, the painter-turned-inventor Samuel Morse strung two copper wires on about 700 chestnut poles beside the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad between Washington and Baltimore. On 24 May 1844, from the Supreme Court chamber in the Capitol, he tapped out the Bible phrase "What hath God wrought" in his dot-and-dash code to his partner Alfred Vail at the railway's Mount Clare station in Baltimore. It was the first long-distance overland electric telegraph in the United States.
moments.why: For the first time a message could travel faster than a horse, a ship or a train. Within two decades telegraph wires crossed the United States (October 1861, ending the Pony Express), a cable under the Atlantic linked Europe and North America in 1866, Britain was wired to India in 1870 and Australia to the world in 1872, and a Pacific cable in 1902 encircled the globe; newspapers, markets, railways and governments began to work in near real time, and once a cable reached the Crimea in 1855, war news arrived in London within hours.
moments.also: Morse was not alone: in Britain William Cooke and Charles Wheatstone patented a needle telegraph in 1837 that became the first commercial telegraph system, while Morse's code, in a modified form, became the international standard in 1865.

moments.title: Indian Rebellion of 1857
moments.summary: On 10 May 1857 Indian soldiers (sepoys) of the British East India Company's army mutinied at Meerut; rebels quickly reached Delhi, where the 81-year-old Mughal ruler Bahadur Shah Zafar was declared Emperor of Hindustan, and the revolt spread through other regiments and civilian uprisings across the upper Gangetic plain and central India. British forces stormed Delhi in September 1857 and defeated the last major rebel army at Gwalior on 20 June 1858.
moments.why: The rebellion led to the dissolution of the East India Company and, under the Government of India Act 1858, to direct rule of India by the British Crown; the last Mughal emperor was exiled and the dynasty ended.

moments.title: Darwin's On the Origin of Species
moments.place: Down House, Downe, Kent (England), Darwin's home
moments.summary: Published on 24 November 1859, Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species argued that populations evolve over generations through natural selection and that the diversity of life arose by common descent, through a branching pattern of evolution. Darwin drew on evidence gathered on the voyage of HMS Beagle in the 1830s and on two decades of later research, and was spurred to publish after receiving a paper from Alfred Russel Wallace, who had reached similar ideas, in June 1858.
moments.why: The book is considered the foundation of evolutionary biology.

sources.title: Wikipedia: On the Origin of Species

moments.title: American Civil War
moments.place: Fort Sumter, Charleston, South Carolina (where the war began)
moments.summary: After Abraham Lincoln, who opposed the expansion of slavery, won the 1860 election, Southern slave states seceded to form the Confederacy, and the war began when Confederate forces bombarded Fort Sumter on 12 April 1861. Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation of 1 January 1863 declared more than 3.5 million enslaved people in Confederate territory free; General Robert E. Lee surrendered at Appomattox Court House on 9 April 1865, and the Thirteenth Amendment banned slavery throughout the United States from December 1865.
moments.why: The deadliest war in US history, it left an estimated 700,000 soldiers dead, preserved the Union and freed four million African Americans from slavery.

moments.title: Meiji Restoration
moments.summary: The arrival of the US Perry Expedition in 1853 and the unequal treaties that followed undermined the Tokugawa shogunate, which had ruled Japan since 1603. On 3 January 1868 an alliance led by the Satsuma and Chōshū domains restored political power to the young Emperor Meiji; Tokugawa resistance was defeated in the Boshin War, and Edo was renamed Tokyo, where the emperor took up residence in 1869.
moments.why: The new government dismantled the shogunal system and set Japan on a course of rapid industrialisation and Westernisation, adopting Western ideas, production methods and technology.

moments.title: Electricity for cities: Edison's Pearl Street station
moments.place: Pearl Street, Lower Manhattan, New York City (USA)
moments.summary: On 4 September 1882 Thomas Edison's Pearl Street Station in Lower Manhattan began generating electricity from coal-fired steam engines and dynamos, sending direct current through the world's first underground urban network to light about 400 of his new incandescent lamps for some 80 customers; by 1884 it served 508 customers with 10,164 lamps. London's Holborn Viaduct station had opened the same year, and in the 1880s and 1890s engineers such as George Westinghouse switched to alternating current, which could be sent over long distances, making large power grids possible.
moments.why: Central power stations turned electricity from a laboratory curiosity into a public utility that could light streets and homes and drive factory motors, which were several times more efficient than small steam engines. Electric power spread to most of humanity in the 20th century: 49 percent of the world's people had electricity in 1970 and 76 percent in 1990, though about 666 million people, most of them in sub-Saharan Africa, still lacked it in 2023.
moments.also: The small town of Godalming in Surrey, England, ran what is believed to be the first public power supply in the autumn of 1881, lighting its streets with hydroelectricity, but it was not a commercial success. In the United States 95 percent of generating capacity was alternating current by 1917.

moments.title: Berlin Conference and the Scramble for Africa
moments.summary: Organised by German chancellor Otto von Bismarck at the request of King Leopold II of Belgium, the Berlin Conference met from 15 November 1884 to 26 February 1885, when fourteen countries signed the General Act regulating European colonisation and trade in Africa, including a common framework for recognising claims backed by 'effective occupation'. As late as the 1870s Europeans controlled about 10 percent of Africa, mostly near the coasts; by 1914 only Ethiopia and Liberia remained outside European control.
moments.why: The conference gave international legal backing to a rapid wave of European claims, and the colonial states carved out in the following decades became the framework from which most modern African countries emerged.

moments.title: Battle of Adwa
moments.summary: On 1 March 1896 the army of Emperor Menelik II, estimated at 73,000 to over 100,000 men and mostly armed with modern rifles bought from France and Russia, routed an Italian colonial force under General Oreste Baratieri that was trying to impose a protectorate on Ethiopia after a dispute over the Treaty of Wuchale. Over 6,000 Italian and colonial troops were killed and about 3,800 captured, while Ethiopian losses are estimated at 4,000 to 7,000 killed; Italy was forced to recognise Ethiopia's sovereignty in the Treaty of Addis Ababa.
moments.why: Adwa kept Ethiopia independent through the Scramble for Africa, and the victory became a rallying point for later African nationalists and the Pan-African movement.
moments.also: Ethiopia remained independent until Fascist Italy occupied it in 1936; Italian rule there ended during World War II.

moments.title: The Wright brothers' first powered flight
moments.place: Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina (USA)
moments.summary: On 17 December 1903, on the windy sand dunes of Kill Devil Hills near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville Wright piloted the Wright Flyer, a fabric-covered biplane with a 12-horsepower petrol engine that he and his brother Wilbur, bicycle makers from Dayton, Ohio, had built with their mechanic Charles Taylor. The first flight lasted 12 seconds and covered 37 m (120 ft); the fourth and last flight of the day, with Wilbur at the controls, covered 260 m (852 ft) in 59 seconds. It was the first sustained, controlled flight of a powered, heavier-than-air aircraft with a person aboard.
moments.why: Within a lifetime aircraft shrank the world: Alcock and Brown flew the Atlantic in 1919, a jet aircraft flew in 1939, and humans landed on the Moon 66 years after Kitty Hawk. Air travel became a mass form of transport, with airlines carrying 4.1 billion passengers in 2017, and by the start of the First World War aircraft were already being used for reconnaissance and attacks on the ground.
moments.also: The Wrights' key breakthrough was not the engine but control: they solved how to steer and balance an aircraft in the air with "wing warping" and a movable rudder and elevator, after testing three full-sized gliders from 1900. The original 1903 Flyer hangs in the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum in Washington.

sources.title: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum: 1903 Wright Flyer

moments.title: World War I
moments.place: Latin Bridge, Sarajevo (Bosnia and Herzegovina), site of the assassination
moments.summary: On 28 June 1914 the Bosnian Serb student Gavrilo Princip assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, in Sarajevo; Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia, and within weeks Europe's alliance system had pulled the great powers into war between the Allies (the Entente) and the Central Powers. Machine guns, artillery, poison gas, aircraft and tanks made it one of the deadliest conflicts in history, with 15 to 22 million deaths, before the armistice of 11 November 1918.
moments.why: The war destroyed the Russian, German, Austro-Hungarian and Ottoman empires, and the peace settlements that followed, including the Treaty of Versailles, left unresolved tensions that helped cause World War II.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand

moments.title: Russian Revolution
moments.summary: Amid military defeats and bread shortages in World War I, the February Revolution of 1917 forced Tsar Nicholas II to abdicate on 15 March (New Style) and ended the monarchy. On 7 November (25 October, Old Style) Vladimir Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power in Petrograd, storming the Winter Palace, seat of the Provisional Government; after victory in the Russian Civil War they founded the Soviet Union on 30 December 1922.
moments.why: Lenin's government created the world's first constitutionally communist state, and the Soviet Union's rivalry with the West shaped much of the 20th century.

moments.title: The 1918 influenza pandemic
moments.place: Haskell County, Kansas (earliest probable recorded cases)
moments.summary: An H1N1 influenza virus caused an exceptionally deadly pandemic at the end of World War I and after; the earliest probable cases were documented in Haskell County, Kansas, in March 1918, though the virus's geographic origin is still uncertain. In two years an estimated 500 million people, nearly a third of the world's population, were infected, and estimates of deaths range from 17 million to 50 million, possibly as high as 100 million, with unusually high mortality among young adults.
moments.why: It was one of the deadliest pandemics in history; it was misleadingly called 'Spanish flu' because wartime censors suppressed news elsewhere while newspapers in neutral Spain reported it freely.

moments.title: Penicillin and the age of antibiotics
moments.summary: In September 1928 the Scottish doctor Alexander Fleming noticed at St Mary's Hospital in London that a Penicillium mould contaminating one of his bacterial cultures had killed the bacteria around it; he called the substance penicillin, but could not purify it. In 1940 a team at the University of Oxford led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain made concentrated penicillin and showed it cured infections, and from 1941 US laboratories and drug companies worked out how to mass-produce it, making 2.3 million doses in time for the D-Day landings in June 1944. Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
moments.why: Penicillin was one of the first medicines that could reliably cure deadly bacterial infections such as those caused by staphylococci and streptococci; in the Second World War it greatly cut deaths and amputations from infected wounds, and after 1945 it became widely available and opened the way to many more antibiotics, making common infections, surgery and childbirth far safer. Overuse has since bred resistant bacteria, which Fleming warned of in 1945: antimicrobial resistance was directly blamed for 1.27 million deaths in 2019.
moments.also: The best mould for mass production came from a mouldy cantaloupe melon bought in a market in Peoria, Illinois, in 1943, and yielded six times as much penicillin as Fleming's strain. Florey chose not to patent penicillin, having been advised that doing so would be unethical.

moments.title: Wall Street Crash and the Great Depression
moments.place: New York Stock Exchange, Wall Street, New York City
moments.summary: After a speculative boom, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell nearly 13 percent on Black Monday, 28 October 1929, and nearly 12 percent the next day, and had lost almost half its value by mid-November. The crash opened the Great Depression: between 1929 and 1932 world GDP fell by an estimated 15 percent, US unemployment reached 25 percent by 1933 and about 9,000 of the country's 25,000 banks failed, while tariffs such as the 1930 Smoot–Hawley Act helped collapse world trade.
moments.why: The Depression brought new government intervention in the economy, such as Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal, and helped fascist movements, including the Nazis in Germany, rise to power.

sources.title: Federal Reserve History: Stock Market Crash of 1929

moments.title: World War II
moments.summary: World War II began on 1 September 1939, when Nazi Germany invaded Poland and Britain and France declared war on Germany; the Soviet Union invaded Poland from the east in mid-September, and Japan had been at war with China since 1937. Fought between the Allies and the Axis powers and involving nearly every country, it ended with Germany's surrender on 8 May 1945 and Japan's on 2 September 1945. It was the deadliest conflict in history: an estimated 60 to 75 million people died, most of them civilians.
moments.why: The United States and the Soviet Union emerged as rival superpowers, setting the stage for the Cold War, while Europe's weakened powers began to lose their colonies in Africa and Asia.

moments.title: The Holocaust
moments.summary: From 1941 to 1945 Nazi Germany and its collaborators systematically murdered around six million Jews, about two-thirds of Europe's Jewish population, in mass shootings across Eastern Europe and in the gas chambers of extermination camps in occupied Poland. At the Auschwitz complex, the deadliest killing centre, at least 1.1 million people were killed, about a million of them Jews, before Soviet troops liberated it on 27 January 1945.
moments.why: The Holocaust was state-sponsored mass murder on an unprecedented scale; the Nazi regime also killed Roma and Sinti, disabled people, Soviet prisoners of war and millions of other civilians.

sources.title: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia: Documenting Numbers of Victims of the Holocaust and Nazi Persecution

moments.title: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
moments.summary: On 6 August 1945 a US B-29 bomber dropped 'Little Boy', a uranium bomb, on Hiroshima, and three days later 'Fat Man', a plutonium bomb, on Nagasaki. By the end of 1945 the bombings had killed an estimated 150,000 to 246,000 people, most of them civilians. Japan announced its surrender on 15 August, six days after Nagasaki and the Soviet Union's declaration of war and invasion of Manchuria, and signed the instrument of surrender on 2 September.
moments.why: They remain the only uses of nuclear weapons in an armed conflict, and they opened the nuclear age.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki

moments.title: The United Nations is founded
moments.place: San Francisco, USA (where the UN Charter was signed)
moments.summary: Delegates of 50 countries met in San Francisco from 25 April to 26 June 1945 to draft the Charter of the United Nations, which they signed on 26 June; it came into force on 24 October 1945 after ratification by China, France, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom, the United States and a majority of the other signatories. Succeeding the League of Nations, the UN was built around a General Assembly of all members, a Security Council in which those five powers hold permanent seats, and an International Court of Justice.
moments.why: With 193 member states today it is the world's largest international organisation, and in 1948 its General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

sources.title: United Nations: History of the UN
Wikipedia: Charter of the United Nations

moments.title: The first electronic computers
moments.place: Moore School of Electrical Engineering, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia (USA)
moments.summary: ENIAC (Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer), built in secret for the US Army by John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert at the University of Pennsylvania, was completed in 1945 and put to work on 10 December that year; it was the first programmable, electronic, general-purpose digital computer. It filled a room, weighed about 27 tonnes and used about 18,000 vacuum tubes, could calculate about a thousand times faster than electromechanical machines, and was programmed with switches and cables by six women mathematicians, among them Kay McNulty, Betty Jennings and Betty Snyder. In Britain, the codebreakers at Bletchley Park had already used Colossus, a programmable electronic machine designed by Tommy Flowers, from early 1944 to read German high-command messages, though it was built for that single job and kept secret until the 1970s.
moments.why: Electronic computers turned calculation, and later almost all information, into something machines could process at enormous speed. The transistor, invented at Bell Labs in 1947, replaced fragile, power-hungry vacuum tubes and let computers shrink from rooms to chips; more than 13 sextillion MOS transistors had been manufactured by 2018, making them the most numerous artificial objects in history, and they run everything from phones and cars to banks, hospitals and power grids.
moments.also: ENIAC's first program was a study for the hydrogen bomb, not the artillery tables it was built for. Germany's Konrad Zuse had completed the electromechanical Z3 computer in Berlin in 1941.

moments.title: Indian independence and Partition
moments.summary: At midnight on 14–15 August 1947 British rule in India ended and two independent dominions, India and Pakistan, came into existence under the Indian Independence Act. The provinces of Punjab and Bengal were divided according to Muslim or non-Muslim majorities, and Partition displaced 12 to 20 million people along religious lines amid communal violence whose death toll is estimated at 200,000 to 2 million.
moments.why: Partition created the states that are today India, Pakistan and Bangladesh, and the contested accession of the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir became a lasting source of conflict between India and Pakistan.

moments.title: The creation of Israel, the 1948 war and the Nakba
moments.summary: On 29 November 1947 the UN General Assembly voted to partition British-ruled Palestine into a Jewish state and an Arab state, with Jerusalem under international administration; Jewish leaders accepted the plan, Palestinian Arab and wider Arab leaders rejected it, and civil war broke out. On 14 May 1948, as the British Mandate ended, David Ben-Gurion proclaimed the State of Israel in Tel Aviv, and the next morning Egypt, Transjordan, Syria and Iraqi forces invaded; when the 1949 armistice agreements ended the war, Israel held about 78 percent of Mandatory Palestine, Transjordan held the West Bank and East Jerusalem, and Egypt held the Gaza Strip. During the fighting an estimated 700,000 to 750,000 Palestinian Arabs, about half the Arab population of Palestine, fled or were expelled from their homes and hundreds of Arab towns and villages were depopulated, events Palestinians call the Nakba (Arabic for "catastrophe").
moments.why: Israelis remember the war as their War of Independence, which secured the Jewish state that the Zionist movement had sought since the late 19th century; Palestinians mark the Nakba each year on 15 May, and the fate of the refugees, whose return or compensation the UN General Assembly called for in December 1948, remains a key issue in the Israeli–Palestinian conflict.
moments.also: Israel lost 6,373 people, about 1 percent of its population; Arab deaths are uncertain, with estimates in the thousands. In the three years after the war a similar number of Jews migrated, fled or were expelled from Arab states, about 260,000 of whom went to Israel.

sources.title: United Nations (Question of Palestine): About the Nakba

moments.title: People's Republic of China proclaimed
moments.summary: After the Chinese Communist Party defeated Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists in the civil war that resumed in full in 1946, Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic of China in Tiananmen Square on 1 October 1949. The Nationalist government of the Republic of China retreated to Taiwan.
moments.why: Communist rule brought sweeping social change to China, and the division between the People's Republic and the government on Taiwan that began in 1949 persists today.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Proclamation of the People's Republic of China

moments.title: Korean War
moments.summary: Korea, a Japanese colony for 35 years, was divided at the 38th parallel into Soviet and US occupation zones in 1945, and rival governments formed in 1948. On 25 June 1950 North Korea invaded the South; a US-led United Nations force came to the South's aid and China and the Soviet Union backed the North, and after two years of attritional fighting an armistice signed on 27 July 1953 created a 4-kilometre-wide Demilitarized Zone along the front line.
moments.why: The war caused around one million military deaths and an estimated 1.5 to 3 million civilian deaths, and left Korea divided under an armistice that has never been replaced by a peace treaty.

moments.title: The structure of DNA: the double helix
moments.summary: On 25 April 1953 the journal Nature published a short paper by James Watson and Francis Crick of the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge proposing that DNA, the molecule that carries genetic information, is a double helix: two strands twisted around each other, held together by pairs of bases in which A always pairs with T and C with G. Their model drew heavily on X-ray diffraction images made at King's College London by Rosalind Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling, above all "Photo 51" of May 1952, which Maurice Wilkins showed Watson without their knowledge; papers by the King's groups appeared in the same issue.
moments.why: The structure explained at once how living things copy and pass on their genetic instructions, since each strand can serve as a template for a new partner, a point the paper noted in its famous last line. It transformed biology, enabled researchers to understand the genetic code, and led to the Human Genome Project, which read most of the human DNA sequence by 2003 at a cost of about $2.7 billion.
moments.also: Watson, Crick and Wilkins received the 1962 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine; Franklin had died in 1958, and the Nobel Committee never makes posthumous nominations.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids: A Structure for Deoxyribose Nucleic Acid

moments.title: Vietnam War
moments.summary: After the First Indochina War ended French rule, Vietnam was divided between the communist North, backed by the Soviet Union and China, and the South, backed by the United States. Direct US military involvement escalated from 1965 and peaked in 1969; US forces withdrew in 1973, North Vietnamese forces captured Saigon on 30 April 1975, and the country was reunified in 1976. Estimates of Vietnamese soldiers and civilians killed range from about 970,000 to 3 million, and some 275,000–310,000 Cambodians, 20,000–62,000 Laotians and 58,220 US service members also died.
moments.why: Both a war of national liberation and a Cold War proxy war, it spilled into Laos and Cambodia, and all three countries ended up under communist governments.

moments.title: The Year of Africa
moments.summary: After Ghana became independent from Britain on 6 March 1957, decolonisation swept the continent, and in 1960 alone seventeen African countries won independence: fourteen from France, two from Britain (Somalia and Nigeria, Africa's most populous country) and one from Belgium (the Congo). The process was often violent, as in the Algerian War (1954–1962) and the Congo Crisis that followed Congolese independence.
moments.why: Between the mid-1950s and 1976 the colonial states created in the Scramble for Africa gave way to independent nations, and Africa emerged as a major force in the United Nations.

moments.title: Cuban Missile Crisis
moments.summary: On 14 October 1962 a US U-2 spy plane photographed Soviet nuclear missile sites being built in Cuba, and President John F. Kennedy imposed a naval 'quarantine' of the island on 22 October. After 13 days of confrontation, Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev announced on 28 October that the missiles would be removed, in return for a US pledge not to invade Cuba and a secret US promise to withdraw its Jupiter missiles from Turkey.
moments.why: Widely considered the closest the Cold War came to full-scale nuclear war, the crisis led to a Moscow–Washington hotline and a treaty banning atmospheric nuclear tests.

sources.title: Office of the Historian (US State Department): The Cuban Missile Crisis, October 1962

moments.title: Apollo 11: humans on the Moon
moments.summary: Launched on a Saturn V rocket from Kennedy Space Center on 16 July 1969, Apollo 11 carried Neil Armstrong, Michael Collins and Buzz Aldrin to the Moon. On 20 July Armstrong and Aldrin landed the lunar module Eagle in the Sea of Tranquility while Collins orbited in the command module Columbia; Armstrong became the first human to walk on the Moon, and the crew returned to Earth on 24 July with 21.5 kg of lunar material.
moments.why: The landing was the culmination of the US–Soviet Space Race and fulfilled President Kennedy's 1961 challenge to land a man on the Moon before the end of the decade.

moments.title: The Internet: ARPANET and TCP/IP
moments.summary: At 10:30 pm on 29 October 1969, UCLA student programmer Charley Kline tried to log in from a computer in Boelter Hall to a computer at the Stanford Research Institute over ARPANET, a network funded by the US Defense Department that broke messages into small "packets"; the remote machine crashed after two characters, so the first message ever sent was "lo", and the login worked about an hour later. During the 1970s Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn designed TCP/IP, a common set of rules that let separate networks join into one "network of networks", and on 1 January 1983, "flag day", ARPANET switched over to it for good, giving the Internet its common language.
moments.why: TCP/IP lets any computer network connect to any other, with no central control, so the Internet could grow from four computers in 1969 and 213 in 1981 to a single worldwide system. With the World Wide Web, email and later smartphones running on top of it, an estimated 6 billion people, about three-quarters of humanity, were using the Internet in 2025, transforming how people communicate, learn, shop, work and organise, although 2.2 billion remain offline.
moments.also: The World Wide Web, invented at CERN in 1989, is a service that runs on the Internet, not the Internet itself. ARPANET drew on the packet-switching ideas of Paul Baran in the US and Donald Davies in Britain.

sources.title: ITU: Facts and Figures 2025 press release

moments.title: China's reform and opening-up
moments.summary: Two years after Mao Zedong's death, the Chinese Communist Party, guided by Deng Xiaoping, launched 'reform and opening-up' on 18 December 1978, gradually opening the economy to markets and foreign investment. Shenzhen, on the border with Hong Kong, was made a special economic zone on 1 May 1980 and grew from a largely rural area into a global metropolis; China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001.
moments.why: Between 1978 and 2018 China reduced extreme poverty by 800 million people, became the world's leading manufacturing power and in 2010 overtook Japan as the world's second-largest economy.

moments.title: Soviet–Afghan War
moments.summary: In December 1979 Soviet forces entered Afghanistan to prop up its communist government against rebel mujahideen, who were backed above all by Pakistan, the United States, the United Kingdom, China, Iran, Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states. Fighting raged through the 1980s, mostly in the countryside; the war killed an estimated one to three million Afghans and drove millions more to flee as refugees, mostly to Pakistan and Iran. The Soviet Union, which lost an estimated 14,453 to 26,000 soldiers, withdrew in February 1989.
moments.why: The war added to the strains on the Soviet Union in its final years, and in Afghanistan fighting continued after the withdrawal until the Taliban seized Kabul and most of the country in 1996.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Dissolution of the Soviet Union

moments.title: The Iranian Revolution
moments.summary: Protests against Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, whose rule many Iranians saw as corrupt, repressive and too dependent on the United States, began in January 1978 after a government-planted newspaper article attacked the exiled cleric Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, and grew into a broad uprising of clerics, liberal nationalists and leftists whose strikes and mass demonstrations paralysed the country. The Shah left Iran on 16 January 1979, Khomeini returned on 1 February to a welcome by several million people, and on 11 February the army declared itself neutral and the monarchy fell. After a referendum in March 1979 Iran became an Islamic Republic, and a new constitution approved in December 1979 made Khomeini its Supreme Leader.
moments.why: The revolution replaced a pro-Western monarchy with a theocratic republic built on Khomeini's doctrine of guardianship of the Islamic jurist (velayat-e faqih), and the seizure of the US embassy in Tehran on 4 November 1979, when 52 Americans were held hostage for 444 days, caused a lasting rupture between Iran and the United States.
moments.also: The death toll is disputed: the Islamic Republic cites 60,000 "martyrs", but historians' estimates for January 1978 to February 1979 are far lower, from about 500 to 3,000.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Casualties of the Iranian Revolution
US State Department, Office of the Historian: The Iranian Hostage Crisis

moments.title: The World Wide Web
moments.summary: In March 1989 Tim Berners-Lee, an English computer scientist at the CERN physics laboratory, proposed a decentralised hypertext system for sharing information. By the end of 1990 he had a working browser, WorldWideWeb, and the first web server; the Web was released to other research institutions in January 1991 and to the whole Internet in August 1991, and on 30 April 1993 CERN made its protocols and code available royalty-free.
moments.why: After the Mosaic browser appeared later in 1993, thousands of websites sprang up within a year, setting off the Web's explosive growth into a global information system.

moments.title: Fall of the Berlin Wall
moments.summary: Amid the revolutions sweeping the Eastern Bloc in 1989, an East German press conference on 9 November prematurely announced that East Germans could travel freely; crowds gathered at Berlin's crossings, and that night puzzled border guards let them through as the world watched on live television. Communist governments fell across Central and Eastern Europe that year, and Germany was reunified on 3 October 1990.
moments.why: The fall of the Wall became a symbol of the collapse of communist rule in Europe and the end of the Cold War.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Fall of the Berlin Wall

moments.title: Dissolution of the Soviet Union
moments.summary: Economic stagnation, the burden of the arms race and foreign wars, nationalist movements in the union republics and the destabilising effects of Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms (glasnost and perestroika) eroded Soviet power. On 8 December 1991 the leaders of Russia, Belarus and Ukraine declared in the Belovezha Accords that the Soviet Union no longer existed; Gorbachev resigned on 25 December, and on 26 December 1991 the USSR was formally dissolved.
moments.why: Fifteen independent states replaced the Soviet Union, with Russia as its recognised successor, ending the Cold War world of two rival superpowers.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Dissolution of the Soviet Union

moments.title: End of apartheid
moments.summary: From 1948 South Africa's white-minority government enforced apartheid, a system of institutionalised racial segregation. In February 1990 President F. W. de Klerk announced the repeal of discriminatory laws and lifted the ban on anti-apartheid groups, and that year released Nelson Mandela after 27 years in prison; negotiations led to the country's first elections open to citizens of all races on 26–29 April 1994, won by Mandela's African National Congress with about 62 percent of the vote.
moments.why: Mandela's inauguration on 10 May 1994 as South Africa's first Black president, heading a Government of National Unity, ended minority rule; he and de Klerk shared the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize for ending apartheid peacefully.

sources.title: Nobel Prize: The Nobel Peace Prize 1993

moments.title: The genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda
moments.summary: On 6 April 1994 a plane carrying Rwanda's president Juvénal Habyarimana and the president of Burundi was shot down as it prepared to land in Kigali (responsibility is still disputed), and within hours Hutu extremists in the army and the Presidential Guard and militias such as the Interahamwe began systematically killing Tutsi civilians and moderate Hutu, among them Prime Minister Agathe Uwilingiyimana. Over about 100 days, incited by local officials and by radio broadcasts that called Tutsi "cockroaches", militias and ordinary villagers killed their neighbours, mostly with machetes, at roadblocks, in homes and in the churches and schools where victims had sought refuge, and hundreds of thousands of women were raped. The killing ended in July when the mainly Tutsi Rwandan Patriotic Front (RPF) rebel army took Kigali on 4 July and the north-west by 18 July.
moments.why: An estimated 500,000 to 800,000 people were killed, most of them Tutsi, while the outside world failed to intervene: after ten Belgian peacekeepers were murdered and countries pulled out their troops, the UN peacekeeping force was cut from 2,165 to 270. The genocide led to the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, and the flight of some two million Hutu refugees into neighbouring countries, mainly Zaire, helped trigger the Congo wars.
moments.also: Death-toll estimates differ: Human Rights Watch estimated at least half a million (about 507,000 Tutsi, roughly three-quarters of Rwanda's Tutsi population), scholarly estimates of Tutsi deaths range from about 500,000 to 662,000, and the Rwandan government's count is over one million.

sources.title: United Nations Outreach Programme on the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda: Historical background
Human Rights Watch (1999), Leave None to Tell the Story: Numbers

moments.title: 9/11 and the war in Afghanistan
moments.place: World Trade Center, New York City
moments.summary: On 11 September 2001, 19 hijackers from the Islamist terrorist organisation al-Qaeda flew airliners into the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center in New York and the Pentagon near Washington; a fourth plane crashed in Pennsylvania after its passengers fought back. The attacks killed 2,977 people. When Afghanistan's Taliban government refused to hand over al-Qaeda's leader Osama bin Laden, a US-led coalition invaded and toppled it, but the Taliban regrouped as an insurgency; after a US–Taliban deal in February 2020 and the withdrawal of US forces, the Taliban captured Kabul on 15 August 2021, and the last US military aircraft left on 30 August.
moments.why: The 20-year war, the longest in US history, killed an estimated 176,000 to 212,000 or more people, including over 46,000 Afghan civilians, and ended with the Taliban's Islamic Emirate restored.

moments.title: The smartphone: the iPhone puts the Internet in every pocket
moments.summary: On 9 January 2007, at the Macworld conference in San Francisco, Apple's Steve Jobs unveiled the iPhone as "a widescreen iPod with touch controls", "a revolutionary mobile phone" and "a breakthrough Internet communicator" in one device; it went on sale in the United States on 29 June 2007. It dropped the physical keyboard and stylus for a multi-touch screen worked with the fingers, and in July 2008 Apple opened the App Store, letting outside developers sell programs for it. Google's Android phones soon followed the same pattern.
moments.why: The smartphone turned the phone into a pocket computer, camera, map, wallet and window on the Internet. Smartphones outsold ordinary mobile phones by early 2013, when shipments passed 1 billion a year, and by 2025 82 percent of people aged 10 and over owned a mobile phone. In countries such as India, Kenya, South Africa, the Philippines and Pakistan most Internet users went online by phone rather than by computer, and in 2008 mobile phones overtook personal computers as the most common way to reach the Internet.
moments.also: Earlier smartphones, such as BlackBerry's, were aimed mainly at business users and relied on keyboards or styluses; the iPhone was aimed at the general public and quickly became Apple's most successful product.

sources.title: ITU Facts and Figures 2025: Mobile phone ownership

moments.title: Global financial crisis
moments.place: Lehman Brothers headquarters, Seventh Avenue, New York City
moments.summary: A US housing boom fuelled by risky subprime mortgages turned to bust, and from early 2007 securities tied to those loans collapsed in value, spreading losses through banks worldwide. The crisis peaked when the investment bank Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy on 15 September 2008, the largest bankruptcy in US history, triggering stock-market crashes and bank runs; governments responded with huge bank bailouts and monetary and fiscal stimulus to prevent a collapse of the financial system.
moments.why: It deepened the Great Recession (December 2007 to June 2009), the longest US downturn since World War II, in which US unemployment peaked at 10 percent, and contributed to crises in Iceland and the eurozone.

sources.title: Federal Reserve History: The Great Recession

moments.title: The Paris Agreement on climate change
moments.summary: On 12 December 2015, at the UN Climate Change Conference (COP21) at Le Bourget near Paris, 195 countries and the European Union adopted by consensus a treaty to hold the rise in global temperature to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C. Instead of imposing targets, it asks every country to set its own plan for cutting greenhouse-gas emissions, a Nationally Determined Contribution, and to submit a stronger one every five years; the agreement was signed in New York on 22 April 2016 and entered into force on 4 November 2016.
moments.why: Unlike the 1997 Kyoto Protocol, which set binding targets for only a limited set of countries, it brought developing countries into emissions planning as well, and almost every country has joined; but emissions kept rising, the United States withdrew in 2020, rejoined in 2021 and withdrew again in 2026, and 2024 was the hottest year on record, more than 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels.

sources.title: United Nations Climate Action: The Paris Agreement
Wikipedia: 2015 United Nations Climate Change Conference

moments.title: COVID-19 pandemic
moments.summary: A new coronavirus, SARS-CoV-2, was first identified in an outbreak in Wuhan, China, in December 2019 and spread worldwide in early 2020; the World Health Organization (WHO) declared a public health emergency on 30 January and described the outbreak as a pandemic on 11 March 2020. Lockdowns, travel restrictions, school closures and remote working transformed daily life, vaccines were rolled out from December 2020, and the WHO declared the global health emergency over in May 2023.
moments.why: About 7 million deaths were officially reported, but the WHO estimated 14.9 million excess deaths in 2020 and 2021 alone, and other estimates put the toll at 19 to 36 million; the pandemic also caused the largest global recession since the Great Depression.

sources.title: WHO: 14.9 million excess deaths associated with the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 and 2021

moments.title: Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine
moments.summary: In 2014, after protests in Kyiv ousted the pro-Russian president Viktor Yanukovych, Russia seized and annexed Crimea and backed separatist forces in the Donbas, where fighting killed about 14,000 people before 2022. On 24 February 2022 President Vladimir Putin announced a "special military operation" and Russian forces invaded from Belarus towards Kyiv, from Crimea in the south and from the Donbas in the east; they withdrew from around Kyiv by April, revealing the Bucha massacre, and Ukrainian counteroffensives retook most of Kharkiv Oblast and the city of Kherson in late 2022. The war then became a costly war of attrition, with Russia occupying roughly a fifth of Ukraine.
moments.why: It is the largest and deadliest war in Europe since the Second World War: estimates of military casualties (killed and wounded) on both sides range from about 1.3 million to 2 million by mid-2026, though all such figures are uncertain, and the UN had verified more than 17,000 civilian deaths, which it believes is an undercount, while 6 to 7 million Ukrainians fled abroad, Europe's largest refugee crisis since 1945.
moments.also: On 2 March 2022 the UN General Assembly voted 141 to 5, with 35 abstentions, to demand that Russia withdraw its forces from Ukraine; many countries imposed sanctions on Russia, and the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Putin and other Russian officials.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Casualties of the Russo-Ukrainian war
UN News: General Assembly resolution demands end to Russian offensive in Ukraine

moments.title: Generative AI: ChatGPT
moments.summary: On 30 November 2022 the San Francisco company OpenAI released ChatGPT, a chatbot, free to use in its basic form, built on a large language model, a generative pre-trained transformer (GPT) trained on huge amounts of text, that could answer questions, write essays and computer code, translate and summarise in everyday language. The models behind it rest on the transformer, a design introduced in 2017 by eight Google researchers in the paper "Attention Is All You Need", which has since been cited more than 150,000 times. ChatGPT gained one million users in five days and 100 million in two months, then the fastest growth of any internet application.
moments.why: ChatGPT brought artificial intelligence that can produce text, images and code into everyday use and sped up an AI boom of rapid investment and public attention; by February 2026 it had 900 million weekly users. It has raised hopes of transforming many professions, and debate over the future of work, cheating in education, misinformation, copyright and the confident but false answers known as "hallucinations".
moments.also: Transformers were first built to improve machine translation; their "attention" mechanism lets a model weigh how every word in a passage relates to every other, which turned out to work for many other tasks.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Attention Is All You Need

journeys.name: Sumerian city-states
journeys.summary: In the marshy south of Mesopotamia, Uruk and its neighbours grew into the world's first cities and, by c. 3300 BCE, the first writing. Through the Early Dynastic period (c. 2900–2334 BCE) rival city-states such as Kish, Ur, Lagash and Umma fought over land and water, until Lugalzagesi united Sumer, only to lose it to Sargon of Akkad. All dates are approximate (middle chronology).

events.text: Late Uruk period: Uruk is the leading city of southern Mesopotamia
events.detail: In the fourth millennium BCE, farming villages on the irrigated plains of southern Mesopotamia grew into the first true cities, and Uruk outgrew them all. In the Late Uruk period it covered roughly 230–250 hectares, with monumental buildings in its Eanna district and perhaps 25,000–50,000 inhabitants, far more than any rival settlement. Uruk-style outposts and colonies, such as the walled town of Habuba Kabira, spread up the Euphrates into Syria. This 'Uruk expansion' made southern Mesopotamia, the heart of the map's Sumerian territory, the most urban and influential region of the Near East.

events.text: Earliest unequivocal written documents (proto-cuneiform) appear at Uruk
events.detail: Running a city of thousands meant keeping track of grain, livestock, labour and rations, and for a long time clay tokens had been used for counting. From about 3300 BCE, in the phase archaeologists call Uruk IV, scribes at Uruk began drawing signs and numbers on clay tablets with a reed stylus: the earliest unequivocal written documents. Almost all of them are administrative records, not stories or laws. Writing gave Sumer's temples and rulers a powerful tool for managing people and goods, and its descendant, cuneiform, would be used across the Near East for more than 3,000 years.

events.text: Jemdet Nasr period: writing becomes more abstract; cities run central administrations
events.detail: After the Uruk expansion faded, the period named after the site of Jemdet Nasr (c. 3100–2900 BCE) saw southern culture continue on a more local scale, limited to south-central Iraq. Writing kept developing: pictures gave way to simpler, more abstract signs, and the script began to take on its wedge-shaped look. Tablets, cylinder seals and large central buildings suggest that a central administration rationed food and organised crafts and farming. A seal impression listing cities such as Ur, Uruk and Larsa hints at close ties between them, the network from which Sumer's city-states would emerge.

events.text: Early Dynastic period begins: rival city-states ruled by kings (lugal)
events.detail: From about 2900 BCE southern Mesopotamia was divided among independent city-states, each a large city controlling the surrounding villages, fields and canals, and each protected by its own god. The most important included Uruk, Ur, Lagash, Adab and Umma, while Kish in the north may have led a larger territorial state. Rulers bore titles such as ensi (governor) or lugal (literally 'big man', meaning king). Because these rival states competed for land and irrigation water, the map shows Sumer as a cluster of cities rather than a single kingdom for the next five centuries.

events.text: Era of Gilgamesh of Uruk and Enmebaragesi of Kish, kings of later legend
events.detail: The early centuries of the Early Dynastic period left almost no contemporary texts, so they are known mainly through later legend. Enmebaragesi of Kish is the earliest king on the Sumerian King List whose name has been found in inscriptions; scholars date him to c. 2700–2600 BCE. Gilgamesh of Uruk was probably a real king of roughly the same era, and a Sumerian poem tells of his revolt against Enmebaragesi's son Agga of Kish. Later generations made Gilgamesh a god and the hero of a famous epic, but the real political map of this 'heroic age' cannot be reconstructed.

events.text: Royal Cemetery of Ur: rich burials with goods traded from the Indus
events.detail: By the 26th century BCE Ur was among the richest cities of Sumer. Its cemetery, excavated by Leonard Woolley in the 1920s, held about 2,000 burials, including sixteen 'royal' tombs in which rulers such as Queen Puabi were buried with attendants, sometimes seventy or more. The graves were filled with gold, silver, lapis lazuli from Afghanistan and carnelian beads that point to trade with the Indus Valley. These treasures show that Sumer, which had to import all its metals, sat at the centre of a trade network reaching from the Gulf to Afghanistan and India.

events.text: Mesilim of Kish arbitrates the border war between Lagash and Umma
events.detail: Lagash and its neighbour Umma were locked in a long quarrel over the Gu-Edin, a fertile irrigated plain on their shared border. Around the middle of the third millennium (c. 2550 BCE by one estimate), Mesilim, king of Kish, who seems to have held some authority over Lagash and Adab, stepped in as arbiter. Claiming the guidance of the god Ishtaran, he fixed a new boundary and set up an inscribed pillar to mark it. The settlement did not last: a later king of Umma, Ush, tore the pillar down, and the border war flared again for generations.

events.text: Eannatum of Lagash defeats Umma; Stele of the Vultures
events.detail: Eannatum of Lagash, grandson of the dynasty's founder Ur-Nanshe, renewed the war for the Gu-Edin. Around 2450 BCE he defeated Ush of Umma, whose army, according to Eannatum's inscription, left 3,600 dead, and then imposed a boundary treaty and grain payments on Umma's next ruler, Enakalle. He celebrated the victory on the Stele of the Vultures, named after the birds shown carrying off enemy heads; its fragments are now in the Louvre. Eannatum also fought Ur, Uruk, Kish, Mari and parts of Elam, making Lagash briefly the strongest power in Sumer, though revolts soon followed.

events.text: Urukagina rules Lagash; Lugalzagesi of Umma conquers Uruk
events.detail: Urukagina (also read Uruinimgina) became ruler of Lagash after Lugalanda and is famous for inscriptions listing changes he made, such as cutting the fees officials charged for burials. Historians now doubt there was one coherent 'reform', and many lines of the texts are hard to interpret. Meanwhile Umma, Lagash's old rival, expanded under Lugalzagesi, who took Uruk in the seventh year of his reign. Lugalzagesi then ravaged Lagash and its temples, leaving Urukagina to rule only from Girsu, and the balance of power in Sumer shifted to Umma and Uruk.

events.text: Lugalzagesi rules all Sumer from Uruk, the first such kingdom on record
events.detail: Having crushed Lagash, Lugalzagesi overthrew the king of Kish and took Ur, Nippur and Larsa, making Uruk his capital. His inscriptions call him 'king of the Land' and claim that the god Enlil gave him all the lands from the Lower Sea (the Gulf) to the Upper Sea (the Mediterranean), though his westward reach may have been little more than a raid. He is the first ruler reliably documented to have united all of Sumer in one kingdom, which the Sumerian King List says lasted 25 years. For a generation the map's many city-states became a single realm centred on Uruk.

events.text: Sargon of Akkad comes to power; Lugalzagesi's kingdom falls to him
events.detail: Sargon built his power at Akkad, a city in central Mesopotamia whose site has never been found; later legend says he had begun as cupbearer to the king of Kish. Lugalzagesi's kingdom now faced this new northern rival. According to Sargon's own inscriptions, three battles were needed to defeat Lugalzagesi; Sargon tore down Uruk's walls and led the captured king in a neck-stock to Enlil's temple at Nippur. The date is debated: Sargon's reign is usually placed from c. 2334 BCE, but the conquest of Sumer is often dated nearer 2300. Sumer's age of independent city-states was over.

reigns.name: Late Uruk period: Uruk the leading city
Early Dynastic I–II: Kish and Uruk (Enmebaragesi, Gilgamesh)
Dynasty of Ur-Nanshe at Lagash (Eannatum, Entemena, Urukagina)

journeys.name: Akkadian Empire
journeys.summary: Sargon of Akkad (r. c. 2334–2279 BCE) conquered Sumer and campaigned from the Gulf to Syria and Elam, creating the first empire to rule all Mesopotamia. His grandson Naram-Sin crushed a great revolt and took the realm to its widest extent, but after Shar-kali-sharri (d. c. 2193 BCE) the state broke apart under Gutian and Amorite pressure and fell c. 2154 BCE. Dates follow the middle chronology and are approximate.

events.text: Sargon comes to power and founds a dynasty ruling from Akkad (site still unknown)
events.detail: Sargon emerged as ruler of Akkad, a small city in central Mesopotamia whose exact site is still unknown; it probably lay near where the Tigris meets the Adhem or Diyala rivers. Almost nothing reliable is known about his rise. Legends written long afterwards call him a usurper who began as cupbearer to King Ur-Zababa of Kish, and some historians suspect he was a vassal of Kish who rebelled. His reign is usually dated c. 2334–2279 BCE, though other estimates run 2316–2277. For perhaps 18 years or more his power seems to have been limited to the north.

events.text: Sargon defeats Lugalzagesi in three battles, razes Uruk's walls and takes Sumer
events.detail: The turning point of Sargon's career was his clash with Lugalzagesi, who ruled a united Sumer from Uruk. According to Sargon's inscriptions, three battles were needed to defeat Lugalzagesi and his allies; Sargon 'conquered fifty governors', razed Uruk's walls and led the captured king in a neck-stock to Enlil's temple at Nippur. The date is debated but is usually put around 2300 BCE. Sumer's cities became provinces under governors, some of them 'sons of Akkad', and for the first time the whole of southern Mesopotamia answered to a single king.

events.text: Sargon takes Mari and claims the 'Upper Country' to the Cedar Forest
events.detail: With Sumer secured, Sargon turned to Syria, then dominated by Mari on the middle Euphrates, Nagar and Ebla. One of his year-names records the destruction of Mari, and an inscription says the god Dagan at Tuttul gave him 'the Upper Land: Mari, Yarmuti and Ebla as far as the Cedar Forest and the Silver Mountains'. Sargon also boasted of 34 victorious battles and of ships from Dilmun, Magan and Meluhha docking at Akkad. These campaigns stretched Akkad's reach towards the Mediterranean and the Taurus, though how firmly the west was held is uncertain, and the date here is approximate.

events.text: Sargon dies; Rimush reconquers rebel cities including Ur, Umma and Lagash
events.detail: Sargon died c. 2279 BCE (other estimates are 2284 or 2277), and his son Rimush inherited an empire whose conquered cities still remembered independence. Rimush's inscriptions describe widespread revolts and the reconquest of Ur, Umma, Adab, Lagash, Der and Kazallu, claiming tens of thousands of enemies killed or captured. He also campaigned east against Elam and Marhashi. His reign was short, about nine years according to the Sumerian King List, and a later tradition says his own courtiers killed him. Still, he held Sargon's empire together and kept Sumer within its borders.

events.text: Manishtushu leads a fleet down the Gulf against 32 kings; takes Anshan
events.detail: Rimush's brother Manishtushu became king c. 2270 BCE and, free of the revolts that had troubled his brother, looked outward. According to his inscription, he sent ships across the 'Lower Sea' (the Persian Gulf), defeated an alliance of 32 cities on the far shore, plundered as far as the silver mines, and brought back black stone for a statue of himself. He also conquered Anshan in Elam, and Akkadian governors came to rule Elam and Pashime on the Iranian coast. He died c. 2255 BCE after about fifteen years, possibly murdered by his courtiers, with Akkad's grip on south-western Iran tightened.

events.text: Naram-Sin succeeds; under him the empire reaches its greatest extent
events.detail: Naram-Sin, Manishtushu's son and Sargon's grandson, ruled c. 2255–2218 BCE, and under him the Akkadian state reached its greatest extent. He defeated the ruler of Magan, fought hill peoples of the Zagros, Taurus and Amanus mountains, and destroyed Armanum and Ebla in Syria, claiming the Amanus, the 'Cedar Mountain' and the Upper Sea. He was the first king to call himself 'King of the Four Quarters', meaning ruler of the whole world. On the map, Akkad's power now stretched from the Gulf and western Iran to northern Syria and the Mediterranean coast.

events.text: Victory Stele: Naram-Sin defeats the Lullubi of the Zagros
events.detail: The Lullubi were a mountain people of the Zagros, astride routes between Mesopotamia and the Iranian plateau. Naram-Sin's army defeated them and their chief Satuni, a victory celebrated on a 2-metre stele of pinkish limestone dated only to his reign. Breaking with older art, it shows the battle climbing diagonally up a mountain, with Naram-Sin at the top wearing a horned helmet, a sign of divinity. Victories like this carried Akkad's power into the Zagros on the empire's eastern edge. Over a thousand years later the Elamite king Shutruk-Nakhunte carried the stele off to Susa; it is now in the Louvre.

events.text: Naram-Sin crushes the Great Revolt and is proclaimed a god
events.detail: At an uncertain point in Naram-Sin's reign, a huge coalition rose against Akkad, led by Iphur-Kish of Kish and Amar-Girid of Uruk and joined by Nippur, Sippar, Kutha, Borsippa and other cities, as well as Amorite highlanders. Naram-Sin claimed that he won nine battles in a single year and captured the kings the rebels had raised. Afterwards, his inscription says, the people of Akkad asked the great gods to make him the god of their city. He became the first Mesopotamian king to claim divinity, and the empire came through intact.

events.text: Shar-kali-sharri succeeds; wars with Gutians, Amorites and Elam
events.detail: Naram-Sin's son Shar-kali-sharri reigned for about 25 years (c. 2218–2193 BCE). His year-names suggest a fairly peaceful reign with recurring clashes: a victory over the Amorites (MAR.TU) at Jebel Bishri in Syria, the capture of a Gutian king, and a battle against Elam and Zahara near Akshak. Economic texts suggest reasonable prosperity. Yet the Gutians were growing stronger and at some point made Adab, in Sumer, their capital. Later tradition held that the empire began to unravel during his reign, as outsiders and restless provinces tested Akkad's strength.

events.text: Shar-kali-sharri dies; anarchy: 'Who was king? Who was not the king?'
events.detail: When Shar-kali-sharri died c. 2193 BCE, no successor could hold the empire together. The Sumerian King List sums up the chaos with a famous question, 'Then who was king? Who was not the king?', naming four rivals, Igigi, Imi, Nanum and Ilulu, who together ruled only three years. Southern cities such as Lagash and Uruk began to reassert their independence, while Gutians, Amorites and Elamites pressed in. Many historians also link the collapse to a severe drought, the '4.2-kiloyear event', that struck Upper Mesopotamia, as Akkad's territory shrank back towards its northern core.

events.text: Reign of Shu-turul ends; Akkad's empire is gone as Gutians dominate
events.detail: After the anarchy, Dudu and then his son Shu-turul ruled a much-reduced kingdom of Akkad in northern Babylonia, including Kish, Tutub, Nippur and Eshnunna. Shu-turul, said to have reigned 15 years, is known only from a few seals and votive objects. With his death c. 2154 BCE the Sumerian King List says kingship passed to Uruk, while the Gutians, based at Adab, became the main regional power and southern cities such as Ur and Lagash ruled themselves. The first empire in Mesopotamian history disappeared from the map, but Sargon and Naram-Sin remained models for later kings.

journeys.name: Third Dynasty of Ur (Neo-Sumerian Empire)
journeys.summary: After the Gutian interlude, Ur-Nammu of Ur (r. c. 2112–2094 BCE) reunited Sumer and Akkad, and his son Shulgi built a centralised, bureaucratic state of some twenty provinces ringed by a military periphery along the Zagros. Amorite incursions, revolts and the breakaway of Isin weakened his successors, and c. 2004 BCE an Elamite coalition sacked Ur. Dates follow the middle chronology and are approximate.

events.text: Ur-Nammu takes power at Ur and founds the Third Dynasty
events.detail: After Akkad fell, Sumer was split between Gutian rulers and revived city-states, until Utu-hengal of Uruk defeated the Gutian king Tirigan. Ur-Nammu, who had governed Ur and may have been Utu-hengal's brother, then took power himself c. 2112 BCE, defeated his former masters at Uruk and conquered Lagash. Taking the title 'King of Sumer and Akkad', he reunited southern Mesopotamia, restored temples and canals, and began the Great Ziggurat of Ur. The oldest surviving law collection, the Code of Ur-Nammu, is linked to him or his son. Sumer was once again a single kingdom, now ruled from Ur.

events.text: Ur-Nammu dies in battle in the eastern highlands; Shulgi begins a 48-year reign
events.detail: Ur-Nammu pushed his rule north-east towards the Diyala valley, probably defeating the Elamite king Puzur-Inshushinak along the way. After about 18 years on the throne he died on the battlefield in the eastern highlands; a later poem, the 'Death of Ur-Nammu', mourns him, and some read it as saying his army abandoned him. His son Shulgi succeeded c. 2094 BCE and reigned for about 48 years, roughly half the life of the whole dynasty. Shulgi would turn his father's kingdom into an empire on the model of Akkad, although his first twenty years are known mostly from temple-building.

events.text: Shulgi, a god by his 21st year, reforms weights, taxes and the bureaucracy
events.detail: Around the middle of his reign Shulgi carried out reforms that reshaped the state, though some may have begun under his father and few can be dated exactly. He reorganised the army, standardised weights and measures, reformed writing and the scribal schools, and unified taxes, including the bala system in which each province took turns supplying the centre. A huge livestock and administrative hub was built at Puzrish-Dagan near Nippur. By his 21st year, and perhaps as early as his 12th, Shulgi had proclaimed himself a god. The result looked like a highly centralised state, at least in its Sumerian core.

events.text: Shulgi destroys Simurrum: first of many campaigns in the Zagros
events.detail: Shulgi's later reign was dominated by wars in the Zagros foothills and along the upper Tigris, lands rich in pasture and trade routes. His 25th year-name records the destruction of Simurrum, a mountain kingdom north of the Diyala; later names boast of destroying it a second, a third and eventually a ninth time, showing how hard such enemies were to hold down. Conquered districts became a defensive, tribute-paying periphery with garrisons and military colonies, rather like the Roman frontier. On the map, Ur's power now reached north-east from Sumer towards the Zagros.

events.text: Shulgi's daughter marries the governor of Anshan in Elam
events.detail: Alongside war, Shulgi used marriage diplomacy with the kingdoms of the Iranian plateau. In his 18th year a daughter became queen of Marhashi, and the name for his 30th year records that the governor of Anshan, in Elam, married another daughter; others married rulers of Pashime. Such ties did not guarantee peace: by his 34th year Shulgi was campaigning against Anshan, and a year-name records its destruction. The kings of Ur also controlled Susa, where Shulgi built temples, so Elam's western lowlands were drawn firmly into Ur's orbit.

events.text: Shulgi builds a wall to keep out Tidnum (Amorite) nomads
events.detail: Amorites (Martu), Semitic-speaking groups from Syria and Upper Mesopotamia often described as tribal and nomadic, had been moving into southern Mesopotamia since late Akkadian times. In his 37th year Shulgi built 'the wall of the land' in the north of Akkad to keep out the Tidnum, an Amorite group. The wall marked the empire's north-western frontier and showed that pressure from the steppe had become a lasting worry. His successors had to reinforce it, and Amorite incursions eventually played a major part in the empire's collapse.

events.text: One campaign defeats Urbilum, Simurrum, Lullubum and Karhar
events.detail: The climax of Shulgi's wars came near the end of his reign. The name for his 45th year boasts that he 'smashed the heads of Urbilum, Simurrum, Lullubum and Karhar in a single campaign'. Urbilum is Arbela (modern Erbil in northern Iraq), and the other lands lay in the Zagros foothills; around the same time he destroyed Kimash and Hurtum near Elam. These victories pushed Ur's ring of tribute-paying border lands to its widest, stretching along the Tigris and the Zagros from Urbilum to Susa, and made Ur the leading power of Mesopotamia.

events.text: Shu-Sin succeeds and builds a new wall against Amorite incursions
events.detail: After Shulgi died, his son Amar-Sin reigned about nine years, followed by Amar-Sin's brother Shu-Sin (c. 2037–2029 BCE). Shu-Sin had to reassert control in the northern and eastern borderlands, where tribute was arriving less regularly, a sign that Ur's grip was loosening. The most threatening danger came from Amorites in the north-west, and after an open revolt he built a new fortified wall between the Euphrates and the Tigris, strengthening Shulgi's defences. Late in his reign much real power lay with his chancellor Aradmu. The borders held for now, but the outer lands were slipping.

events.text: Ibbi-Sin succeeds; within three years the central archives dry up
events.detail: Ibbi-Sin, probably Shu-Sin's son, came to the throne c. 2028 BCE and reigned for 24 years while the empire fell apart. The archives of the main administrative centres in the heartland dry up after his third year, a sign that the central bureaucracy had lost control of the provinces. Eastern lands such as Anshan and Susa broke away, Eshnunna became independent, and Amorite raids grew more violent. In his seventh and eighth years the price of grain rose to some 60 times normal, pointing to famine. On the map, Ur's empire shrank towards the city of Ur itself.

events.text: Ishbi-Erra holds Isin under his own year-names, breaking from Ur
events.detail: Ishbi-Erra, an official described as a 'man of Mari', had been sent by Ibbi-Sin to buy grain at Isin and Kazallu. According to letters preserved as later school exercises, whose authenticity is uncertain, he complained that Amorite raids stopped him shipping it and asked to be made governor of Isin and Nippur. By Ibbi-Sin's eighth year he was dating documents by his own year-names, in effect declaring independence at Isin. His power grew as Ibbi-Sin's declined, splitting the former empire in two, and his dynasty of Isin would later present itself as Ur's heir.

events.text: Elamites under Kindattu sack Ur, ending the dynasty
events.detail: By the end Ibbi-Sin held little beyond the city of Ur. Around 2004 BCE (middle chronology) an army from Elam and the Shimashki highlands of the Zagros, led by King Kindattu, sacked Ur and carried Ibbi-Sin off in chains to Elam, where he died. The disaster was remembered in the 'Lament for Sumer and Ur', which describes the city reduced to ruin mounds. The Elamites occupied Ur until Ishbi-Erra of Isin drove them out. The fall of Ur ended the last great Sumerian state, and Mesopotamia split into rival Amorite-led kingdoms such as Isin and Larsa.

journeys.name: Old Babylonian Empire (Hammurabi)
journeys.summary: Hammurabi (r. c. 1792–1750 BCE) turned Babylon from one Amorite kingdom among many into the master of Mesopotamia, conquering Larsa, Mari and Eshnunna and issuing his famous law code. Under his son Samsu-iluna revolts wrecked the southern cities and the far south broke away as the Sealand dynasty; a shrunken kingdom lasted until the Hittite king Mursili I sacked Babylon c. 1595 BCE. Dates follow the middle chronology and are approximate.

events.text: Hammurabi succeeds Sin-muballit as king of Babylon
events.detail: Since the fall of Ur, Mesopotamia had been divided among kingdoms ruled by Amorite dynasties. Babylon was a secondary city where an Amorite dynasty had taken root about a century earlier and built a modest kingdom including Kish, Sippar and Borsippa. When Hammurabi succeeded his father Sin-muballit in 1792 BCE (middle chronology), he was surrounded by stronger neighbours: Rim-Sin's Larsa in the south, Eshnunna in the Diyala valley, and Shamshi-Adad's kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia, with whom Babylon kept good relations. For two decades he mostly built temples and canals.

events.text: Hammurabi conquers Larsa and annexes Rim-Sin's kingdom in the south
events.detail: After helping to repel an Elamite invasion of Mesopotamia, Hammurabi turned on Rim-Sin of Larsa, the long-reigning king who had earlier absorbed Isin and Uruk. Citing Rim-Sin's poor support against Elam and alleged raids, he launched a lightning war with help from his ally Zimri-Lim of Mari. Larsa was besieged until its defenders ran short of food; Babylonian troops took the walls and brought Rim-Sin out alive. With Larsa annexed in 1763 BCE (some accounts say 1764), Hammurabi controlled all of southern Mesopotamia and took the old title 'king of Sumer and Akkad'.

events.text: Hammurabi takes Mari on the Euphrates; its palace is destroyed by 1759
events.detail: Mari, on the middle Euphrates, was a rich trading kingdom whose palace archives of more than 25,000 tablets are a key source for this age. Its king Zimri-Lim had been Hammurabi's ally, but the two fell out, apparently over Babylonian ambitions in the Jebel Sinjar region. The course of the war is not recorded, but the outcome is clear: Mari was captured around 1761 BCE and destroyed by 1759, ending its archive. Babylon now controlled the Euphrates route towards Syria, and the map's Babylonian realm stretched far upstream.

events.text: Ekallatum in Assyria is subjugated; Eshnunna has already been beaten
events.detail: North of Babylon, Eshnunna in the Diyala valley had been weakened by the Elamite war. Hammurabi first allied with its new king, Silli-Sin, who married one of his daughters, but then defeated it, a victory named in his 32nd year. The name for his next year boasts that he subjugated Mari and 'the many cities of Subartu', including Ekallatum on the Tigris, once the seat of Shamshi-Adad's son Ishme-Dagan, and Assyria was reduced to a vassal. Babylon was now master of almost all Mesopotamia, from the Gulf to the upper Tigris.

events.text: Code of Hammurabi set up late in his reign
events.detail: Near the end of his reign, Hammurabi had his laws inscribed on stone monuments. The best-preserved copy is a basalt stele 2.25 metres tall, topped by a relief of the king before Shamash, the sun god and god of justice. Its prologue says the gods chose him 'to prevent the strong from oppressing the weak', and its rulings, written as 'if this, then that' cases, cover crime, family, property and trade, including 'an eye for an eye'. The exact date is uncertain (often c. 1753 BCE). Taken to Susa as Elamite plunder centuries later, the stele was found in 1901 and is now in the Louvre.

events.text: Hammurabi dies; his son Samsu-iluna succeeds
events.detail: Hammurabi died around 1750 BCE, in the 43rd year of his reign, apparently after a long illness; his son Samsu-iluna seems to have been running the kingdom in his final months. In four decades Hammurabi had turned Babylon from one Amorite kingdom among many into the master of Mesopotamia, and the city would remain the region's leading centre for over a thousand years. But his empire had been won by conquest within a single lifetime, and many newly conquered cities still remembered independence. Samsu-iluna inherited a realm that would soon start to shrink.

events.text: Rim-Sin II's revolt spreads to 26 cities; first known Kassite attack repelled
events.detail: In Samsu-iluna's ninth year (c. 1741 BCE), a man calling himself Rim-Sin, perhaps a nephew of the king Hammurabi had defeated, led a revolt from Larsa. It spread to some 26 cities, including Uruk, Ur and Isin in the south and Eshnunna in the north. Within a year Samsu-iluna broke the northern rebels and had the king of Eshnunna executed. That same year he turned back an invading Kassite army, the earliest known mention of the people who would later rule Babylonia. The kingdom survived the shock, but the south remained at war.

events.text: Samsu-iluna retakes Larsa; Ur and Uruk sacked, the south largely abandoned
events.detail: For several years Samsu-iluna's armies fought Rim-Sin II's forces across the borderlands between Babylon, Sumer and Elam. Eventually he attacked Ur, pulled down its walls and sacked it, then did the same to Uruk and Isin, before finally defeating Larsa.
