wars.name: Hundred Years' War
wars.summary: The kings of England held the Duchy of Aquitaine (Gascony) as vassals of the French crown, a long source of friction. When Philip VI confiscated it in 1337, Edward III answered by claiming the French throne through his mother. The war that followed was a series of campaigns broken by long truces. In the Edwardian phase England won at Sluys, Crécy and Poitiers, captured King John II and gained an enlarged Aquitaine at Brétigny in 1360. Under Charles V the French recovered almost everything. Henry V reopened the war, won at Agincourt in 1415, conquered Normandy and, allied with Burgundy during a French civil war, was named heir to France by the Treaty of Troyes. Joan of Arc's relief of Orléans in 1429 and Burgundy's return to the French side in 1435 turned the tide; with better artillery and a professional army, France took Normandy and Gascony, leaving England only Calais after Castillon in 1453.
wars.casualties: Estimates are very uncertain: one widely repeated compilation counts about 185,000 soldiers killed in battle and some 556,000 military deaths in all, while raiding, famine and the Black Death killed far more civilians, especially in France.

events.label: May 1337
events.text: Philip VI confiscates Aquitaine; Edward III claims France
events.detail: Edward III held Gascony, the remnant of the Duchy of Aquitaine, as a vassal of the French king, and the French crown had long sought to assert its sovereignty there. In May 1337 Philip VI's Great Council declared the duchy forfeit, citing Edward's breach of his duties as vassal and his shelter of Philip's enemy Robert of Artois. Edward replied by reviving his claim to the French throne through his mother Isabella, sister of the last Capetian king.

events.label: 26 Jan 1340
events.text: Flemish towns proclaim Edward III King of France
events.detail: The cloth towns of Flanders depended on English wool, and Edward courted them and other Low Countries princes as allies. On 26 January 1340 he received homage as king of France from Guy, half-brother of the count of Flanders, and the civic authorities of Ghent, Ypres and Bruges proclaimed him their king. Adopting the French title let his Flemish supporters claim they were loyal to the true king of France rather than rebels against their overlord.

events.label: 24 Jun 1340
events.text: English fleet destroys the French navy at Sluys
events.detail: Edward sailed from England with a fleet of some 120–150 ships and found the much larger French fleet drawn up in defensive formation in the inlet off Sluys in Flanders. Attacking in the afternoon with the wind and sun behind them, the English almost destroyed the French fleet. England dominated the Channel for the rest of the war, which kept the fighting on French soil and made a French invasion of England impractical.

events.text: War of the Breton Succession becomes a second front
events.detail: With Edward's money running out, the war might have ended, but the death of the duke of Brittany in 1341 started a succession dispute between John of Montfort and Charles of Blois, nephew of Philip VI. Edward backed Montfort and Philip backed Blois, and for years the war centred on Brittany, where towns such as Vannes changed hands several times. The English-backed Montfort finally won the duchy in 1364.

events.label: 12 Jul 1346
events.text: Edward III invades Normandy and sacks Caen
events.detail: Edward landed at Saint-Vaast-la-Hougue on the Cotentin peninsula with complete surprise and marched south, his soldiers razing towns and looting as they went. The army captured the rich city of Caen in a single day, then turned north-east, pillaging toward the Low Countries. Finding the Seine bridges destroyed, Edward crossed at Poissy near Paris and then forded the Somme at Blanchetaque, slipping away from Philip's pursuing army.

events.label: 26 Aug 1346
events.text: English longbowmen rout the French at Crécy
events.detail: Unable to outmarch Philip VI, Edward chose a defensive position near Crécy. Genoese mercenary crossbowmen were driven back in an archery duel by English and Welsh longbowmen, and the French knights then launched a series of disordered cavalry charges into arrow fire and dismounted men-at-arms. The French suffered heavy losses, including many nobles, and Philip had allowed the attack to begin before his army was ready.

events.label: 17 Oct 1346
events.text: Scots invade England and are defeated at Neville's Cross
events.detail: Scotland had been bound to France by the Auld Alliance since 1295. Philip appealed to the Scots to relieve the pressure by invading northern England, and King David II led an army south. Near Durham, at Neville's Cross, it was defeated and David himself was captured. The defeat greatly reduced the Scottish threat to England for the following years and freed Edward to continue his campaign in France.

events.text: Calais falls to the English after a long siege
events.detail: After Crécy, Edward marched north unopposed and besieged the Channel port of Calais, which held out until it surrendered in 1347. The town became England's main base in France, letting it land and supply troops safely in the north. Calais stayed English long after the war ended, until the French retook it in 1558. Together with Crécy and Neville's Cross, its capture capped a run of English successes in 1346–1347.

events.text: The Black Death reaches Paris
events.detail: The plague pandemic that swept Europe arrived in Paris in 1348 and killed a very large share of the population of both kingdoms; estimates for France run to 6–12 million deaths, 30–60 percent of the population, and for England 2–3 million. Fighting was largely suspended while the epidemic raged. The losses strained recruitment and royal finances on both sides, and English campaigning on a large scale resumed only in 1355.

events.text: The Black Prince's great raid from Gascony to Narbonne
events.detail: Edward III's eldest son, Edward of Woodstock, later called the Black Prince, led a chevauchée, a mounted raid designed to ruin the enemy's lands and revenue, from Bordeaux across southern France. His army pillaged Avignonet, Castelnaudary, Carcassonne and Narbonne. Such raids, repeated throughout the war, burned towns and crops and fell hardest on the peasants of France rather than on its armies.

events.label: 19 Sep 1356
events.text: Black Prince captures King John II at Poitiers
events.detail: On a second raid the Black Prince was overtaken near Poitiers by King John II. The French, some 14,000–16,000 strong, attacked about 6,000 Anglo-Gascons in a strong defensive position. A mounted force led by the Gascon captal de Buch, hidden in a wood, struck their flank and cut off their retreat, and John and many nobles were captured. With the king a prisoner, his son the Dauphin Charles ruled as regent amid growing disorder.

events.label: Easter 1360
events.text: Hailstorm devastates Edward's army: 'Black Monday'
events.detail: Edward invaded France a third time, hoping to be crowned at Reims, but the city held out for five weeks, and the Dauphin refused battle. After skirmishes outside Paris the English moved toward Chartres, where a freak hailstorm struck their camp at Easter and killed more than 1,000 men. The disaster pushed Edward to negotiate when the French approached him.

events.label: 8 May 1360
events.text: Treaty of Brétigny gives England a greatly enlarged Aquitaine
events.detail: Drafted at Brétigny near Chartres and ratified at Calais in October, the treaty gave Edward full sovereignty over a much larger Aquitaine, including Gascony, Poitou, Saintonge, Limousin and other lands, plus Calais and Ponthieu. In return he gave up Normandy, Touraine, Anjou and Maine and his claim to the French crown. John II's ransom was set at three million écus, with hostages held as guarantee.

events.text: War resumes as Charles V backs Gascon lords and Castile
events.detail: In Castile's civil war the Black Prince restored Peter of Castile by winning the battle of Nájera, but the campaign left him in debt. His new hearth tax in Aquitaine provoked Gascon lords to appeal to Charles V, who summoned the prince to Paris; the prince refused, and war broke out again in 1369. That year Henry of Trastámara, backed by France, killed Peter, and Castile became an important French naval ally.

events.text: Castilian fleet defeats the English off La Rochelle
events.detail: Castile's new Trastámara regime repaid French support with naval help. In 1372 a Castilian fleet defeated an English fleet off La Rochelle, an important port in western France. The defeat weakened English control of the sea routes to Aquitaine, and under the cautious strategy of Charles V and his constable Bertrand du Guesclin, who avoided pitched battles, the French steadily took back English-held towns.

events.text: By Charles V's death, England holds only Calais and a few ports
events.detail: Charles V's small professional army under du Guesclin had pushed the English back so far that when the king died in 1380, the vast lands won at Brétigny had shrunk to Calais and a few coastal towns. The Black Prince had died in 1376 and Edward III in 1377, and England, ruled for the boy king Richard II, faced heavy war taxation and the Peasants' Revolt of 1381.

events.label: 18 Jun 1389
events.text: Truce of Leulinghem begins a long pause in the war
events.detail: With the war unpopular in England and neither side able to pay for major campaigns, negotiations led to the three-year Truce of Leulinghem, signed on 18 June 1389. Renewed several times, it brought a long lull. In the following decades Charles VI of France suffered bouts of madness, and the rivalry of the dukes of Burgundy and Orléans turned into civil war between Burgundians and Armagnacs, both of which sought English help.

events.label: 25 Oct 1415
events.text: Henry V wins a crushing victory at Agincourt
events.detail: Henry V landed in August 1415 and took Harfleur after a long siege. Marching toward Calais with a tired, hungry army, he was forced to fight a much larger French army near Agincourt. English archers and men-at-arms on a narrow, muddy field inflicted catastrophic losses, killing many leaders of the Armagnac faction. Fearing an attack, Henry ordered most of the French prisoners, perhaps thousands, to be killed.

events.label: 10 Sep 1419
events.text: Murder of John the Fearless drives Burgundy into alliance with England
events.detail: Henry conquered Normandy, taking Caen in 1417 and Rouen in January 1419. Meanwhile the Burgundians had seized Paris in 1418. On 10 September 1419 Duke John the Fearless of Burgundy was killed by one of the Dauphin Charles's attendants during a meeting on the bridge at Montereau, and his son Philip the Good allied formally with England. The Anglo-Burgundian alliance gave Henry control of Paris and much of northern France.

events.label: 21 May 1420
events.text: Treaty of Troyes makes Henry V heir to the French throne
events.detail: Sealed at Troyes with the insane Charles VI, the treaty disinherited the Dauphin Charles and named Henry and his heirs successors to the French crown. Charles VI remained king for life, and Henry married his daughter Catherine of Valois. Henry entered Paris later that year. The Dauphin, holding much of France south of the Loire, rejected the treaty, so the war became a contest between two claimants.

events.label: 17 Aug 1424
events.text: English destroy the Dauphin's army at Verneuil
events.detail: Henry V died in August 1422, two months before Charles VI, leaving a baby son, Henry VI, as king of England and, by the treaty, of France. His brother the Duke of Bedford ran English France. At Verneuil in Normandy, Bedford's archers devastated a Franco-Scottish army, virtually destroying the Dauphin's field army and ending the Scots' role as a major force in France for the rest of the war.

events.label: Apr–May 1429
events.text: Joan of Arc helps lift the English siege of Orléans
events.detail: The English had besieged Orléans, the key to the Loire valley, since October 1428, and hunger threatened to force its surrender. Joan of Arc, a peasant girl who said God had sent her to drive out the English, persuaded the Dauphin to send her there, and she entered the city on 29 April. Within days the revived French attacked the English forts and the siege was lifted, followed by victories along the Loire and at Patay.

events.label: 16 Jul 1429
events.text: The Dauphin is crowned Charles VII at Reims
events.detail: The victory at Patay, where French cavalry broke the English rearguard and captured John Talbot, opened the road through English- and Burgundian-held country to Reims, the traditional coronation city. Charles was crowned there on 16 July 1429, strengthening his claim against the Treaty of Troyes. An attack on Paris in September failed, and Henry VI was crowned king of France in Paris in 1431.

events.label: 30 May 1431
events.text: Joan of Arc is burned at the stake in Rouen
events.detail: Burgundian troops captured Joan at Compiègne in May 1430 and handed her to the English. At Rouen, the seat of English government in France, a church court led by Pierre Cauchon, bishop of Beauvais and an ally of the English, convicted her, and she was burned on 30 May 1431. A later church inquiry overturned the verdict about 25 years afterwards, and she became a lasting French national symbol.

events.label: Sep 1435
events.text: Burgundy changes sides at the Congress of Arras
events.detail: England, France and Burgundy met at Arras in the summer of 1435 in what has been called Europe's first real peace congress. The English demands were seen as unrealistic, and after they left, Philip the Good of Burgundy made peace with Charles VII in the Treaty of Arras, recognising him as king. The loss of its main ally was a severe blow to England, and the treaty returned Paris to the French king.

events.label: 15 Apr 1450
events.text: French victory at Formigny completes the recovery of Normandy
events.detail: During long truces Charles VII reorganised his army into a professional force with powerful artillery that could take castles in days. The French retook Rouen in 1449. At Formigny an English army marching to relieve Caen was attacked by the Count of Clermont and then struck in flank and rear by Arthur de Richemont. It was the last significant English field army in Normandy, and the remaining strongholds soon fell.

events.label: 17 Jul 1453
events.text: French artillery defeats the English at Castillon
events.detail: Charles VII turned to Gascony, England's last province; Bordeaux surrendered in 1451, but its people, largely sympathetic to the English, welcomed back an army under John Talbot in October 1452. At Castillon, Talbot attacked a French camp laid out by the artillery master Jean Bureau and was cut down by its cannon. Talbot and his son were killed in what is usually considered the last battle of the war.

events.label: 19 Oct 1453
events.text: Bordeaux surrenders, ending English rule in Gascony
events.detail: The fall of Bordeaux ended English rule in Gascony and the fighting of the Hundred Years' War. England kept only Calais. No peace treaty was signed until 1475, when the Treaty of Picquigny formally ended the war, and English and later British monarchs kept the title king of France until the early nineteenth century. Defeat abroad fed the discontent that led to the Wars of the Roses in England.

wars.name: Wars of the Roses
wars.summary: The Wars of the Roses were a series of English civil wars for the throne between two branches of the royal Plantagenet family: the House of Lancaster and the House of York, both descended from Edward III. Defeat in the Hundred Years' War, powerful private retinues and the weak rule of the mentally unstable Lancastrian king Henry VI fed rivalries at court, and Richard, Duke of York, pressed his own claim. Fighting began at St Albans in 1455. York was killed at Wakefield in 1460, but his son seized the crown as Edward IV and crushed the Lancastrians at Towton in 1461. After the Earl of Warwick changed sides, Henry VI was briefly restored in 1470, but Edward won back the throne at Barnet and Tewkesbury in 1471. When Edward's brother took the throne as Richard III in 1483, the Lancastrian heir Henry Tudor defeated and killed him at Bosworth in 1485, married Edward IV's daughter Elizabeth of York, and beat a last Yorkist challenge at Stoke Field in 1487.
wars.casualties: Estimates vary widely: one modern compilation suggests about 105,000 killed in battle over the whole period, while many historians think the fighting was more limited, and the 28,000 dead reported after Towton is generally considered an exaggeration.

events.label: 22 May 1455
events.text: First Battle of St Albans: York captures Henry VI
events.detail: Henry VI's mental instability and the dominance at court of his Beaufort relatives, above all Edmund Beaufort, Duke of Somerset, drove Richard, Duke of York, and his allies the Neville earls of Salisbury and Warwick to take up arms. They defeated a royal army in the streets of St Albans, north of London. Somerset was killed and the king captured, and a parliament then appointed York Lord Protector. The battle is traditionally taken as the start of the wars.

events.label: 23 Sep 1459
events.text: Yorkists defeat a larger Lancastrian army at Blore Heath
events.detail: Queen Margaret of Anjou, determined to protect the rights of her young son Edward, had been raising support for the Lancastrian cause. When the Earl of Salisbury marched to join York with about 5,000 men, a Lancastrian force twice that size under Lord Audley ambushed him at Blore Heath in Staffordshire. The Lancastrians were defeated and Audley was killed, and open war resumed after four years of uneasy peace.

events.label: Autumn 1459
events.text: Yorkist army scatters at Ludford Bridge; leaders flee abroad
events.detail: The Yorkist leaders gathered near Ludlow, but at Ludford Bridge their army fell apart when Warwick's professional troops from Calais, under Andrew Trollope, defected to the king. York fled to Ireland with his second son, Edmund, while Warwick and Salisbury sailed to Calais with York's heir, Edward, Earl of March. The Lancastrians appeared to have won, but the exiles soon prepared to return.

events.label: 10 Jul 1460
events.text: Yorkists win at Northampton and capture the king again
events.detail: Warwick and Edward of March landed from Calais and marched north against the royal army. At Northampton, by the River Nene, they defeated the forces loyal to Henry VI; the Duke of Buckingham, the Earl of Shrewsbury and other Lancastrian lords were killed defending the king, who was taken prisoner. It was the first battle in England in which artillery was used. Queen Margaret fled north and then to Scotland.

events.label: 25 Oct 1460
events.text: Act of Accord makes York heir to the throne
events.detail: Returning from Ireland, York laid his hand on the empty throne in Parliament to signal his claim, shocking even his allies. Unable to decide the claim on legal grounds, the lords reached a compromise in the Act of Accord: Henry VI would remain king for life, but the throne would then pass to York and his heirs, disinheriting Henry's son, Prince Edward. Queen Margaret and many Lancastrian nobles refused to accept it.

events.label: 30 Dec 1460
events.text: Richard of York killed at Wakefield
events.detail: Margaret and the Lancastrian lords massed their armies in the north, and York marched to confront them, and was near Sandal Magna, by Wakefield, at the end of December. In what recent research suggests was a small-scale skirmish rather than a full battle, York, his son Edmund, Earl of Rutland, and the Earl of Salisbury were captured and killed. York's claim passed to his eldest son, Edward, Earl of March.

events.label: 2 Feb 1461
events.text: Edward of March wins at Mortimer's Cross
events.detail: In the Welsh Marches, York's son Edward defeated a Lancastrian army at Mortimer's Cross. At dawn a parhelion made three suns appear in the sky; Edward reassured his frightened troops that it stood for the Holy Trinity and showed God's blessing, and he later took the 'sun in splendour' as his personal badge. The captured Owen Tudor, husband of Henry V's widow Catherine of Valois, was executed by his troops.

events.label: 17 Feb 1461
events.text: Lancastrians win the Second Battle of St Albans and free Henry
events.detail: Margaret's army, moving south after Wakefield, met Warwick, who had the captive Henry VI with him, astride Watling Street at St Albans. Warwick's entrenched army was defeated and the king was freed. Yet the Lancastrian cause was unpopular in London, where the queen's army had been promised the freedom to plunder on its march south, and the citizens refused to let it in. Warwick joined Edward, and the two hurried to London, where Edward was proclaimed king as Edward IV.

events.label: 29 Mar 1461
events.text: Edward IV crushes the Lancastrians at Towton
events.detail: Edward marched north to settle the war. On Palm Sunday, near Towton in Yorkshire, perhaps 50,000 men fought for about ten hours in a snowstorm; the wind blew snow into the faces of the Lancastrian archers, whose arrows fell short. It was probably the largest and bloodiest battle ever fought on English soil. Many Lancastrians were killed in the rout, Henry fled the country, and Edward was formally crowned in June.

events.label: 15 May 1464
events.text: Last Lancastrian army in the north destroyed at Hexham
events.detail: Lancastrian resistance continued in the far north, where a rising for Henry broke out in spring 1463. After truces with Scotland and France cut off foreign help, a Yorkist force under John Neville destroyed the main Lancastrian army at Hexham; its commanders, including the Duke of Somerset, were captured and executed. Henry VI was later caught hiding near the River Ribble and imprisoned in the Tower of London.

events.label: 26 Jul 1469
events.text: Warwick turns on Edward IV; royal army beaten at Edgcote
events.detail: Warwick, once Edward's chief supporter, was alienated when the king married Elizabeth Woodville against his advice in 1464, promoted her family and turned away from Warwick's policy of friendship with France. In 1469 Warwick rebelled, hoping to replace Edward with his brother George, Duke of Clarence. Rebels led by 'Robin of Redesdale' defeated a royal army at Edgcote, its commanders were executed, and Edward was held prisoner until Warwick, lacking support, had to let him resume his rule.

events.label: 3 Oct 1470
events.text: Readeption: Warwick restores Henry VI to the throne
events.detail: After a failed rising in 1470, Warwick and Clarence fled to France, where Louis XI reconciled Warwick with his old enemy Queen Margaret. They invaded through Dartmouth and Plymouth in September, Edward was forced to flee abroad, and Warwick freed Henry VI from the Tower. Henry, now too frail to rule unaided, was restored as king on 3 October 1470, with Warwick in effective control. The map keeps the Yorkist colour for this brief restoration.

events.label: 14 Mar 1471
events.text: Edward IV returns, landing at Ravenspurn
events.detail: With some money, ships and men from his brother-in-law Charles the Bold of Burgundy, and backing from Flemish merchants, Edward landed at Ravenspurn in Yorkshire, his ships scattered by bad weather. Hull refused to let him in, but with the Earl of Northumberland's support he gathered troops as he marched south. The restored Lancastrian regime was divided, and Clarence deserted Warwick to rejoin his brother. Bad weather kept Queen Margaret and her son, with French troops, from crossing the Channel to reinforce Warwick.

events.label: 14 Apr 1471
events.text: Warwick 'the Kingmaker' killed at Barnet
events.detail: On Easter Day the armies met near Barnet, north of London, in thick mist. In the confusion, the star badge of the Lancastrian Earl of Oxford was mistaken for Edward's sun, and Lancastrians attacked their own men. Edward's determined assault broke Warwick's army; Warwick and his brother John Neville were killed in the rout. Victory at Barnet began fourteen years of Yorkist rule.

events.label: 4 May 1471
events.text: Lancastrian heir killed at Tewkesbury; Henry VI dies
events.detail: Margaret and Prince Edward landed at Weymouth on the day of Barnet and, with an army raised in the West Country, marched north to join Jasper Tudor's Lancastrians in Wales. Edward IV caught them at Tewkesbury and completely defeated them. Prince Edward, the Lancastrian heir, was killed, and many Lancastrian nobles died in the battle or were executed after it. Henry VI died in the Tower soon afterwards, probably murdered. Edward ruled securely until his death in 1483.

events.label: 26 Jun 1483
events.text: Richard III takes the throne; the princes disappear
events.detail: Edward IV died in April 1483, leaving his twelve-year-old son Edward V, with the boy's uncle Richard, Duke of Gloucester, as Lord Protector. Before the coronation, Edward IV's marriage was declared invalid and his children illegitimate, and an assembly proclaimed Richard king. Edward V and his younger brother, the 'Princes in the Tower', were not seen in public after that summer; their fate remains a mystery.

events.label: Oct–Nov 1483
events.text: Buckingham's rebellion fails; the duke is executed
events.detail: Former supporters of Edward IV, joined by Richard's one-time ally the Duke of Buckingham, rose against the new king in October 1483, backed by Edward's widow Elizabeth Woodville and Lady Margaret Beaufort, mother of the exiled Lancastrian claimant Henry Tudor. Storms wrecked Henry's attempt to invade from Brittany, Richard easily put down the revolt, and Buckingham was executed at Salisbury on 2 November.

events.label: 7 Aug 1485
events.text: Henry Tudor lands in Wales with French support
events.detail: Henry Tudor, descended from Edward III through his mother Margaret Beaufort, had promised to marry Elizabeth of York, Edward IV's eldest daughter, which won over many Yorkists. With French troops he sailed from Harfleur and landed at Mill Bay, near Dale on Milford Haven, in his native Wales. He marched inland gathering support, while Richard III mustered his army to intercept him.

events.label: 22 Aug 1485
events.text: Richard III killed at Bosworth; Henry Tudor becomes king
events.detail: Near Market Bosworth in Leicestershire, Richard's larger army attacked, but the Earl of Northumberland did not join in and the Stanleys held back. Richard gambled on a charge to kill Henry himself; Sir William Stanley's men then intervened and Richard was killed, the last English king to die in battle. Henry was crowned Henry VII, and Bosworth is often seen as the end of the Plantagenet dynasty. The exact battlefield site is disputed.

events.label: 18 Jan 1486
events.text: Henry VII marries Elizabeth of York, uniting the two claims
events.detail: Crowned at Westminster Abbey on 30 October 1485, Henry VII kept his promise and married Elizabeth of York. Their children would inherit both the Lancastrian and Yorkist claims, a union later symbolised by the Tudor rose, which combined the white rose of York with the red rose that Henry adopted for Lancaster. Their first son, Arthur, was born that September. Yet plots by Yorkist sympathisers continued.

events.label: May 1487
events.text: Yorkist rebels gather in Ireland around the pretender Lambert Simnel
events.detail: Yorkist plotters presented a boy, Lambert Simnel, as the imprisoned Earl of Warwick, Clarence's son and the male heir of York. John de la Pole, Earl of Lincoln, Richard III's nephew, went to Burgundy, where his aunt Margaret, Duchess of Burgundy, gave him money and soldiers. The rebel fleet reached Dublin on 4 May 1487, where the Earl of Kildare helped recruit Irish troops before the invasion of England.

events.label: 16 Jun 1487
events.text: Henry VII defeats the last Yorkist rising at Stoke Field
events.detail: Lincoln's army of German and Swiss mercenaries, Irish troops and English Yorkists met Henry at East Stoke in Nottinghamshire. The battle may have been slightly larger than Bosworth, with heavier casualties, and Henry won a crushing victory; Lincoln and most of the other Yorkist commanders fell fighting. Simnel was captured and pardoned, and given work in the royal kitchen. It was the last battle between rival claimants descended from Lancaster and York.

wars.name: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire
wars.summary: In 1519 Hernán Cortés sailed from Cuba with a few hundred Spaniards, defying the governor who had cancelled his expedition. Landing on the Gulf coast, he won over the Totonacs of Cempoala, who resented Aztec tribute, and after a series of battles made an alliance with Tlaxcala, the Aztecs' unconquered enemy. In November 1519 Moctezuma II received him in Tenochtitlan, and Cortés soon held the emperor hostage. A massacre of Aztec nobles in May 1520 set off an uprising, and on La Noche Triste (30 June 1520) the Spaniards and their allies fled the city with heavy losses. Sheltered by Tlaxcala, Cortés rebuilt his forces while smallpox ravaged the Valley of Mexico and killed the new emperor, Cuitláhuac. From Texcoco, with thirteen brigantines and tens of thousands of Indigenous allies, he besieged Tenochtitlan from May 1521. The city fell on 13 August 1521, when Cuauhtémoc was captured, and New Spain was built on its ruins.
wars.casualties: Estimates vary widely: about 1,800 Spaniards are estimated to have died over the whole campaign and many thousands of their Indigenous allies, while an estimated 100,000 to 240,000 Aztec warriors and civilians were killed, besides the far larger toll of the 1520 smallpox epidemic.

sides.name: Spain and its Indigenous allies (Tlaxcala, Totonacs, Texcoco and others)

events.label: 10 Feb 1519
events.text: Cortés's expedition leaves Cuba
events.detail: Two earlier Spanish voyages had touched the coasts of Yucatán and the Gulf of Mexico and heard of a rich empire inland. Diego Velázquez, governor of Cuba, chose Hernán Cortés to lead a third expedition, then cancelled his commission. Cortés sailed anyway in February 1519 with 11 ships carrying about 630 men, a few horses and some cannon, following the route of the first voyage along the Yucatán coast.

events.label: 24 Mar 1519
events.text: Potonchán makes peace and gives Cortés the interpreter Malintzin
events.detail: After defeating the Chontal Maya of Potonchán, on the Tabasco coast, in two battles, Cortés received their submission on 24 March 1519, with gifts that included twenty enslaved women. One of them, a Nahua woman the Spaniards called Doña Marina and the Nahuas Malintzin, spoke both Maya and Nahuatl. Working with Gerónimo de Aguilar, a shipwrecked Spaniard who spoke Maya, she let Cortés talk to the Aztecs, and she became his chief interpreter and adviser.

events.label: 22 Apr 1519
events.text: Cortés lands on the Gulf coast near San Juan de Ulúa
events.detail: The fleet anchored off San Juan de Ulúa, and the Spaniards came ashore on Good Friday, 22 April 1519. Envoys of the Aztec emperor Moctezuma II soon arrived with lavish gifts, and Cortés tried to impress them with a display of cannon fire and horses. The gifts were meant to persuade the strangers to leave, but they only convinced Cortés that great wealth lay inland.

events.label: Jun 1519
events.text: Veracruz is founded and the Totonacs of Cempoala ally with Cortés
events.detail: To escape the authority of Governor Velázquez, Cortés had his men found a town, La Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz, whose council named him its captain. At Cempoala, capital of the Totonacs, he persuaded the ruler Xicomecoatl to rebel against the Aztecs, and Moctezuma's tax collectors were seized. Cortés then sank his ships so that his men could not return to Cuba.

events.label: 2–5 Sep 1519
events.text: Battles with the Tlaxcalans
events.detail: Marching inland from 16 August with Totonac porters and warriors, the Spaniards entered the lands of Tlaxcala, a confederacy that had resisted the Aztecs for generations. Otomí and Tlaxcalan armies attacked them in a series of battles from 2 to 5 September 1519 and the fighting went on for days. Unable to destroy the Spaniards, and seeing them as enemies of Moctezuma, Tlaxcala's leaders chose to make peace.

events.label: 23 Sep 1519
events.text: Cortés enters Tlaxcala: the alliance that decided the war
events.detail: On 23 September 1519 Cortés entered the city of Tlaxcala, welcomed by its rulers Maxixcatzin and Xicotencatl the Elder, who saw the Spaniards as allies against the Aztecs. Tlaxcala had been encircled and blockaded by the empire for decades. Its warriors, porters and supplies, and its refuge after defeats, would make the conquest possible: tens of thousands of Tlaxcalans fought beside the Spaniards to the end.

events.label: 18 Oct 1519
events.text: The Cholula massacre
events.detail: Moctezuma's envoys steered Cortés through Cholula, a great sacred city that had broken with Tlaxcala to become an Aztec tributary. Claiming that the Cholulans planned an ambush, and urged on by his Tlaxcalan allies, Cortés had the city's nobles seized and killed in the main temple courtyard, and the city was sacked. Cortés reported about 3,000 dead and other witnesses far more; the massacre frightened other cities into negotiating.

events.label: 8 Nov 1519
events.text: Moctezuma receives Cortés in Tenochtitlan
events.detail: Crossing the mountains between the volcanoes, the Spaniards and their allies entered Tenochtitlan along the southern causeway on 8 November 1519. The island capital had an estimated 60,000 to more than 300,000 people, one of the largest cities in the world. Moctezuma met Cortés on the causeway and lodged the Spaniards in the palace of his father Axayacatl, at the heart of the city.

events.label: 14 Nov 1519
events.text: Cortés takes Moctezuma hostage
events.detail: After Aztec forces on the coast killed several Spaniards left at Veracruz, Cortés and his captains forced Moctezuma to move into the Spaniards' quarters, where he was held from 14 November 1519. The emperor kept ruling in name, under Cortés's control, and was made to swear allegiance to the Spanish king and hand over his treasure, while resentment grew among the Aztec nobility.

events.label: May 1520
events.text: Massacre at the Great Temple during the Toxcatl festival
events.detail: Cortés had left Pedro de Alvarado in charge of the small garrison in Tenochtitlan. During the festival of Toxcatl in May 1520, Alvarado, suspecting a plot, had his men close the temple courtyard and attack the unarmed nobles and dancers, killing many. The city rose in arms, and the Spaniards and their Tlaxcalan allies were besieged in their palace. Moctezuma, still a captive, was made to call for calm.

events.label: 27 May 1520
events.text: Cortés defeats Narváez at Cempoala
events.detail: Governor Velázquez sent Pánfilo de Narváez with some 900 Spaniards and 19 ships to arrest Cortés, and Narváez made Cempoala his base. Leaving Tenochtitlan with a few hundred men, Cortés attacked by night on 27 May 1520 with Chinantec allies, captured Narváez and won over most of his soldiers with promises of riches. Some of the newcomers carried smallpox, which then spread inland.

events.label: 30 Jun 1520
events.text: La Noche Triste: the Spaniards flee Tenochtitlan
events.detail: Cortés returned to the besieged palace on 24 June, but the city's nobles had chosen a new ruler, Cuitláhuac, and Moctezuma was killed in late June, by stones from his own people according to the Spaniards, by the Spaniards according to Aztec accounts. On the rainy night of 30 June 1520 Cortés broke out along the Tlacopan causeway. Hundreds of Spaniards and thousands of Tlaxcalans were killed, drowned or captured, and most of the treasure was lost.

events.label: 7 Jul 1520
events.text: Battle of Otumba
events.detail: The survivors retreated north around the lakes, harassed all the way. On 7 July 1520, on the plain near Otumba, a large Aztec army blocked their road to Tlaxcala. Cortés and his horsemen charged the Aztec commander, the cihuacoatl Matlatzincatl, and killed him, and the Aztec army broke off. Days later the exhausted, mostly wounded Spaniards reached Tlaxcala, whose rulers refused Aztec offers and kept the alliance.

events.label: Aug 1520
events.text: The Tepeaca campaign
events.detail: To rebuild his reputation and secure the roads to the coast, Cortés led Spaniards and Tlaxcalans against Tepeaca, an Aztec tributary whose people had killed Spaniards, from early August 1520. Tepeaca was defeated and became an allied town. Other tributary towns, seeing the Aztecs unable to protect them, began to change sides, while Cortés received reinforcements from ships arriving on the coast.

events.label: 4 Dec 1520
events.text: Smallpox kills the emperor Cuitláhuac
events.detail: Smallpox, unknown in the Americas, spread through the Valley of Mexico from the autumn of 1520 for about seventy days. Many thousands died, and others starved because no one was well enough to feed them. The emperor Cuitláhuac died on 4 December 1520, after ruling for eighty days; he was succeeded early in 1521 by Cuauhtémoc. The epidemic also struck Tlaxcala, killing the ruler Maxixcatzin.

events.label: 26 Dec 1520
events.text: Cortés marches on Texcoco, which becomes his base
events.detail: On the day after Christmas 1520 Cortés left Tlaxcala with his Spaniards and more than 10,000 Tlaxcalan warriors under Chichimecatecuhtli, and crossed into the Valley of Mexico. At Texcoco, once the Aztecs' partner in the Triple Alliance, he installed a friendly ruler, Ixtlilxochitl II. Texcoco, on the eastern shore of the lake, became the base from which the siege of Tenochtitlan was prepared.

events.label: Apr 1521
events.text: Cortés circles the lakes and fights at Xochimilco
events.detail: Having won over Chalco and Tlalmanalco and beaten Aztec forces around Chalco in March 1521, Cortés set out in April with some 20,000 allied warriors on a circuit of the southern and western lakeshore. He fought a hard battle at Xochimilco, Tenochtitlan's ally, then found Coyoacán, Tlacopan and Azcapotzalco deserted, and returned to Texcoco, where thirteen brigantines built from Tlaxcalan timber were nearly ready.

events.label: 26 May 1521
events.text: The siege of Tenochtitlan begins
events.detail: Three columns, each of about 200 Spaniards and 8,000 Indigenous warriors, took up positions on the lakeshore at Tlacopan under Pedro de Alvarado, Coyoacán under Cristóbal de Olid and Iztapalapa under Gonzalo de Sandoval. Alvarado and Olid cut the aqueduct from Chapultepec that carried the city's fresh water. Cortés launched the thirteen brigantines, which scattered the Aztec canoes and took control of the lake.

events.label: 30 Jun 1521
events.text: Aztec victory on the causeway: Spanish prisoners sacrificed
events.detail: Cortés ordered a combined push into the city towards the great market of Tlatelolco but failed to fill in a breach behind his men. The Aztecs counter-attacked, Cortés was wounded and nearly captured, and dozens of Spaniards were taken alive and sacrificed at the Great Temple in sight of their comrades. Many allies briefly left the besiegers, but the blockade held and famine spread in the city.

events.label: 1 Aug 1521
events.text: The besiegers reach the marketplace of Tlatelolco
events.detail: Advancing street by street along the causeways, the Spaniards and their allies razed each district they took and used the rubble to fill the canals. By the start of August they had broken into the market square of Tlatelolco, in the north of the island, where Alvarado's men set fire to the temple. The defenders, starving and drinking brackish water, were penned into the last corner of the city.

events.label: 13 Aug 1521
events.text: Tenochtitlan falls and Cuauhtémoc is captured
events.detail: On 13 August 1521 Cuauhtémoc tried to escape across the lake by canoe and was captured by one of Sandoval's brigantines, and the last defenders surrendered. Tens of thousands had died in the siege, and allied warriors killed many of the survivors. The Aztec Empire ended; its tributary cities passed under Spanish rule, and Mexico City, capital of New Spain, was built on the ruins.

sources.title: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire (Wikipedia)

wars.name: Imjin War (Japanese invasions of Korea)
wars.summary: Having unified Japan, Toyotomi Hideyoshi planned to conquer Ming China and demanded passage through Korea. When the Joseon court refused, about 158,000 Japanese troops landed at Busan in May 1592. Armed with arquebuses and hardened by Japan's civil wars, they took Hanseong (Seoul) in less than three weeks and Pyongyang in July, while Katō Kiyomasa pushed into the far north-east. But Admiral Yi Sun-sin's navy won a string of victories that cut Japanese supply lines by sea, Korean Righteous Armies rose behind the lines, and in early 1593 a Ming army retook Pyongyang. The Japanese fell back to forts on the south coast while Ming and Japanese envoys negotiated. The talks collapsed in 1596, and in 1597 Hideyoshi sent a second invasion, which destroyed the Korean fleet but was halted short of Hanseong at Jiksan and at sea at Myeongnyang. Hideyoshi's death in September 1598 led Japan to withdraw; at Noryang in December Yi Sun-sin was killed in the last battle. The war devastated Korea and strained the Ming treasury.
wars.casualties: Estimated at well over a million Korean civilian and military deaths, with tens of thousands of Koreans carried off to Japan, more than 100,000 Japanese and over 30,000 Ming soldiers killed, though all figures are uncertain.

events.label: 23–24 May 1592
events.text: Japanese armies land at Busan and storm its fortress
events.detail: Having unified Japan, Toyotomi Hideyoshi demanded passage through Korea to conquer Ming China, and when the Joseon court refused he sent an army of about 158,800 soldiers, labourers and sailors in nine divisions. Konishi Yukinaga's First Division landed at Busan on 23 May 1592. The next day it stormed the fortress of Busanjin, commanded by Chŏng Pal, killing most of the garrison and many townspeople. Korea, at peace for two centuries, was badly prepared, and its defences in the south collapsed.

events.label: 25 May 1592
events.text: Dongnae falls after a last stand by its governor
events.detail: Konishi's troops moved on to the walled town of Dongnae just north of Busan. Its prefect, Song Sanghyŏn, refused to let them pass, and the town was stormed after hours of fighting; about 3,000 defenders were killed by Korean count. The other Japanese divisions landed behind the first, and three columns, under Konishi, Katō Kiyomasa and Kuroda Nagamasa, began a race north along separate roads towards the capital, Hanseong (Seoul).

events.label: 3 Jun 1592
events.text: Konishi routs General Yi Il at Sangju
events.detail: The court sent General Yi Il south to stop the invaders on the central road, but he found only a few hundred raw troops at Sangju. On 3 June 1592 Konishi's veterans, armed with thousands of arquebuses, surrounded and destroyed his small army; Yi Il escaped and fled north. The Japanese musketeers, trained in the long civil wars of the Sengoku period, were far superior to Korean troops in open battle in the early months of the war.

events.label: 7 Jun 1592
events.text: Sin Rip's army is destroyed at Chungju
events.detail: General Sin Rip, Korea's most famous commander, chose not to hold the Choryong pass and instead deployed his cavalry on open ground at Tangeumdae, near Chungju, with rivers behind it. On 7 June 1592 Konishi's arquebusiers broke the Korean charges and drove the army into the rivers, where many drowned; Sin Rip took his own life. Chungju was the last organised defence before the capital, and King Seonjo fled north.

events.label: 10 Jun 1592
events.text: Konishi's First Division enters the abandoned capital Hanseong
events.detail: The court had already left Hanseong, and parts of the city, including the offices holding the slave registers, had been looted and burned by its own people. Konishi's division reached the capital first, on 10 June 1592, less than three weeks after landing, with Katō's division arriving soon after. King Seonjo withdrew to Pyongyang and later to Uiju on the Chinese border, and the Korean court appealed to the Ming emperor, its overlord, for help.

events.label: 16 Jun 1592
events.text: Yi Sun-sin wins his first victory, at Okpo
events.detail: While Japan's armies swept north, the navy of Jeolla province under Admiral Yi Sun-sin sailed east from its base at Yeosu. On 16 June 1592 it surprised a Japanese transport fleet anchored at Okpo on Geoje island and destroyed 26 ships without losing one of its own. It was the first of a series of naval victories, won with sturdy panokseon warships and heavy cannon, that began to threaten the Japanese supply line from Busan.

events.label: 6–7 Jul 1592
events.text: The Japanese cross the Imjin River
events.detail: A Korean army of about 10,000 held the north bank of the Imjin river, the barrier on the road from Hanseong to Pyongyang, and the Japanese waited there for two weeks without boats. Then the Japanese feigned a retreat; the Korean troops crossed in pursuit and were ambushed and destroyed on 6–7 July 1592. The road north lay open: Kato turned north-east into Hamgyong province, while Konishi and Kuroda marched on Pyongyang.

events.label: 19–24 Jul 1592
events.text: Konishi takes Pyongyang
events.detail: King Seonjo fled Pyongyang on 19 July 1592, and the panic his departure caused spread to the defenders. A Korean night attack across the Taedong river failed, and when the retreating troops showed the Japanese a ford, the defenders abandoned the city. Konishi's First Division entered Pyongyang on 24 July and found its granaries intact. Konishi halted there, waiting for supplies and reinforcements that the Korean navy and guerrilla attacks were making ever harder to deliver.

events.label: 15 Aug 1592
events.text: Yi Sun-sin destroys a Japanese fleet off Hansan Island
events.detail: Hideyoshi ordered his admirals to destroy the Korean navy. Wakisaka Yasuharu's fleet of about 73 ships was lured out of the narrow strait of Gyeonnaeryang into open water off Hansan Island, where Yi Sun-sin's 56 warships, including turtle ships, closed round it in a crane-wing formation. On 15 August 1592 most of the Japanese fleet was destroyed. Hansan ended Japanese plans to supply their armies by sea along the west coast.

events.label: 23 Aug 1592
events.text: A first Ming force is beaten back at Pyongyang
events.detail: The Ming court was busy with a revolt at Ningxia, but it sent a small force of about 6,000 men under General Zu Chengxun across the Yalu. On 23 August 1592 it attacked Pyongyang in heavy rain, broke into the city and was cut to pieces in the streets by Konishi's musketeers; Zu escaped with a few survivors. The defeat convinced the Ming that a much larger army would be needed, while envoys bought time with truce talks.

events.label: 30 Aug 1592
events.text: Katō Kiyomasa reaches Hoeryong and captures two Korean princes
events.detail: Katō Kiyomasa's Second Division of more than 20,000 men crossed to the east coast, took Hamhung, the capital of Hamgyong province, and beat the provincial army at Songjin on 23 August. On 30 August it entered Hoeryong near the Tumen river, where two Korean princes and the governor had already been seized by local people and handed over. Katō even raided across the Tumen against the Jurchens. But Korean partisans soon rose across Hamgyong and retook its northern towns.

events.label: 8–13 Nov 1592
events.text: Kim Si-min repels a Japanese army at Jinju
events.detail: Jinju guarded the road from Gyeongsang into the rich province of Jeolla, which had escaped invasion and fed the Korean war effort. About 30,000 Japanese troops besieged the fortress, held by Kim Si-min with some 3,800 soldiers and a few thousand irregulars and 170 newly made arquebuses. After six days of assaults with siege towers and ladders the Japanese gave up on 13 November, having lost heavily; Kim Si-min was mortally wounded. Jinju became a symbol of Korean resistance, alongside the Righteous Armies.

events.label: 6–8 Feb 1593
events.text: Ming and Korean troops retake Pyongyang
events.detail: In January 1593 a Ming army of about 40,000 under Li Rusong crossed the Yalu and, with Korean troops and monk soldiers, reached Pyongyang on 5 February. Its cannon battered the walls, and after three days of assaults Konishi abandoned the city on the night of 8 February and retreated south, losing thousands of men. The Japanese gave up most of the north. Katō Kiyomasa, in danger of being cut off, withdrew from Hamgyong province in the following weeks.

events.label: 27 Feb 1593
events.text: The Japanese halt Li Rusong's advance at Byeokjegwan
events.detail: Confident after Pyongyang, Li Rusong pushed on towards Hanseong with an advance force, mostly cavalry. At the post station of Byeokjegwan, north of the capital, on 27 February 1593 it ran into a much larger Japanese army under Kobayakawa Takakage and was driven back with heavy losses in the mud. Li withdrew to Kaesong and then Pyongyang, and the two sides settled into a stalemate along the line from Kaesong to Hanseong.

events.label: 14 Mar 1593
events.text: Kwon Yul's garrison beats off a Japanese assault at Haengju
events.detail: General Kwon Yul fortified the hill fort of Haengjusanseong on the Han river west of Hanseong with about 2,300 soldiers, monks and townspeople. On 14 March 1593 some 30,000 Japanese attacked it in waves through the day, but the defenders, using cannon, rocket carts and stones, held out until the Japanese withdrew. Haengju, with Korean naval raids and the Ming burning of Japanese grain stores at Yongsan, left the army in Hanseong short of food.

events.label: May 1593
events.text: The Japanese abandon Hanseong and fall back to the south coast
events.detail: Short of food, hit by disease and harassed by guerrillas, the Japanese commanders agreed in peace talks with the Ming envoy Shen Weijing to evacuate the capital and withdraw to the Busan area, while the Ming army would also pull back. They left Hanseong in the spring of 1593 and retreated to a chain of castles, the wajō, built along the southern coast of Gyeongsang province from Ulsan to Geoje, which they held for the rest of the war.

events.label: 20–27 Jul 1593
events.text: The Japanese take Jinju and massacre its defenders
events.detail: Hideyoshi was determined to avenge the failure at Jinju. In July 1593 a Japanese army of about 90,000, the largest single force of the war, besieged the fortress, defended by a few thousand soldiers and crowded with civilians. After a week of assaults the walls were breached and the city fell on 27 July; the Japanese killed its defenders and much of its population, Korean sources counting 60,000 dead. They then withdrew to their coastal forts.

events.text: Peace talks collapse at Osaka
events.detail: For three years Ming and Japanese negotiators, chiefly Shen Weijing and Konishi Yukinaga, misrepresented each side's demands to their masters in order to keep the truce. Hideyoshi expected Ming surrender of territory and a princess, while the Ming believed he had asked to become a tributary king. When the deception came out at his audience with the Ming envoys at Osaka Castle in 1596, Hideyoshi was enraged and ordered a second invasion of Korea.

events.label: 28 Aug 1597
events.text: The Korean navy is destroyed at Chilcheollyang
events.detail: In 1597 more than 140,000 Japanese troops crossed to Korea. Yi Sun-sin had been removed from his command after a Japanese plot, and his successor Won Gyun was ordered to attack the Japanese fleet. On 28 August 1597, off Geoje island near Chilcheollyang, his tired fleet was surprised at night by a much larger Japanese navy. Most of the Korean fleet, by one count 188 ships, was destroyed, and Won Gyun was killed. The sea route to the west coast now lay open to Japan.

events.label: 23–26 Sep 1597
events.text: The Japanese storm Namwon
events.detail: Japan's second offensive aimed at Jeolla province, which had escaped the first invasion. The Left Army of about 50,000 under Ukita Hideie besieged Namwon, held by about 3,000 Ming soldiers under Yang Yuan and a few hundred Koreans. The town fell on the night of 26 September after four days; Yang Yuan broke out with about 100 men, but most of the defenders and many townspeople were killed. The Japanese went on to take Jeonju.

events.label: 16 Oct 1597
events.text: Ming troops stop the Japanese advance at Jiksan
events.detail: While the Left Army swept Jeolla, the Japanese Right Army under Mōri Hidemoto and Katō Kiyomasa marched north through Chungcheong towards Hanseong. On 16 October 1597 its vanguard under Kuroda Nagamasa met a Ming force of about 8,000 infantry and cavalry near Jiksan, south of the capital, and was driven back after a hard fight. Jiksan was the farthest the Japanese got towards Hanseong in the second invasion; with winter coming, their armies turned back towards the south coast.

events.label: 26 Oct 1597
events.text: Yi Sun-sin's 13 ships defeat a Japanese fleet at Myeongnyang
events.detail: Restored to command after Chilcheollyang, Yi Sun-sin had only 13 warships left. He waited for the Japanese fleet, at least 133 warships, in the narrow Myeongnyang strait off Jindo island, where a powerful tidal current runs. On 26 October 1597 his ships held the strait for hours, sinking or disabling about 30 Japanese vessels, and when the tide turned the Japanese withdrew. The victory stopped the Japanese navy from advancing along the west coast to support their armies.

events.label: 29 Jan – 19 Feb 1598
events.text: Ming–Korean armies fail to take Ulsan castle
events.detail: The Japanese held the winter in new coastal castles, and the Ming general Yang Hao led about 50,000 Ming and Korean troops against the new Japanese castle at Ulsan. Its garrison held out through repeated assaults until a Japanese relief army arrived; on 19 February 1598 the allies broke off the siege and retreated with heavy losses. A stalemate followed along the south coast, from Ulsan to Suncheon.

events.label: 18 Sep 1598
events.text: Toyotomi Hideyoshi dies; Japan decides to withdraw
events.detail: Hideyoshi died at Fushimi Castle on 18 September 1598, leaving his five-year-old son Hideyori as heir. The Council of Five Elders that now governed Japan kept his death secret and ordered the armies in Korea home. Meanwhile allied armies attacked the Japanese castles at Sacheon and Suncheon in October 1598 and were beaten off, but the Japanese prepared to evacuate their forts and sail back to Japan.

events.label: 16 Dec 1598
events.text: Noryang: the last battle; Yi Sun-sin is killed
events.detail: Konishi Yukinaga was blockaded at Suncheon by the Korean and Ming fleets, and Shimazu Yoshihiro sailed with about 500 ships to rescue him. Yi Sun-sin and the Ming admiral Chen Lin intercepted the relief fleet in the Noryang strait before dawn on 16 December 1598 and destroyed about half of it. Yi was killed by a gunshot at the height of the battle. Konishi escaped round the south of Namhae island, and on 21 December the last Japanese commanders sailed from Busan for Japan.

wars.name: Thirty Years' War
wars.summary: The war began as a revolt by Protestant nobles in Bohemia against their Habsburg king, Ferdinand, who was elected Holy Roman Emperor in 1619. It grew into a struggle over religion and power across the Holy Roman Empire, as Denmark, Sweden and finally France intervened against the Austrian and Spanish Habsburgs and the Catholic League led by Bavaria. Imperial armies crushed Bohemia in 1620 and Denmark in 1626, and the Edict of Restitution of 1629 alarmed Protestant rulers. Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden then won at Breitenfeld in 1631 but was killed at Lützen in 1632. After the Swedish defeat at Nördlingen in 1634, most German princes made peace with the emperor in 1635, but Catholic France joined Sweden in open war on the Habsburgs. Exhausting campaigns followed until the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, which recognised Calvinism alongside Catholicism and Lutheranism, gave Sweden and France territory, confirmed Dutch independence from Spain and recognised the Swiss Confederation as independent of the Empire.
wars.casualties: An estimated 4.5 to 8 million soldiers and civilians died, most from famine and disease, and the population of Germany is thought to have fallen from about 18–20 million to 11–13 million.

events.label: 23 May 1618
events.text: Defenestration of Prague: Bohemian Protestants revolt
events.detail: Bohemia's Protestant nobles feared that their new Habsburg king, the devout Catholic Ferdinand, would roll back the religious freedoms they had won. At Prague Castle a group of them threw two of the king's regents and their secretary out of a high window; all three survived. The act was an open challenge to Habsburg rule, and the rebels set up their own government and raised an army. The local revolt became the opening of a thirty-year European war.

events.label: Aug 1619
events.text: Bohemia deposes Ferdinand and chooses Frederick V of the Palatinate
events.detail: In August 1619 the Bohemian Estates rescinded Ferdinand's election as their king and offered the crown to Frederick V, the Calvinist Elector Palatine; in the same month Ferdinand was elected Holy Roman Emperor. Frederick entered Prague in October. By accepting, he turned a Bohemian dispute into a quarrel among the Empire's princes. Ferdinand secured help from Maximilian of Bavaria and the Catholic League, and from Spain, while Gabriel Bethlen of Transylvania attacked Habsburg Hungary in support of the rebels.

events.label: 8 Nov 1620
events.text: Battle of White Mountain: the Bohemian revolt is crushed
events.detail: An imperial and Catholic League army under Tilly and Bucquoy, with Spanish troops, met the Bohemian army under Christian of Anhalt on a low plateau outside Prague. The rebels were routed in about an hour and Tilly entered Prague the next day. Frederick fled, mocked as the 'Winter King'. Twenty-seven rebel leaders were later executed in the Old Town Square, and much of the Protestant nobility went into exile as their lands were confiscated and Bohemia was forcibly re-Catholicised.

events.label: May 1622
events.text: Catholic armies win at Wimpfen and overrun the Palatinate
events.detail: With Bohemia lost, the war moved to Frederick's own lands on the Rhine. Spanish troops had already occupied part of the Palatinate, and in May and June 1622 Tilly defeated Protestant armies at Wimpfen and Höchst; Frankenthal surrendered in March 1623. The emperor rewarded Maximilian of Bavaria with Frederick's title of elector, confirmed in February 1623. Transferring an electoral vote from a Protestant to a Catholic prince alarmed Protestant rulers inside and outside the Empire.

events.label: 27 Aug 1626
events.text: Battle of Lutter: Tilly defeats Christian IV of Denmark
events.detail: King Christian IV of Denmark, also a prince of the Empire as Duke of Holstein, had entered the war in 1625 as champion of the Protestant cause in northern Germany. At Lutter am Barenberge Tilly's Catholic League army beat him comprehensively: he lost at least a third of his army, all his artillery and most of his baggage, and many German allies deserted him. Imperial troops under Wallenstein then pushed into Denmark's Jutland peninsula.

events.label: Mar 1629
events.text: Emperor Ferdinand II issues the Edict of Restitution
events.detail: At the height of his power, Ferdinand II ordered that church lands taken over by Protestant rulers since the Peace of Passau of 1552 be returned to the Catholic Church. Enforcing it would have stripped Lutheran princes of bishoprics and abbeys across northern Germany, and imperial commissioners began confiscations with army backing. The edict turned even moderate, previously loyal Lutheran states such as Saxony and Brandenburg against the emperor and helped open the way for Swedish intervention.

events.label: Jun 1629
events.text: Treaty of Lübeck takes Denmark out of the war
events.detail: Defeated on land and with Jutland occupied, Christian IV made peace with the emperor at Lübeck in June 1629. He kept Schleswig and Holstein and recovered his Danish lands, but gave up his claims to the north German bishoprics of Bremen and Verden and promised not to interfere in the Empire again. The Danish phase of the war ended with Habsburg power reaching the Baltic coast, which worried Sweden.

events.label: Jul 1630
events.text: Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden lands in Pomerania
events.detail: Concerned by imperial power on the Baltic and presenting himself as protector of German Protestants, King Gustavus Adolphus landed in Pomerania with nearly 18,000 troops. By the Treaty of Bärwalde in 1631, Cardinal Richelieu's Catholic France agreed to subsidise the Swedish army, putting rivalry with the Habsburgs ahead of religion. Sweden's well-drilled army, with mobile field artillery, was to change the course of the war.

events.label: 20 May 1631
events.text: Sack of Magdeburg: some 20,000 people killed
events.detail: The Protestant city of Magdeburg had allied with Sweden and was besieged by Catholic League forces. On 20 May troops under Pappenheim, part of Tilly's army, stormed the walls; the city burned and was plundered for days. Around 20,000 defenders and civilians are estimated to have died, and of roughly 25,000 inhabitants only about 5,000 survived. The massacre shocked Protestant Europe and helped persuade many rulers to stand against the emperor.

events.label: 17 Sep 1631
events.text: Battle of Breitenfeld: first great Swedish victory
events.detail: Saxony, threatened by Tilly's army, finally allied with Sweden. Near Leipzig the combined Swedish-Saxon army met Tilly; the Saxons were routed early, but the Swedes held and broke the imperial army, which lost about two-thirds of its men. It was the Catholic side's first major defeat of the war. Gustavus marched into southern and western Germany, and several Protestant states joined him.

events.label: 16 Nov 1632
events.text: Battle of Lützen: Sweden wins but Gustavus Adolphus is killed
events.detail: The emperor had recalled Wallenstein to raise a new army. At Lützen, southwest of Leipzig, the Swedes narrowly defeated him in a confused, foggy battle, and Wallenstein's cavalry general Pappenheim was mortally wounded. But Gustavus Adolphus, riding to rally his infantry, ran into enemy cavalry and was shot dead. Sweden's chancellor Axel Oxenstierna kept the war going, but without its king the Protestant coalition lost much of its drive.

events.label: 25 Feb 1634
events.text: Wallenstein is assassinated at Eger (Cheb)
events.detail: Albrecht von Wallenstein, the emperor's most powerful general, had grown wealthy and independent and was suspected at court of secret talks with the enemy. Ferdinand II dismissed him, and on 25 February 1634 officers of his own army murdered him at Eger (Cheb) in Bohemia. Command of the imperial army passed to the emperor's son, the future Ferdinand III, tightening Habsburg control of the war effort.

events.label: 6 Sep 1634
events.text: Battle of Nördlingen: crushing defeat for Sweden
events.detail: An imperial army under the future Ferdinand III, joined by a Spanish army marching north from Italy, met the Swedes and their German allies at Nördlingen in Swabia. The Protestant army was destroyed. Sweden's position in southern Germany collapsed, and its German allies began to look for terms with the emperor, while France, fearing a Habsburg triumph, prepared to enter the war openly.

events.label: May 1635
events.text: France declares war on Spain
events.detail: Until now Richelieu had fought the Habsburgs by paying others. After Nördlingen, France declared war on Spain in May 1635 and in March 1636 formally allied with Sweden by the Treaty of Wismar. From this point the conflict was less a German religious war than a contest between Bourbon France and the Habsburgs, fought in the Low Countries, along the Rhine and in Italy as well as Germany.

events.label: May 1635
events.text: Peace of Prague: Saxony and most German princes make peace with the emperor
events.detail: Days after France's declaration, the emperor and Saxony agreed the Peace of Prague, and most Lutheran princes, including Brandenburg, soon accepted it. In return the emperor effectively set aside the Edict of Restitution, and the princes merged their forces into an imperial army. The treaty might have ended the German war, but Sweden, now backed by France, fought on, and Saxony found itself at war with its former Swedish ally.

events.label: Oct 1636
events.text: Battle of Wittstock: Sweden recovers in the north
events.detail: In October 1636 a Swedish army under Johan Banér defeated an imperial and Saxon army at Wittstock in Brandenburg. The victory restored Sweden's position in northern Germany after the disaster of Nördlingen. Campaigning across Brandenburg, Saxony and Pomerania devastated the region, as armies of all sides lived off the land, spreading hunger and disease among civilians. Wittstock also showed that Sweden, now paid by France, could fight on without its German allies.

events.label: Dec 1638
events.text: Breisach falls to Bernard of Saxe-Weimar
events.detail: Bernard of Saxe-Weimar, a German Protestant general now paid by France, besieged the Rhine fortress of Breisach, which surrendered in December 1638. Breisach guarded the route by which Spain moved troops from Italy to the Netherlands along the Rhine, and its loss made Spanish reinforcement of Flanders much harder. After Bernard's death in 1639 France took over his army and his conquests in Alsace.

events.label: Oct 1642
events.text: Second Battle of Breitenfeld: Swedish victory near Leipzig
events.detail: On almost the same ground as Gustavus Adolphus's victory of 1631, a Swedish army under Lennart Torstensson defeated an imperial army in October 1642. The win let Sweden occupy Leipzig and much of Saxony and keep up pressure on the Habsburg lands. Peace talks were by now being arranged, but each side fought on to improve its bargaining position. Torstensson, Sweden's ablest general after Gustavus, would lead its armies to their greatest successes over the next three years.

events.label: 19 May 1643
events.text: Battle of Rocroi: France defeats Spain's army of Flanders
events.detail: Spain's army in the Netherlands invaded northern France and besieged the fortress of Rocroi. A French army under the young Duke of Enghien, later the Great Condé, attacked and destroyed it, including its famed infantry regiments. Rocroi became a symbol of the end of Spain's military dominance in Europe, though the Franco-Spanish war went on until 1659. The battle was fought just days after the death of King Louis XIII, and it secured the start of the young Louis XIV's reign.

events.label: Mar 1645
events.text: Battle of Jankau: Swedes rout the imperial army in Bohemia
events.detail: Torstensson's Swedish army invaded Bohemia and in March 1645 destroyed an imperial army at Jankau (Jankov), southeast of Prague. Swedish troops then advanced towards Vienna. The defeat left the emperor with few soldiers, and in the same year Saxony made a truce with Sweden. Ferdinand III's negotiators at Münster and Osnabrück now had to accept far more concessions. Imperial losses were so heavy that the Habsburg lands lay open to Swedish raids.

events.label: 14 Mar 1647
events.text: Truce of Ulm: Bavaria pauses its war with France and Sweden
events.detail: With Franco-Swedish armies ravaging his lands, Maximilian of Bavaria, the emperor's most important German ally, agreed a truce with France and Sweden at Ulm. The emperor was left almost alone in Germany. Maximilian broke the truce later that year and rejoined the emperor, but the episode showed how close the Habsburg side was to exhaustion. Bavaria had fought for the Catholic side since 1619, and its wavering showed that even the most loyal allies wanted peace on almost any terms.

events.label: 30 Jan 1648
events.text: Peace of Münster: Spain recognises Dutch independence
events.detail: At Münster, Spain and the Dutch Republic signed a separate peace ending the Eighty Years' War, which had resumed alongside the German war in 1621. Spain recognised the United Provinces as a sovereign state. Freed of its Dutch war, Spain kept fighting France, but the treaty removed one strand of the wider conflict months before the main settlement. The Dutch, who had fought Spain on and off for eighty years, emerged as a leading trading and naval power.

events.label: May 1648
events.text: Battle of Zusmarshausen: last imperial field army defeated
events.detail: A combined French and Swedish army under Turenne and Wrangel caught the retreating imperial and Bavarian army at Zusmarshausen, west of Augsburg, in May 1648 and defeated it. Bavaria lay open to plunder, and the emperor had no army left capable of resisting in southern Germany. The defeat pushed Ferdinand III to settle quickly on the terms being negotiated in Westphalia.

events.label: Jul 1648
events.text: Swedes storm Prague Castle and the Lesser Town
events.detail: In the war's last months a Swedish force surprised Prague, seizing the castle and the Malá Strana (Lesser Town) on the left bank in July 1648 and carrying off rich booty, including treasures from the imperial collections. The Old Town across the river held out until news of peace arrived. The war thus ended in the city where it had begun thirty years earlier.

events.label: 24 Oct 1648
events.text: Peace of Westphalia signed at Münster and Osnabrück
events.detail: Two treaties concluded with France (at Münster) and Sweden (at Osnabrück) ended the war. Calvinism was recognised alongside Catholicism and Lutheranism, with 1624 as the reference year for each territory's religion. Sweden gained Western Pomerania, Bremen-Verden and an indemnity; France gained Metz, Toul, Verdun and lands in Alsace; Brandenburg gained Farther Pomerania; Bavaria kept an electorate and the Palatine heir received a new one; and the Swiss Confederation was recognised as independent of the Empire.
