wars.name: Paraguayan War (War of the Triple Alliance)
wars.summary: In 1864 Brazil intervened in a civil war in Uruguay against the Blanco government, an ally of Paraguay. Paraguay's president, Francisco Solano López, who had warned that he would treat an occupation of Uruguay as a threat, seized a Brazilian steamer in November and invaded Brazil's province of Mato Grosso. When Argentina refused his army passage, Paraguay attacked Corrientes in April 1865, and Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay, now under a pro-Brazilian government, signed the Treaty of the Triple Alliance. Brazil's victory at Riachuelo gave the allies the rivers, and Paraguay's invading armies were destroyed or surrendered by late 1865. The allies invaded Paraguay in 1866, won at Tuyutí but were bloodily repulsed at Curupayty; under the Marquess of Caxias they took the fortress of Humaitá in 1868 and Asunción in January 1869. López fought on as a guerrilla until Brazilian troops killed him at Cerro Corá on 1 March 1870. Paraguay lost territory and a large share of its people.
wars.casualties: Estimates vary widely, from about 150,000 to 500,000 deaths in all; Paraguay may have lost 60–70 percent of its population of about 420,000–450,000, by one estimate, while Brazil lost an estimated 50,000 soldiers and Argentina about 18,000, many of them to disease and hunger.

events.label: 12 Oct 1864
events.text: Brazilian troops invade Uruguay
events.detail: Brazil backed the Colorado rebel Venancio Flores against Uruguay's Blanco government of Atanasio Aguirre, which had rejected Brazilian demands over border raids. Paraguay's president, Francisco Solano López, warned in August that he would regard any occupation of Uruguay as an attack on the balance of the Platine region. Brazil ignored him, and on 12 October 1864 Brazilian troops crossed into Uruguay.

events.label: 12 Nov 1864
events.text: Paraguay seizes the Brazilian steamer Marquês de Olinda
events.detail: The Brazilian steamer Marquês de Olinda, carrying the new governor of Mato Grosso up the Paraguay River, called at Asunción on 11 November 1864. López sent the warship Tacuarí after her; on 12 November she was stopped near Concepción and brought back, and all aboard were arrested. The same day Paraguay broke off diplomatic relations with Brazil. A month later López launched his first offensive.

events.label: 27 Dec 1864
events.text: Paraguay invades Mato Grosso and attacks Fort Coimbra
events.detail: Two Paraguayan columns invaded the Brazilian province of Mato Grosso. One, carried up the Paraguay River, attacked Fort Coimbra on 27 December 1864; its garrison of 154 men held out for three days before slipping away upriver. Albuquerque and Corumbá fell in January 1865, and the overland column took Dourados, Miranda and Nioaque, and Coxim in April, but the Paraguayans did not push on to Cuiabá.

events.label: 20 Feb 1865
events.text: The Uruguayan War ends with Flores in power
events.detail: After a Brazilian and Colorado siege, the Blanco stronghold of Paysandú fell on 2 January 1865, and the allies closed in on Montevideo. On 20 February 1865 the Blanco government gave way and Venancio Flores took power. Paraguay had lost its ally in Uruguay before its own army could arrive, and Flores's Uruguay sided with Brazil. Montevideo had been left isolated before it gave in.

events.label: 23 Mar 1865
events.text: Paraguay's Congress votes for war with Argentina
events.detail: In January 1865 López asked Argentina to let 20,000 Paraguayan soldiers cross the province of Corrientes to strike at Brazil; President Bartolomé Mitre refused. A Paraguayan congress met in March and on 23 March voted for war with Argentina, accusing it of favouring Brazil, and made López a field marshal. The declaration was sent to Buenos Aires on 29 March.

events.label: 13 Apr 1865
events.text: Paraguayan forces seize Corrientes
events.detail: On 13 April 1865 a Paraguayan squadron sailed down the Paraná, attacked two Argentine warships at Corrientes, and troops under General Wenceslao Robles took the city. Robles then advanced south along the river, taking Bella Vista, Empedrado and Goya, while the provincial government withdrew inland and Corrientes militia fought a guerrilla war. The attack brought Argentina into the war. Argentina declared war in early May.

events.label: 1 May 1865
events.text: Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay sign the Treaty of the Triple Alliance
events.detail: On 1 May 1865 Brazil, Argentina and Flores's Uruguay signed a secret treaty in Buenos Aires, naming Argentina's president Bartolomé Mitre allied commander-in-chief. They pledged to fight until López was removed and laid down Paraguay's future borders in their own favour. The treaty was meant to stay secret, but Britain obtained a copy and published it in 1866. Uruguay's Flores commanded his own small army.

events.label: 11 Jun 1865
events.text: Battle of Riachuelo: Brazil destroys Paraguay's navy
events.detail: On 11 June 1865 a Paraguayan squadron attacked the Brazilian fleet of Admiral Francisco Manoel Barroso on the Paraná below Corrientes. Barroso rammed and sank or wrecked most of the Paraguayan ships. The battle gave the allies control of the rivers up to Paraguay's border, cut the invading armies' supply lines and, for practical purposes, decided the outcome of the war.

events.label: 12 Jun 1865
events.text: A Paraguayan army invades Rio Grande do Sul
events.detail: In May 1865 some 12,000 Paraguayans under Colonel Antonio de la Cruz Estigarribia crossed into Argentine territory south of Encarnación and marched down the Uruguay River. Estigarribia took the Brazilian town of São Borja on 12 June and then Itaqui, while a smaller column under Major Pedro Duarte advanced down the Argentine bank of the river. Brazilian commanders in the province could offer little resistance at first.

events.label: 17 Aug 1865
events.text: Battle of Yatay
events.detail: Duarte's column, about 3,200 strong, had occupied Paso de los Libres on the Argentine bank opposite Uruguaiana, which Estigarribia entered on 5 August without supporting him. On 17 August 1865 an allied army under Venancio Flores attacked Duarte's position by the Yatay stream and destroyed his column; most of its men were killed or taken prisoner. Estigarribia, across the river, did not intervene.

events.label: 18 Sep 1865
events.text: Estigarribia surrenders at Uruguaiana
events.detail: Besieged in Uruguaiana by Brazilian, Argentine and Uruguayan forces, with Emperor Pedro II, Mitre and Flores present, Estigarribia's starving garrison surrendered on 18 September 1865, against López's orders, and some 5,500 men became prisoners. López then pulled his armies out of Argentina and Brazil, and the war moved to Paraguay's own borders. Some of the prisoners were sold into slavery by Brazilian officers.

events.label: 3 Nov 1865
events.text: The Paraguayan army completes its withdrawal from Corrientes
events.detail: On 3 October López ordered the southern army to leave Argentine territory. It evacuated the city of Corrientes on 22 October, looting the river towns as it went, and by 3 November 1865 some 27,000 men had recrossed the Paraná at Paso de la Patria with about 100,000 head of cattle. Corrientes's provincial government returned to its capital the same day.

events.label: 16 Apr 1866
events.text: The allies cross the Paraná and invade Paraguay
events.detail: After months of gathering in camps north of Corrientes, the allied armies crossed the Paraná into Paraguay on 16 April 1866. General Manuel Luís Osório led the landing and beat back Paraguayan counterattacks around the fort of Itapirú. The allies pushed inland towards the swamps and trenches guarding the fortress of Humaitá, and were checked at Estero Bellaco on 2 May.

events.label: 24 May 1866
events.text: Battle of Tuyutí, the largest battle of the war
events.detail: Hoping to destroy the allied army in one blow, López attacked its camp at Tuyutí on 24 May 1866 with about 23,000–25,000 men against some 32,000–35,000 allies. The attack nearly succeeded but was broken by allied resistance and Brazilian artillery. Paraguay lost about 12,000–13,000 killed and wounded, losses it could not replace, while the allies suffered some 4,000–6,000 casualties. Both armies then dug in for months.

events.label: 22 Sep 1866
events.text: Battle of Curupayty: a bloody allied defeat
events.detail: After taking the fort of Curuzú on 3 September 1866 and a failed peace meeting between López and Mitre, the allies made a frontal assault on the Paraguayan trenches at Curupayty on 22 September, supported by Brazilian warships. General José E. Díaz's defenders held, and the allies lost between about 4,000 and 8,000 men, against at most a few hundred Paraguayans. Allied offensives stopped for ten months.

events.label: 22 Jul 1867
events.text: Caxias begins the march around Humaitá
events.detail: The Marquess of Caxias, Brazil's commander from late 1866, rebuilt the disease-ridden allied army and on 22 July 1867 began a wide flanking march east and north around the fortress of Humaitá. On 2 November Brazilian troops took Tayí on the Paraguay River north of the fortress, cutting its land link with Asunción; López's counterattack at the second battle of Tuyutí the next day failed.

events.label: 19 Feb 1868
events.text: Brazilian ironclads force the passage of Humaitá
events.detail: Humaitá's river batteries and a chain across the Paraguay River had blocked the allied fleet for two years. On 19 February 1868 Brazilian ironclads ran past the batteries under heavy fire, giving the allies control of the river and threatening Asunción. In early March López left the fortress with most of its garrison, crossing to the Chaco shore and moving north.

events.label: 26 Jul 1868
events.text: The fortress of Humaitá falls
events.detail: The remaining garrison of Humaitá, starving after a long siege, beat off an allied assault on 16 July 1868. On the night of 24–25 July Colonel Francisco Martínez led the last defenders out across the river, and on 26 July the allies occupied the empty fortress. Trapped on the Chaco shore, about 1,300 survivors surrendered on 5 August. Humaitá had blocked the allied advance for more than two years.

events.label: 6–11 Dec 1868
events.text: Ytororó and Avay: Caxias attacks the Paraguayans from behind
events.detail: López had fortified a line on the Pikysyry stream south of Asunción. Caxias built a road through the Chaco swamps, carried his army round the line and recrossed the river at Villeta. Turning south to attack from the rear, the Brazilians forced the bridge at Ytororó on 6 December 1868 at heavy cost, and on 11 December destroyed a Paraguayan division at Avay.

events.label: 21–27 Dec 1868
events.text: Battle of Lomas Valentinas
events.detail: From 21 to 27 December 1868 the allies attacked López's last entrenched army at Lomas Valentinas, near Itá Ybaté. After days of fighting the Paraguayan positions were overrun, though López escaped with a small escort. The garrison of the riverside fort of Angostura, cut off, surrendered on 30 December, and the road to Asunción lay open. Caxias's call on López to surrender on 24 December had been refused.

events.label: 1 Jan 1869
events.text: Allied troops occupy Asunción
events.detail: Brazilian troops entered the evacuated Paraguayan capital on 1 January 1869, and Caxias arrived on 5 January. About 30,000 allied soldiers were soon quartered there and looted almost every building. Caxias, ill, considered the war won and left; Brazil set up a provisional Paraguayan government, while López withdrew east into the hills of the Cordillera and raised a new army.

events.label: 12 Aug 1869
events.text: Battle of Piribebuy
events.detail: Emperor Pedro II's son-in-law, the Count of Eu, took command in 1869 and led some 20,000 men into the Cordillera. On 12 August 1869 they stormed Piribebuy, López's temporary capital, defended by about 1,600 poorly armed men and boys. After five hours of fighting the town fell; its hospital was burned and the government's archives were lost. Some 730 of the defenders were killed.

events.label: 16 Aug 1869
events.text: Battle of Acosta Ñu, the 'Children's Battle'
events.detail: Covering López's retreat on 16 August 1869, about 3,500 Paraguayans, most of them boys, faced more than 20,000 Brazilian and Argentine soldiers on the plain of Acosta Ñu. They were overwhelmed, with some 2,000 killed. It was the last major battle of the war, and Paraguay remembers it every 16 August as Children's Day. López himself escaped north with the survivors.

events.label: 1 Mar 1870
events.text: López is killed at Cerro Corá and the war ends
events.detail: With a few hundred followers López retreated into the forests of the north-east, pursued by Brazilian columns. On 1 March 1870 troops under General José Antônio Correia da Câmara surprised his camp at Cerro Corá. López, wounded and refusing to surrender, was killed. Allied troops occupied Paraguay until 1876, and peace treaties gave disputed lands to Brazil and Argentina. He had refused every offer to surrender.

wars.name: First Italo-Ethiopian War
wars.summary: Italy had held the Red Sea port of Massawa since 1885 and built the colony of Eritrea on the plateau behind it. In 1889 Emperor Menelik II signed the Treaty of Wuchale with Italy, but its Italian text made Ethiopia an Italian protectorate while the Amharic text did not, and in 1893 Menelik repudiated it. In January 1895 Italian colonial troops under General Oreste Baratieri defeated Ras Mengesha of Tigray at Coatit and Senafe, then occupied Adigrat, Adwa and Mekelle and declared Tigray annexed. Menelik called up the nobility of the whole empire and marched north with an army of over 100,000, many armed with modern rifles. His forces overran an Italian outpost at Amba Alagi in December 1895 and forced the fort at Mekelle to surrender in January 1896. On 1 March 1896 Baratieri attacked near Adwa and his army was routed. In the Treaty of Addis Ababa of October 1896 Italy recognised Ethiopia's full independence, a victory that became a symbol for anti-colonial and Pan-African movements.
wars.casualties: At Adwa alone an estimated 6,000 Italian and colonial troops and 4,000–7,000 Ethiopians were killed; estimates for the whole war run to about 9,000 Italian and colonial dead and about 10,000 Ethiopian.

events.label: 13 Jan 1895
events.text: Italians repel Ras Mengesha's invasion of Eritrea at Coatit
events.detail: Menelik had repudiated the Treaty of Wuchale in 1893, and in December 1894 Bahta Hagos led a revolt against Italian rule in Eritrea, which was quickly crushed. Suspecting Ras Mengesha Yohannes, the ruler of Tigray, Governor Baratieri moved against him. Mengesha crossed into Eritrea with about 19,000 men, but on 13 January 1895 a colonial force of under 4,000, mostly Eritrean askaris, beat him at Coatit, opening the war.

events.label: 15 Jan 1895
events.text: Baratieri routs Mengesha's retreating army at Senafe
events.detail: Mengesha withdrew towards Tigray, but Baratieri caught up with his camp in the Senafe basin on the evening of 15 January 1895. Italian mountain guns shelled the camp from the heights over two days, and the Tigrayan army broke up with heavy losses. The defeat left Tigray open to invasion, and Baratieri gathered his troops at Senafe for an advance south across the border.

events.label: 25 Mar 1895
events.text: Italian troops occupy Adigrat in Tigray
events.detail: Crossing from Eritrea into the Ethiopian province of Tigray, Baratieri's army occupied the town of Adigrat on 25 March 1895. It became the main Italian base in Tigray, supporting further advances south. The Italians hoped that disaffected rulers such as Ras Mengesha, Negus Tekle Haymanot of Gojjam and the Sultan of Aussa would join them, but Ethiopia's nobility instead rallied to the emperor.

events.label: 2 Apr 1895
events.text: Italians occupy Adwa and declare Tigray annexed to Eritrea
events.detail: On 2 April 1895 Italian troops entered Adwa, the main town of western Tigray, and Baratieri issued a proclamation annexing Tigray to the colony of Eritrea. With the rainy season approaching, the Italians paused their advance. Menelik meanwhile sought help abroad, but France chose Italian goodwill over an alliance with him; Russia, which disliked a Catholic power ruling an Orthodox nation, sent arms.

events.label: 17 Sep 1895
events.text: Menelik II calls the Ethiopian nobility to war
events.detail: On 17 September 1895 Menelik issued a proclamation summoning the men of Ethiopia to join his army at Were Ilu. Regional rulers who had resented his rise, among them Ras Mengesha of Tigray, answered the call. Over the following months an army of more than 100,000 assembled and marched north, armed with tens of thousands of modern rifles bought from France, Russia and even Italy.

events.label: 9 Oct 1895
events.text: Italians push south past Debra Ailà and take Mekelle
events.detail: In October the Italians resumed their advance. On 9 October 1895 colonial battalions under General Giuseppe Arimondi drove Mengesha's rearguard from the pass of Debra Ailà, near Antalo. Mekelle, the Tigrayan capital, was occupied without a fight after Mengesha withdrew on Menelik's advice, and in October the Italians built a fort by the church of Enda Iyesus above the town. Advanced detachments went on south to the mountain stronghold of Amba Alagi.

events.label: 7 Dec 1895
events.text: Ethiopians overrun the Italian outpost at Amba Alagi
events.detail: Major Pietro Toselli held Amba Alagi with about 2,000 Eritrean askaris. On 7 December 1895 the vanguard of Menelik's army under Ras Makonnen, joined by Ras Mengesha and Ras Welle, attacked from several sides and overran the position. Toselli and most of his men were killed. Arimondi, coming up from Mekelle with reinforcements, could only collect a few hundred survivors and fall back north, leaving a garrison in the unfinished fort at Mekelle.

events.label: 18 Dec 1895
events.text: Ras Makonnen surrounds the Italian fort at Mekelle
events.detail: Major Giuseppe Galliano held the fort above Mekelle with about 1,150 askaris and 200 Italians and two mountain guns. Ras Makonnen's troops surrounded it on 18 December 1895 and a frontal assault a few days later was repulsed with heavy losses. Galliano was ordered to hold on while Baratieri concentrated the rest of the Italian army at Adigrat. In early January 1896 Menelik himself arrived with the main imperial army.

events.label: 21 Jan 1896
events.text: Mekelle garrison surrenders and is allowed to leave
events.detail: After two weeks of bombardment the Ethiopians cut the fort off from its water supply and beat back attempts to retake the well. With his men dying of thirst, Galliano agreed to surrender with his commanders' permission on 21 January 1896. Menelik let the garrison march out with its weapons and gave it mules to rejoin Baratieri. The escort also let the emperor move his army west, through passes the Italians did not guard, towards Adwa.

events.label: Feb 1896
events.text: Menelik moves on Adwa; Baratieri follows with his army
events.detail: Rather than attack the fortified Italian base at Adigrat, Menelik marched his army west by way of Hawzen to the plain around Adwa. Fearing an invasion of Eritrea, Baratieri left Adigrat and moved his army towards Adwa to face him. Both armies were short of food: the Ethiopian host had exhausted the countryside, while the Italians, at the end of a long supply line, had provisions for only a few more days.

events.label: 29 Feb 1896
events.text: Baratieri and his generals decide to attack
events.detail: On the evening of 29 February 1896 Baratieri, who knew he was about to be replaced by General Antonio Baldissera and was under pressure from Rome to win, met his four brigade commanders. With supplies running out, he suggested retreating towards Asmara, but the generals argued for an attack. Believing Menelik could field only about 30,000 men, Baratieri ordered an advance by night to positions overlooking the Ethiopian camp.

events.label: 1 Mar 1896
events.text: Battle of Adwa: Menelik's army routs the Italians
events.detail: About 17,700 Italian and Eritrean troops in four brigades marched overnight on separate mountain tracks and lost touch with each other. At dawn on 1 March 1896 Albertone's brigade ran into the Ethiopian army, perhaps 73,000 to 100,000 strong, and the others were attacked in turn and cut off. By noon the Italian army was in flight, abandoning its artillery. Over 6,000 Italian and colonial troops were killed and about 3,800 captured.

events.label: 10 Mar 1896
events.text: Crispi's government falls in Rome after the defeat
events.detail: News of Adwa reached Italy by telegraph almost at once and set off riots and demonstrations in several cities. Prime Minister Francesco Crispi, the main champion of colonial expansion in Ethiopia, was forced to resign, leaving office on 10 March 1896. Menelik offered peace if Italy publicly renounced its claim to a protectorate, but broke off talks when Italy asked for conditions. Talks went slowly while Italian prisoners remained in Ethiopian hands.

events.label: 18 May 1896
events.text: Italians evacuate Adigrat, their last foothold in Tigray
events.detail: General Baldissera reorganised the defeated army in Eritrea and relieved the Italian garrison left behind at Adigrat. Menelik insisted on its surrender as a condition of the peace talks, and on 18 May 1896 Baldissera evacuated the fort. The Italians withdrew behind the Mareb river, which became the border between Eritrea and Ethiopia, and Menelik returned to his capital, Addis Ababa.

events.label: 26 Oct 1896
events.text: Treaty of Addis Ababa: Italy recognises Ethiopian independence
events.detail: After months of negotiation, Italy agreed in August to abrogate the Treaty of Wuchale without conditions, and the Treaty of Addis Ababa was signed on 26 October 1896. Italy recognised Ethiopia's independence, paid for the upkeep of its prisoners and kept Eritrea up to the Mareb, Belesa and Muna rivers. Britain and France soon signed treaties treating Ethiopia as an equal, and it stayed independent until the Italian invasion of 1935.

wars.name: First World War
wars.summary: The First World War began a month after the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914. Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia, and within days the alliance system drew in the great powers. Germany and Austria-Hungary, joined by the Ottoman Empire in 1914 and Bulgaria in 1915, formed the Central Powers. Serbia, Russia, France, Belgium and the British Empire formed the Allies, or Entente, joined by Japan (1914), Italy (1915), Portugal and Romania (1916), and the United States, Greece, Siam, China and Brazil (1917). After the Marne the Western Front froze into trench warfare, while fighting spread to Eastern Europe, the Alps, the Balkans, the Middle East, Africa, East Asia and the oceans. Revolution took Russia out of the war in 1917–18. Germany's spring offensive of 1918 failed, Allied counter-offensives followed, and the Central Powers signed armistices between September and 11 November 1918. Four empires collapsed, and the peace treaties redrew the map of Europe and the Middle East.
wars.casualties: An estimated 15 to 22 million soldiers and civilians died, with many millions more wounded.

members.clio: United Principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia

events.label: 28 Jun 1914
events.text: Archduke Franz Ferdinand assassinated in Sarajevo
events.detail: Bosnia had been annexed by Austria-Hungary in 1908, angering Serbian nationalists. On 28 June 1914 Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb student, shot the heir to the Habsburg throne and his wife in Sarajevo. Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia and, assured of German backing, sent Belgrade an ultimatum it expected to be refused. The crisis of July 1914 turned a regional quarrel into a confrontation between Europe's two armed alliance blocs.

events.label: 28 Jul 1914
events.text: Austria-Hungary declares war on Serbia
events.detail: Serbia accepted most of the ultimatum but not all of it, and on 28 July Austria-Hungary declared war. Russia mobilised in support of Serbia; Germany declared war on Russia on 1 August and on France on 3 August. Mobilisation timetables and alliance commitments meant that a Balkan war became a continental one in under a week, before diplomacy could slow it down.

events.label: 4 Aug 1914
events.text: Germany invades Belgium; Britain declares war
events.detail: Germany's war plan aimed to knock out France quickly by swinging through neutral Belgium before turning east against Russia. German troops crossed the Belgian border on 4 August and besieged the fortresses of Liège. Britain, a guarantor of Belgian neutrality under the 1839 treaty, declared war on Germany the same day, bringing in its whole empire, including India, the dominions and its African colonies.

events.label: 23–30 Aug 1914
events.text: Germany crushes a Russian army at Tannenberg
events.detail: Russia attacked East Prussia sooner than Germany expected, forcing it to move troops east. Between 23 and 30 August German forces under Hindenburg and Ludendorff encircled and destroyed the Russian Second Army near Tannenberg, taking a very large number of prisoners. Russia was driven out of East Prussia, but its offensive had drawn German strength away from France at a critical moment.

events.label: 5–12 Sep 1914
events.text: The First Battle of the Marne halts the German advance
events.detail: German armies sweeping through Belgium and northern France came within reach of Paris by early September. From 5 to 12 September French and British forces counter-attacked along the River Marne, opening a gap between German armies and forcing them to retreat to the Aisne. The quick victory Germany had planned was lost; both sides dug in, and trenches soon ran from the Channel coast to Switzerland.

events.label: 29 Oct 1914
events.text: Ottoman warships raid Russia's Black Sea ports
events.detail: The Ottoman Empire had signed a secret alliance with Germany in August. On 29 October Ottoman warships, led by two ex-German cruisers, shelled Russian ports on the Black Sea. Russia declared war on 1 November and Britain and France followed. Ottoman entry closed the Straits to Allied supplies for Russia and opened new fronts in the Caucasus, Mesopotamia, Sinai and Palestine.

events.label: 7 Nov 1914
events.text: Japan captures Germany's Chinese base at Tsingtao
events.detail: Japan, allied to Britain since 1902, declared war on Germany on 23 August 1914 and moved against German possessions in Asia and the Pacific. Japanese forces, with a smaller British contingent, besieged the German naval base at Tsingtao on China's Shandong peninsula, which fell on 7 November. Japan also took Germany's island colonies north of the equator, extending its reach in East Asia.

events.label: 22 Apr 1915
events.text: Germany uses poison gas on a large scale at Ypres
events.detail: On the Western Front neither side could break the trench lines. At the start of the Second Battle of Ypres, on 22 April 1915, German troops released chlorine gas against French and Algerian positions, opening a gap they could not exploit. Both sides went on to use chemical weapons throughout the war, and gas became one of the conflict's most feared features.

events.label: 24 Apr 1915
events.text: Armenian deportations and massacres begin
events.detail: On the night of 23–24 April 1915 Ottoman authorities arrested hundreds of Armenian community leaders in Constantinople. Deportations of Armenians from Anatolia followed, with death marches towards the Syrian desert and mass killings. Estimates of the dead range from about 600,000 to 1.5 million. Almost all historians outside Turkey describe these events as genocide; the Turkish government rejects that term.

events.label: 25 Apr 1915
events.text: Allied landings at Gallipoli
events.detail: Britain and France hoped to force the Dardanelles, take Constantinople and open a sea route to Russia. After a naval attack failed, British, French, Australian, New Zealand and Indian troops landed on the Gallipoli peninsula on 25 April 1915. Ottoman forces held the heights, and months of costly fighting followed. The Allies abandoned the campaign and withdrew their last troops in December 1915 and January 1916.

events.label: 7 May 1915
events.text: A German U-boat sinks the liner Lusitania
events.detail: Germany had declared the waters around Britain a war zone in February 1915, using submarines against merchant shipping. On 7 May a U-boat torpedoed the British liner Lusitania off southern Ireland, killing more than a thousand passengers and crew, among them over a hundred Americans. The sinking turned American opinion against Germany, which for a time restricted submarine attacks to avoid war with the United States.

events.label: 23 May 1915
events.text: Italy declares war on Austria-Hungary
events.detail: Italy had stayed neutral in 1914 despite its prewar alliance with Germany and Austria-Hungary. After the Allies secretly promised it Austrian territory, Italy declared war on Austria-Hungary on 23 May 1915, though not on Germany until August 1916. A new front opened along the Alps and the Isonzo River, where repeated Italian offensives over the next two years gained little ground at great cost.

events.label: 14 Oct 1915
events.text: Bulgaria joins the Central Powers; Serbia is overrun
events.detail: Bulgaria, seeking territory lost in the Balkan Wars, declared war on Serbia on 14 October 1915. Attacked by German and Austro-Hungarian armies from the north and Bulgarians from the east, Serbia was conquered in little more than a month. Its army retreated across the Albanian mountains to the Adriatic coast and was evacuated by Allied ships, later fighting again on the Salonika front.

events.label: 21 Feb 1916
events.text: The Battle of Verdun begins
events.detail: Germany attacked the fortress city of Verdun on 21 February 1916, aiming to wear down the French army in a battle France could not refuse. The fighting lasted until 18 December, when French counter-attacks had retaken most of the lost ground. Combined French and German casualties are estimated at roughly 700,000 to 975,000, and Verdun became a symbol of the war's attrition.

events.label: 31 May–1 Jun 1916
events.text: Britain and Germany fight the naval Battle of Jutland
events.detail: Britain's Royal Navy blockaded Germany, and the German High Seas Fleet hoped to destroy part of the British Grand Fleet. The two fleets met in the North Sea off Denmark on 31 May and 1 June 1916, the war's largest naval battle. Britain lost more ships and men, but the German fleet returned to port and did not seek another major fleet action, so the blockade held.

events.label: 4 Jun 1916
events.text: Russia's Brusilov Offensive breaks the Austro-Hungarian line
events.detail: To relieve pressure on France and Italy, Russian armies under General Aleksei Brusilov attacked along a wide front in Galicia and Volhynia on 4 June 1916. Short, surprise bombardments broke the Austro-Hungarian lines, and huge numbers of prisoners were taken. Germany had to send reinforcements east, and the offensive's early success encouraged Romania to join the Allies, but Russian losses were also very heavy.

events.label: 10 Jun 1916
events.text: Sharif Hussein launches the Arab Revolt at Mecca
events.detail: Britain had promised in letters to Sharif Hussein of Mecca to support Arab independence in return for a rising against the Ottomans. On 10 June 1916 his forces attacked the Ottoman garrison at Mecca. Backed by British gold, weapons and officers such as T. E. Lawrence, Arab forces under his son Faisal took Aqaba in July 1917 and reached Damascus at the end of September 1918.

events.label: 1 Jul 1916
events.text: The Battle of the Somme begins
events.detail: Britain and France attacked along the River Somme on 1 July 1916, partly to relieve Verdun. On the first day the British army suffered about 57,500 casualties, including some 19,200 dead, the worst single day in its history. The battle lasted until 18 November and gained only a few miles; British, French and German losses together exceeded a million, and tanks made their first appearance there.

events.label: 27 Aug 1916
events.text: Romania enters the war on the Allied side
events.detail: Encouraged by the Brusilov Offensive and promised Austro-Hungarian Transylvania, Romania declared war and began hostilities against Austria-Hungary on 27 August 1916. German, Austro-Hungarian, Bulgarian and Ottoman forces counter-attacked from two sides, and Bucharest fell on 6 December. Romania's government and army held on in Moldavia but, isolated after Russia's collapse, signed a separate peace in May 1918, then re-entered the war on 10 November 1918.

events.label: 15 Mar 1917
events.text: Revolution in Petrograd forces the Tsar to abdicate
events.detail: War losses, food shortages and distrust of the government fuelled protests in Petrograd from 8 March 1917 (February in Russia's old calendar). Troops joined the crowds, and Tsar Nicholas II abdicated on 15 March. A Provisional Government kept Russia in the war, but its 1917 summer offensive failed and the army began to disintegrate, while soviets of workers and soldiers competed for power.

events.label: 6 Apr 1917
events.text: The United States declares war on Germany
events.detail: Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare on 1 February 1917, gambling that it could starve Britain before American forces arrived. The intercepted Zimmermann telegram, in which Germany proposed an alliance with Mexico, further angered American opinion. The United States declared war on Germany on 6 April 1917 as an 'associated power', and its troops reached the Western Front in growing numbers through 1918.

events.label: 24 Oct 1917
events.text: Austro-German breakthrough at Caporetto
events.detail: On 24 October 1917 Austro-Hungarian and German divisions, using gas and infiltration tactics, broke the Italian line at Caporetto on the Isonzo. The Italian army fell back to the Piave River, losing very large numbers of men, many of them as prisoners. Britain and France rushed divisions to Italy, General Cadorna was replaced as commander, and the new line on the Piave held through the winter and against a final Austro-Hungarian offensive in June 1918.

events.label: 7 Nov 1917
events.text: The Bolsheviks seize power in Russia
events.detail: Led by Lenin, the Bolsheviks overthrew the Provisional Government in Petrograd on 7 November 1917 (25 October in the old calendar), promising peace, land and bread. The new government agreed an armistice with the Central Powers on 15 December. Peace talks opened at Brest-Litovsk. Russia's withdrawal let Germany move many divisions to the Western Front for a final offensive, while Russia itself slid into a long civil war between the Bolsheviks and their opponents.

events.label: 11 Dec 1917
events.text: British forces enter Jerusalem
events.detail: After failing twice at Gaza, the British Egyptian Expeditionary Force under General Allenby broke through the Ottoman line at Beersheba and Gaza in autumn 1917. On 11 December Allenby entered Jerusalem on foot. British troops had also taken Baghdad in March, and the Balfour Declaration of 2 November had promised support for a Jewish national home in Palestine, shaping the region's postwar history.

events.label: 3 Mar 1918
events.text: Russia makes peace at Brest-Litovsk
events.detail: Soviet Russia signed the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk with Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria on 3 March 1918. Russia gave up Finland, the Baltic lands, Poland, most of Belarus and Ukraine, and Kars, Ardahan and Batum in the Caucasus. German troops occupied much of this territory, though Germany still kept large forces in the East. The treaty ended the Eastern Front for the Central Powers and was annulled after Germany's defeat in November 1918.

events.label: 21 Mar 1918
events.text: Germany launches its Spring Offensive in the West
events.detail: With divisions freed from Russia, Germany tried to win in the West before American strength could tell. Operation Michael began on 21 March 1918 near Saint-Quentin and drove the British back many miles; further offensives followed into July, reaching the Marne again. The attacks gained ground but cost Germany its best troops and failed to break the Allied armies, now under a single commander, Ferdinand Foch.

events.label: 8 Aug 1918
events.text: Allied victory at Amiens opens the Hundred Days Offensive
events.detail: After stopping the last German attack on the Marne in July, the Allies struck back. On 8 August British, Australian, Canadian and French forces attacked east of Amiens with tanks, aircraft and artillery and advanced several miles in a day. A series of Allied offensives followed, including the American-led Meuse–Argonne offensive from 26 September, pushing German armies back towards their own border.

events.label: 19–25 Sep 1918
events.text: Allenby routs the Ottoman armies at Megiddo
events.detail: In Palestine, British Empire forces under Allenby, with Arab Revolt forces on their flank, attacked the Ottoman line on 19 September 1918. Cavalry broke through and the Ottoman armies in Palestine collapsed within days. Damascus was reached at the end of September, and the Ottoman Empire signed the Armistice of Mudros on 30 October, after Bulgaria had already signed an armistice on 29–30 September.

events.label: 3 Nov 1918
events.text: Austria-Hungary signs an armistice after Vittorio Veneto
events.detail: Italy launched its offensive at Vittorio Veneto on 24 October 1918 as Austria-Hungary was breaking up into national states. The Austro-Hungarian army disintegrated, and on 3 November an armistice was signed at Villa Giusti near Padua, taking effect the next day. The Habsburg monarchy dissolved within days, as Czechoslovakia, Hungary and the new South Slav state went their own ways. Germany was now the only Central Power still fighting.

events.label: 11 Nov 1918
events.text: Germany signs the armistice at Compiègne
events.detail: With its allies gone, its armies in retreat and revolution spreading at home, Germany sought terms. Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicated on 9 November, and German delegates signed the armistice in a railway carriage in the forest of Compiègne early on 11 November; fighting stopped at 11 a.m. The peace treaties followed, including the Treaty of Versailles with Germany on 28 June 1919.

wars.name: Second World War
wars.summary: The Second World War began when Nazi Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939 and Britain and France declared war; Japan had been at war with China since July 1937. Germany, with the Soviet Union bound to it by a non-aggression pact, overran Poland, Denmark, Norway, the Low Countries and France by June 1940, when Italy joined it. The Tripartite Pact of September 1940 tied Germany, Italy and Japan together as the Axis, later joined by Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria and others. Germany's invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941 and Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941 brought the Soviet Union and the United States into the Allied coalition alongside Britain, China and the exiled governments. After turning points at Midway, Guadalcanal and Stalingrad, the Allies invaded Italy and France while the Red Army advanced from the east. Germany surrendered on 8 May 1945. Japan, after the atomic bombings and the Soviet declaration of war, announced its surrender on 15 August and signed it on 2 September 1945.
wars.casualties: An estimated 60 million to more than 75 million people died, most of them civilians, including about six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust.

members.clio: French Mandate for Syria and Lebanon
French Mandate for Syria and Lebanon

events.label: 1 Sep 1939
events.text: Germany invades Poland
events.detail: In August 1939 Germany and the Soviet Union signed a non-aggression pact that secretly divided eastern Europe between them. On 1 September German forces invaded Poland from the west, north and south, using massed armour and air power. Poland's army fought for over a month, but Warsaw surrendered in late September and the last Polish units in early October, and Poland was partitioned.

events.label: 3 Sep 1939
events.text: Britain and France declare war on Germany
events.detail: Britain and France had guaranteed Poland's independence, and when Germany ignored their demand to withdraw they declared war on 3 September 1939. Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and Canada followed within days, and India was committed by its viceroy. Little fighting followed in the West for months, the so-called Phoney War, while the war at sea began at once, with U-boats attacking Allied shipping in the Atlantic.

events.label: 17 Sep 1939
events.text: The Soviet Union invades eastern Poland
events.detail: Under the secret terms of its pact with Germany, the Soviet Union invaded Poland from the east on 17 September 1939, and the two powers divided the country. The Soviet Union went on to force bases on the Baltic states, invade Finland in November 1939 in the Winter War, and annex the Baltic states and parts of Romania in 1940, though it stayed formally neutral in the wider war.

events.label: 9 Apr 1940
events.text: Germany invades Denmark and Norway
events.detail: Germany wanted Norway's ports for its navy and U-boats and to protect iron-ore shipments from Sweden through Narvik. On 9 April 1940 it invaded Denmark, which capitulated within hours, and Norway, where British, French and Polish troops landed to help. The Allies withdrew in early June as France collapsed, and the Norwegian army on the mainland surrendered on 10 June; Norway's king and government went into exile in London.

events.label: 10 May 1940
events.text: Germany attacks France and the Low Countries
events.detail: On 10 May 1940 Germany invaded the Netherlands, Belgium and Luxembourg. Its main armoured thrust came through the Ardennes, crossing the Meuse at Sedan and racing to the Channel, cutting off the Allied armies in Belgium. The Netherlands surrendered within days and Belgium at the end of May, while more than 340,000 Allied troops were evacuated from Dunkirk by early June.

events.label: 10 Jun 1940
events.text: Italy declares war on Britain and France
events.detail: Mussolini's Italy, allied to Germany by the Pact of Steel in 1939, stayed out of the fighting until France was clearly beaten. On 10 June 1940 Italy declared war on Britain and France and attacked in the Alps. Italy's entry spread the war to the Mediterranean, North Africa and East Africa, where Italian colonies bordered British-held Egypt, Sudan and Kenya.

events.label: 22 Jun 1940
events.text: France signs an armistice; the Vichy regime follows
events.detail: With Paris taken on 14 June, Marshal Philippe Pétain's new government sought terms. The armistice was signed on 22 June in the forest of Compiègne, in the carriage used in 1918. Germany occupied the north and the Atlantic coast, while a French government based at Vichy ran the rest and the colonies. In London, General Charles de Gaulle called on the French to keep fighting, founding Free France.

events.label: 10 Jul 1940
events.text: The Battle of Britain begins
events.detail: Germany needed control of the air before it could invade Britain. From 10 July to 31 October 1940 the Luftwaffe attacked shipping, airfields and then cities, but the Royal Air Force, aided by radar, was not defeated. Hitler postponed the planned invasion indefinitely. It was Germany's first major defeat of the war. Night bombing of British cities, the Blitz, continued from September 1940 until May 1941.

events.label: 27 Sep 1940
events.text: Germany, Italy and Japan sign the Tripartite Pact
events.detail: On 27 September 1940 Germany, Italy and Japan signed the Tripartite Pact in Berlin, pledging to support each other against any new enemy, a warning aimed at the United States. Hungary, Romania and Slovakia joined in November 1940, Bulgaria in March 1941, and Croatia after its creation. Thailand allied with Japan in December 1941 and declared war on Britain and the United States in January 1942.

events.label: 6 Apr 1941
events.text: Axis invasion of Yugoslavia and Greece
events.detail: Italy had invaded Greece in October 1940 but was driven back into Albania, and British troops arrived to help Greece. On 6 April 1941 Germany, with Italian and Hungarian forces, invaded Yugoslavia, whose government had just been overthrown for joining the Axis, and Greece. Both were conquered within weeks, Crete fell in May, and Yugoslavia was carved up, including a new Axis-aligned Independent State of Croatia.

events.label: 22 Jun 1941
events.text: Germany invades the Soviet Union
events.detail: On 22 June 1941 Germany and its allies, including Romania, Finland and Hungary, launched Operation Barbarossa, a vast invasion along a front from the Baltic to the Black Sea. Huge Soviet armies were encircled and German forces reached the outskirts of Leningrad and Moscow by late 1941, where a Soviet counter-offensive in December pushed them back. The Soviet Union now joined Britain as an ally.

events.label: 7 Dec 1941
events.text: Japan attacks Pearl Harbor and Western colonies in Asia
events.detail: After the United States embargoed oil exports over Japan's occupation of French Indochina, Japan struck. On 7 December 1941 its carrier aircraft attacked the US Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor, killing 2,403 Americans, while other forces attacked the Philippines, Guam, Wake, Malaya, Thailand and Hong Kong. The United States declared war on Japan the next day, and Germany and Italy declared war on the United States on 11 December.

events.label: 20 Jan 1942
events.text: Nazi officials coordinate the 'Final Solution' at Wannsee
events.detail: Mass shootings of Jews by German units in the occupied Soviet Union had begun in 1941. On 20 January 1942 SS General Reinhard Heydrich convened senior officials at a villa at Wannsee in Berlin to coordinate the deportation of Europe's Jews to be killed, mostly in occupied Poland. Through killing centres such as Auschwitz-Birkenau, the Nazis and their collaborators murdered about six million Jews in the Holocaust.

events.label: 15 Feb 1942
events.text: Singapore surrenders to Japan
events.detail: Japanese forces landed in Malaya in December 1941 and advanced rapidly down the peninsula. Singapore, Britain's main base in Asia, surrendered on 15 February 1942, and about 80,000 British, Indian, Australian and local troops became prisoners. Churchill called it the worst disaster in British military history. By May Japan had also taken the Dutch East Indies, the Philippines and most of Burma.

events.label: 4–7 Jun 1942
events.text: The US Navy defeats Japan at Midway
events.detail: Japan tried to draw the remaining US carriers into a decisive battle by attacking Midway atoll. Forewarned by codebreakers, US aircraft sank all four Japanese fleet carriers in the attacking force, Akagi, Kaga, Sōryū and Hiryū, between 4 and 7 June 1942, for the loss of the carrier Yorktown. Japan could not replace the ships and trained aircrew, and the battle is widely seen as a turning point in the Pacific.

events.label: 7 Aug 1942
events.text: US Marines land on Guadalcanal
events.detail: Japan was building an airfield on Guadalcanal in the Solomon Islands that threatened links between the United States and Australia. US Marines landed on 7 August 1942 in the first major Allied land offensive against Japan. Months of fighting on land, at sea and in the air followed, until Japan evacuated its last troops on 9 February 1943, ceding the initiative in the Pacific to the Allies.

events.label: 8 Nov 1942
events.text: Allied landings in Vichy North Africa (Operation Torch)
events.detail: Days after the British victory at El Alamein in Egypt, American and British forces landed in Vichy-ruled Morocco and Algeria on 8 November 1942. After brief fighting, Admiral Darlan ordered French forces to stop on 10 November, and French North Africa went over to the Allies. Germany responded by occupying the rest of France on 11 November. Axis forces in Tunisia surrendered by 13 May 1943.

events.label: 2 Feb 1943
events.text: The German Sixth Army surrenders at Stalingrad
events.detail: German forces had attacked Stalingrad on the Volga in the summer of 1942 and nearly taken the city by November. On 19 November the Red Army counter-attacked against the Romanian armies on the flanks and encircled the German Sixth Army. Its commander, Friedrich Paulus, surrendered on 2 February 1943, and about 235,000 Axis soldiers were captured. The Soviet Union kept the initiative on the Eastern Front for the rest of the war.

events.label: 5 Jul 1943
events.text: The Battle of Kursk
events.detail: Germany's last major offensive in the East began on 5 July 1943, when its armies attacked the Soviet salient around Kursk from north and south. Soviet forces had prepared deep defences and held, and on 12 July they launched their own counter-offensive. Kursk, which included some of the largest tank battles of the war, ended Germany's ability to mount strategic offensives on the Eastern Front.

events.label: 9 Jul 1943
events.text: Allied invasion of Sicily; Italy changes sides
events.detail: After victory in North Africa, the Allies invaded Sicily on 9 July 1943. Mussolini was deposed on 25 July, and the new Italian government signed an armistice, announced on 8 September, as the Allies landed on the mainland. Germany occupied most of Italy, freed Mussolini and set up a puppet state in the north, while the royal government joined the Allies as a co-belligerent.

events.label: 6 Jun 1944
events.text: D-Day: the Allied landings in Normandy
events.detail: After years of preparation, Allied forces landed on five Normandy beaches, Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno and Sword, on 6 June 1944, preceded by airborne drops. More than 156,000 soldiers came ashore on the first day in the largest seaborne invasion in history, carried by about 5,000 ships. After weeks of hard fighting the Allies broke out in late July and advanced across France.

events.label: 22 Jun 1944
events.text: Operation Bagration destroys German Army Group Centre
events.detail: Three years to the day after the German invasion, the Red Army launched a massive offensive in Belarus on 22 June 1944. Army Group Centre's front collapsed, Minsk was liberated on 4 July, and by August Soviet forces had reached the Vistula near Warsaw and the border of East Prussia. With about 450,000 German casualties, it was among the heaviest German defeats of the war.

events.label: 25 Aug 1944
events.text: Paris is liberated; Romania leaves the Axis
events.detail: As Allied armies broke out of Normandy and landed in southern France, the French Resistance rose in Paris, and French and American troops entered the city on 25 August 1944. Two days earlier a coup in Romania had taken it out of the Axis, and Bulgaria followed in September. Romania's oilfields were lost to Germany, and by the autumn it was losing allies and territory on every front.

events.label: 23–26 Oct 1944
events.text: The Battle of Leyte Gulf
events.detail: US forces landed on Leyte in the Philippines on 20 October 1944. Japan sent almost its whole remaining fleet to attack the landings, and from 23 to 26 October the largest naval battle of the war was fought around the islands. The Japanese navy suffered crippling losses and never again sailed in comparable force. The battle also saw the first organised kamikaze attacks.

events.label: 16 Dec 1944
events.text: Germany's Ardennes offensive: the Battle of the Bulge
events.detail: With the Allies nearing Germany's western border, Hitler gambled on a surprise winter offensive through the Ardennes on 16 December 1944, aiming to split the Allied armies and retake Antwerp. German forces made a deep bulge in the American line but were held at key points such as Bastogne, and the offensive was repulsed by mid-January 1945, using up Germany's last reserves in the West.

events.label: 1 Apr 1945
events.text: US forces invade Okinawa
events.detail: The Allies needed bases close to Japan for the planned invasion. US forces landed on Okinawa on 1 April 1945 and fought until organised resistance ended on 22 June, under waves of kamikaze attacks at sea. About 94,000 Japanese soldiers and some 12,500 Americans died, and estimates of Okinawan civilian deaths range from 40,000 to 150,000, foreshadowing the cost of invading Japan itself.

events.label: 8 May 1945
events.text: Germany surrenders unconditionally
events.detail: Soviet forces stormed Berlin in late April 1945 while American and British armies advanced from the west; Hitler killed himself on 30 April. German commanders signed an unconditional surrender at Reims on 7 May and a definitive act in Berlin-Karlshorst, which took effect at 23:01 on 8 May. The Western Allies celebrate Victory in Europe Day on 8 May, while Russia marks Victory Day on 9 May.

events.label: 6 Aug 1945
events.text: The United States drops an atomic bomb on Hiroshima
events.detail: Japan rejected the Allied demand for unconditional surrender issued at Potsdam in July. On 6 August 1945 a US bomber dropped an atomic bomb on Hiroshima, and a second destroyed much of Nagasaki on 9 August. Estimates of deaths by the end of 1945 are 90,000–166,000 in Hiroshima and 60,000–80,000 in Nagasaki. Historians still debate whether the bombings were justified.

events.label: 9 Aug 1945
events.text: The Soviet Union invades Japanese-held Manchuria
events.detail: At Yalta in February 1945 Stalin had agreed to join the war against Japan within about three months of Germany's defeat. The Soviet Union declared war on 8 August and invaded Manchuria an hour later, and Mongolia joined on 10 August. Soviet forces quickly overran Manchukuo, Inner Mongolia, northern Korea, southern Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands, removing Japan's last hope of a negotiated peace.

events.label: 2 Sep 1945
events.text: Japan signs the instrument of surrender
events.detail: After the atomic bombings and the Soviet attack, Emperor Hirohito ordered acceptance of the Allied terms, and his recorded announcement of surrender was broadcast on 15 August 1945. Japanese representatives signed the instrument of surrender aboard the USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay on 2 September 1945, ending the Second World War. Japan was occupied, and its overseas empire was dismantled.

wars.name: 1948 Arab–Israeli War
wars.summary: On 29 November 1947 the UN General Assembly voted to partition British-ruled Palestine into Jewish and Arab states, with Jerusalem under international control. Jewish leaders accepted the plan; Palestinian Arab leaders and the Arab states rejected it, and civil war broke out between Jewish and Palestinian Arab forces. Israel declared independence on 14 May 1948 as the British Mandate ended, and the next day the armies of Egypt, Transjordan, Syria, Iraq and Lebanon, with a Saudi contingent, entered the country. Fighting alternated with UN truces until early 1949. Israel emerged in control of about 78 percent of former Mandatory Palestine; Transjordan held the West Bank and East Jerusalem, and Egypt the Gaza Strip, along armistice lines later called the Green Line. Israelis remember the war as their War of Independence. For Palestinians it is the Nakba ("catastrophe"): about 750,000 people fled or were expelled, over 400 villages were depopulated, and Israel did not allow the refugees to return.
wars.casualties: An estimated 6,373 Israelis (about 4,000 soldiers and 2,400 civilians), 3,700–7,000 soldiers of the Arab armies and 3,000–13,000 Palestinian Arab fighters and civilians were killed.

events.label: Nov 1947
events.text: UN votes to partition Palestine; civil war breaks out
events.detail: Britain, which had ruled Palestine under a League of Nations mandate since the 1920s, handed the question of its future to the United Nations. On 29 November 1947 the General Assembly adopted Resolution 181, dividing the country into a Jewish state and an Arab state with Jerusalem under UN control. Jewish leaders accepted; Palestinian Arab leaders and the Arab states rejected it. Fighting between Jewish and Palestinian Arab militias began immediately and grew into a civil war while British troops prepared to leave.

events.label: 5 Apr 1948
events.text: Operation Nachshon fights to open the road to Jerusalem
events.detail: By early 1948 Palestinian Arab irregulars had cut the road from the coast, leaving Jewish West Jerusalem short of food and arms. From 5 to 20 April the Haganah, the main Jewish militia, launched Operation Nachshon to open the route through the hills, its first brigade-sized offensive. The fighting around Castel, where the Palestinian commander Abd al-Qadir al-Husayni was killed, marked a shift from defence to attack under Plan Dalet, which aimed to secure the territory of the planned Jewish state and its approaches.

events.label: 9 Apr 1948
events.text: Deir Yassin massacre
events.detail: On 9 April fighters of the Irgun and Lehi, right-wing Jewish militias, supported by the Haganah and Palmach, attacked the Arab village of Deir Yassin west of Jerusalem. At least 107 villagers, many of them women, children and elderly people, were killed; for decades a figure of about 254 was widely cited, but recent scholarship puts the toll near 110. News of the killings spread fear across Palestine and greatly accelerated the flight of Arab civilians from their homes.

events.label: 13 Apr 1948
events.text: Hadassah medical convoy ambushed in Jerusalem
events.detail: Four days after Deir Yassin, Arab fighters ambushed a convoy carrying doctors, nurses, patients and Haganah escorts to the Hadassah Hospital on Mount Scopus, an isolated Jewish enclave in north-east Jerusalem. The vehicles were trapped and set alight in the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood, and 78 Jews, most of them medical staff, were killed. The attack was described as a reprisal for Deir Yassin and showed how the civil war had become a cycle of attacks on civilians.

events.label: 21 Apr 1948
events.text: Haganah captures Haifa; most Arab residents leave
events.detail: Haifa, a mixed port city of about 140,000 people, roughly half of them Arabs, was a key target as British forces withdrew. On 21–22 April the Haganah's Carmeli Brigade seized the city. Around 15,000 Arabs fled or were expelled during the fighting, and by mid-May only about 4,000 of some 65,000–70,000 Arab residents remained. Jaffa and other Arab towns fell in the following weeks, and the exodus became one of the central events of the Nakba.

events.label: 13 May 1948
events.text: Kfar Etzion falls; massacre of defenders
events.detail: The Etzion bloc, four Jewish settlements between Bethlehem and Hebron, lay deep in territory allotted to the Arab state and had been besieged for months. On 13 May, the day before the Mandate ended, the Arab Legion and local Arab irregulars overran Kfar Etzion. Many of the defenders were killed after they had surrendered, and the other settlements of the bloc surrendered the next day. Israelis came to remember the massacre as one of the war's defining losses.

events.label: 14 May 1948
events.text: Israel declares independence as the Mandate ends
events.detail: With the British Mandate due to expire at midnight, David Ben-Gurion read Israel's Declaration of Independence in Tel Aviv on the afternoon of 14 May 1948. The United States granted the new provisional government de facto recognition the same day, and the Soviet Union soon followed with full recognition. The declaration turned the civil war into an interstate war: Arab governments had announced that their armies would intervene once British rule ended.

events.label: 15 May 1948
events.text: Arab armies enter Palestine
events.detail: On 15 May the armies of Egypt, Transjordan, Syria and Iraq crossed into former Mandatory Palestine, and Lebanon joined on the northern border; a Saudi formation fought under Egyptian command. Transjordan's Arab Legion moved mainly into areas allotted to the Arab state and around Jerusalem. Egyptian columns advanced up the coast towards Tel Aviv and through the Negev. Palestinians commemorate 15 May each year as Nakba Day, marking the loss of their homeland.

events.label: 20 May 1948
events.text: Syrian attack on the Deganias is repulsed
events.detail: Syria's army advanced south of the Sea of Galilee and on 20 May attacked Degania Alef and Degania Bet, the oldest kibbutzim in the Jordan Valley. Defenders with few heavy weapons stopped the tanks at the perimeter, and by 21 May the Syrians had pulled back. The Syrian front then settled into a stalemate, with Syria holding small areas west of the old border until the armistice of July 1949.

events.label: 25 May 1948
events.text: Israeli assault on Latrun fails
events.detail: The Arab Legion's hold on the police fort at Latrun again cut the main road to Jerusalem. On 24–25 May the newly formed Israel Defense Forces attacked it in Operation Bin Nun A, using units that included recently arrived immigrants, and were driven back with heavy losses; further attacks in late May and June also failed. Israel instead built a rough bypass, nicknamed the 'Burma Road', to supply West Jerusalem.

events.label: 28 May 1948
events.text: Jewish Quarter of Jerusalem's Old City surrenders
events.detail: From mid-May the Arab Legion fought Jewish forces for control of Jerusalem. The Jewish Quarter of the walled Old City, held by a small garrison, was surrounded and shelled. On 28 May it surrendered; its residents were expelled to West Jerusalem and the defenders taken prisoner. Jerusalem was left divided, with Transjordan holding the Old City and East Jerusalem until 1967.

events.label: 29 May 1948
events.text: Egyptian advance halted near Isdud
events.detail: Egypt's main column pushed up the coastal road and by 28 May reached a destroyed bridge north of the Arab town of Isdud (modern Ashdod), about 30 kilometres from Tel Aviv. From 29 May to 3 June Israeli forces counter-attacked in Operation Pleshet, using Israel's first fighter aircraft. The Egyptians dug in and advanced no further north, and the line held until the first truce.

events.label: 11 Jun 1948
events.text: First UN truce begins
events.detail: The UN Security Council had demanded a ceasefire, and the Swedish diplomat Count Folke Bernadotte, appointed UN Mediator, negotiated a four-week truce that took effect on 11 June. Both sides used the pause to rearm despite an arms embargo; Israel received aircraft and weapons from Czechoslovakia and absorbed thousands of new recruits. When fighting resumed on 8 July, the military balance had shifted in Israel's favour.

events.label: 12 Jul 1948
events.text: Lydda and Ramle captured; 50,000–70,000 residents expelled
events.detail: In the 'Ten Days' of fighting between the truces, Israel launched Operation Dani to secure the road from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem. Lydda was captured on 11 July and Ramle on 12 July, and hundreds of people were killed in Lydda. On 12 July Ben-Gurion authorised the expulsion of both towns' civilians, and some 50,000–70,000 people were forced to walk east towards Arab Legion lines in summer heat. It was the largest single expulsion of the war.

events.label: Sep 1948
events.text: Arab League sets up the All-Palestine Government in Gaza
events.detail: The second UN truce began on 18 July. In September the Arab League established an All-Palestine Government in Gaza, claiming authority over the whole of Palestine. It was led by figures close to the exiled Palestinian leader Amin al-Husseini but depended entirely on Egypt, which controlled the Gaza Strip. Transjordan's King Abdullah opposed it and moved to absorb the West Bank, which he annexed in 1950.

events.label: 17 Sep 1948
events.text: UN Mediator Folke Bernadotte assassinated
events.detail: Bernadotte had proposed a settlement that would give the Negev to the Arab side and western Galilee to Israel, plans opposed by Israelis and Arabs alike. On 17 September members of Lehi, a militant Jewish group, ambushed his motorcade in Jerusalem's Katamon quarter, killing him and the French officer Colonel André Serot. Israel's government outlawed Lehi, but the killers were never convicted. The UN later handed his duties to a Conciliation Commission.

events.label: 21 Oct 1948
events.text: Israel takes Beersheba in Operation Yoav
events.detail: On 15 October Israel broke the second truce with Operation Yoav, an offensive against Egyptian forces in the south. It cut the Egyptian lines, encircled an Egyptian brigade in the Faluja pocket, where it held out until the armistice, and on 21 October captured Beersheba, the main town of the Negev. Most of the town's Arab population had already fled. The operation opened the route to the southern Negev.

events.label: 29 Oct 1948
events.text: Operation Hiram takes the Upper Galilee
events.detail: Starting on 24 October, Israeli forces attacked the Arab Liberation Army, a force of volunteers from Arab countries, and Syrian and Lebanese units in the Upper Galilee. Within about 60 hours the whole region was in Israeli hands, and Israeli troops briefly occupied villages inside southern Lebanon. Arab losses were estimated at 400 dead and 550 captured; killings of civilians were reported in several villages, and many inhabitants fled north into Lebanon.

events.label: 22 Dec 1948
events.text: Operation Horev drives Egyptian forces from the Negev
events.detail: On 11 December the UN General Assembly passed Resolution 194, saying refugees wishing to return home and live in peace should be allowed to do so, or receive compensation. Days later, on 22 December, Israel launched Operation Horev to expel the Egyptian army from the Negev. Israeli columns crossed briefly into Egyptian Sinai before British pressure forced a withdrawal, and fighting near Rafah in early January 1949 led Egypt to accept armistice talks.

events.label: 24 Feb 1949
events.text: Israel and Egypt sign an armistice at Rhodes
events.detail: Under UN mediator Ralph Bunche, Israeli and Egyptian delegates negotiated on the Greek island of Rhodes and signed the first armistice of the war on 24 February 1949. Egypt kept the Gaza Strip, crowded with refugees; the besieged brigade at Faluja was allowed to go home, and the village passed to Israel. Lebanon signed on 23 March and Transjordan on 3 April; Iraq withdrew its troops without a separate agreement.

events.label: 10 Mar 1949
events.text: Israeli forces reach the Red Sea at Umm Rashrash
events.detail: In Operation Uvda, launched on 5 March, Israeli brigades raced south through the Negev, an area allotted to Israel under the partition plan but not yet occupied. On 10 March they reached the abandoned police post of Umm Rashrash on the Gulf of Aqaba and raised a hand-inked flag, a moment Israel regards as the end of the fighting. The site became the port of Eilat, giving Israel access to the Red Sea.

events.label: 20 Jul 1949
events.text: Israel–Syria armistice ends the war
events.detail: The last armistice, with Syria, was signed on 20 July 1949 after months of talks on the Jordan River front; Syria withdrew from most of the land it held west of the border, which became demilitarised zones. The armistice lines, later called the Green Line, held until 1967. About 750,000 Palestinian refugees lived in camps in Gaza, the West Bank, Jordan, Lebanon and Syria, and Israel barred their return. In the following years hundreds of thousands of Jews left or were expelled from Arab countries, many settling in Israel.
